- `extensions/runway/video-generation-provider.ts` uses the same unguarded helper and omits the request config entirely.

Already guarded on main, so no longer part of this issue:
- `minimax` routes through `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded`.
- `xai` routes through `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded` in `extensions/xai/video-generation-transport.ts`.
- `vydra` routes through `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded` in `extensions/vydra/shared.ts` (after #105884 merged).

So this issue is now byteplus and runway only. My fix PR #111912 is closed: the patch worked, but it gated on a maintainer decision about whether the generic guarded download helper should become a public `provider-http` SDK export, and it went stale waiting for that. If the answer is no, the same guard can be applied per provider without a shared helper. Leaving this issue as the tracker.

external_evidence.title: Video-generation providers fetch the result URL with no SSRF guard (byteplus, minimax, xai, runway, vydra)
external_evidence.description:
## Summary

Five bundled video-generation providers (byteplus, minimax, xai, runway, vydra) fetch the generated-video bytes from a URL taken directly out of the provider's own JSON status/completion response, using a plain unguarded `fetchWithTimeout` call that never re-applies the SSRF guard (DNS pinning, private/loopback/link-local address blocking) that the same providers correctly apply to their submit/poll requests. If the upstream provider API is compromised, MITM'd, or configured with a malicious/self-hosted-compatible base URL, it can set that video/download URL to an internal address (cloud metadata service, loopback admin port, internal service) and OpenClaw will fetch it and save the response bytes as the generated video attachment.

## Environment

- Commit: `8656c3b357f62b230752f2da37c0c9eb584382a8` (origin/main at time of filing)
- Surface: bundled model-provider plugins, video generation capability, agent-tool path (`src/agents/tools/video-generate-tool.ts`)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure any of `byteplus`, `minimax`, `xai`, `runway`, or `vydra` as a video-generation provider (default configuration, no `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork`/custom request policy needed).
2. Have the agent call the video-generate tool against that provider.
3. The upstream provider's status/completion response (compromised endpoint, malicious custom `baseUrl`, or on-path MITM) sets its `video_url` / `download_url` / result-URL field to a private/loopback/link-local address, for example `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>` or `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/admin`.

## Expected

The download step should re-apply the same SSRF guard (`fetchWithSsrFGuard` / `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded`) used for the submit/poll requests, blocking private/loopback/link-local targets by default the same way `extensions/fal` and `extensions/google` already do for the identical "fetch the URL the JSON body told us to fetch" step.

## Actual

The download call goes through `fetchProviderDownloadResponse` / `fetchProviderOperationResponse` (`src/media-understanding/shared.ts:250-298`) or, for vydra, `fetchWithTimeout` directly (`extensions/vydra/shared.ts:244`). Both bottom out in `fetchWithTimeout` (`src/utils/fetch-timeout.ts:179-195`), which is a bare `fetchFn(url, { ...init, signal })` with no DNS pinning, no private-IP/link-local block, and no `dispatcherPolicy`/`allowPrivateNetwork` argument at all. There is also no check that the returned URL's host matches the provider's own configured origin. Real behavior proof below confirms the unguarded providers connect to and return bytes from an attacker-supplied loopback address, while a guarded sibling provider (fal) blocks the identical URL before any connection is attempted.

## Root cause

Each provider resolves `allowPrivateNetwork`/`dispatcherPolicy` once via `resolveProviderHttpRequestConfig` and correctly threads it into the submit `postJsonRequest` call, but never passes it into the download helper, which was written before the SSRF-guard threading pattern existed and was never updated:

- `extensions/byteplus/video-generation-provider.ts:202-224` (`downloadBytePlusVideo`), resolved config never passed through: `extensions/byteplus/video-generation-provider.ts:292` destructures `allowPrivateNetwork`/`dispatcherPolicy`, call site at `:399`-`:406` drops both before calling `downloadBytePlusVideo`.
- `extensions/minimax/video-generation-provider.ts:222-243` (`downloadVideoFromUrl`) and `extensions/minimax/video-generation-provider.ts:248-291` (`downloadVideoFromFileId`, itself fetching an unguarded metadata request at `:258` before an unguarded download at `:279`); call site `:430`-`:443`.
- `extensions/xai/video-generation-provider.ts:351-373` (`downloadXaiVideo`); call site `:482`-`:487`.
- `extensions/runway/video-generation-provider.ts:320-346` (`downloadRunwayVideos`, looping over every task output URL); call site `:448`-`:449`.
- `extensions/vydra/shared.ts:236-263` (`downloadVydraAsset`, which does not even go through the shared `fetchProviderDownloadResponse` helper, calling `fetchWithTimeout` directly), called from `extensions/vydra/video-generation-provider.ts:126-132`.

```ts
// src/utils/fetch-timeout.ts:179-195
export async function fetchWithTimeout(
  url: string,
  init: RequestInit,
  timeoutMs: number,
  fetchFn: typeof fetch = fetch,
): Promise<Response> {
  const { signal, cleanup } = buildTimeoutAbortSignal({
    timeoutMs: Math.max(1, timeoutMs),
    operation: "fetchWithTimeout",
    url,
  });
  try {
    return await fetchFn(url, { ...init, signal });
  } finally {
    cleanup();
  }
}
```

No caller of this function for these five providers' download step ever routes through `fetchWithSsrFGuard` / `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded`.

## Sibling surfaces

`extensions/google/video-generation-provider.ts:242,344`, `extensions/fal/video-generation-provider.ts:208-220` (via `fetchWithSsrFGuard`), and `extensions/openrouter/video-generation-provider.ts:380-395` (via `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded`) all correctly re-apply the SSRF guard to this exact same "download the URL the provider's JSON body told us to fetch" step, so the fix pattern already exists in this codebase; it was simply never applied to byteplus, minimax, xai, runway, or vydra.

`together` (`extensions/together/video-generation-provider.ts`) has the same class of gap, but it is already covered by open PR #102136 ("fix(together): apply configured request policy to video generation requests"), which is unmerged as of this filing. Together is intentionally out of scope for this issue; please track it under #102136 instead.

I also checked open PR #101854 ("fix: guard generated video downloads [AI]") to confirm it does not cover this. Its diff touches only `src/cli/capability-cli.ts` and `src/cli/capability-cli.test.ts`, a separate, CLI-only download path for `openclaw infer video generate`. It never touches any of the five provider modules above or the agent-tool path (`src/agents/tools/video-generate-tool.ts:751-758`, where `saveMediaBuffer` persists the downloaded bytes as a deliverable attachment). #101854 is not a duplicate of this issue.

### Related open PRs (reviewed but do not close this gap on current main)

Three more open, unmerged PRs attempt a similar "apply configured request policy" change for three of these five providers. None of them are merged, so `main` is unaffected today, but they are worth flagging so this issue is not mis-triaged as already covered:

- #102096 (byteplus) and #102134 (runway) add a guarded download path, but only take it `if (allowPrivateNetwork || dispatcherPolicy)` is explicitly configured by the operator; with no custom request policy configured (the default, and the exact scenario in this report), both PRs fall back to the same unguarded `fetchProviderOperationResponse`/`fetchProviderDownloadResponse` call and would leave this SSRF gap open even after merging as currently written.
- #102072 (minimax) always routes the download through `fetchWithTimeoutGuarded` (passing `undefined` guard options when no policy is configured, which still applies the guard's default private-network block), so if merged as currently written it would fully close this gap for minimax specifically.
- #102094 (dashscope) is a similar PR for a provider not in this report's scope; not reviewed in detail here.

xai and vydra have no open PR addressing this at all.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: xai, byteplus, minimax, runway, and vydra video-generation providers fetch the completion payload's video/download URL with a plain unguarded fetch, so an attacker-controlled loopback/private-network URL in that JSON field gets connected to and its bytes returned as the generated video, unlike guarded sibling providers (fal, google, openrouter) which block the same URL shape by default.
Real environment tested: the real production `generateVideo()` entry points of `extensions/xai/video-generation-provider.ts`, `extensions/byteplus/video-generation-provider.ts`, and (for contrast) the guarded `extensions/fal/video-generation-provider.ts`, driven end to end at commit 8656c3b357f62b230752f2da37c0c9eb584382a8 (origin/main). Only the true external network boundary (`globalThis.fetch`) was replaced with a router that serves crafted submit/poll JSON responses when the URL matches the provider's own hostname, and otherwise transparently forwards to the real underlying fetch implementation; the SSRF-guard code itself (DNS resolution, hostname/IP policy checks, dispatcher selection in `src/infra/net/fetch-guard.ts` and `src/infra/net/ssrf.ts`) ran completely unmodified for all three providers.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: a real HTTP server was started on `127.0.0.1` on an ephemeral port; each provider's crafted completed-task JSON response set its `video_url` / `download_url` / `video.url` field to that server's `/secret-metadata` path; each provider's real `generateVideo()` was invoked end to end (submit, poll, download) with default configuration (no `allowPrivateNetwork`/dispatcher policy overrides).
Evidence after fix:
```
[xai] attacker video.url=http://127.0.0.1:41513/secret-metadata local_server_hits=["/secret-metadata"] downloaded_bytes=LEAKED-INTERNAL-BYTES-9f3c2a
[byteplus] attacker video_url=http://127.0.0.1:41513/secret-metadata local_server_hits=["/secret-metadata"] downloaded_bytes=LEAKED-INTERNAL-BYTES-9f3c2a
[fal] attacker video.url=http://127.0.0.1:41513/secret-metadata local_server_hits=[] generateVideo_rejected_with=Blocked hostname or private/internal/special-use IP address
```
Observed result after fix: xai and byteplus both connected to the attacker-supplied loopback address and returned its bytes as the generated video asset's buffer; fal, whose download step re-applies the SSRF guard, never connected to the loopback server at all and its call was rejected with a blocked-hostname error before any socket was opened. minimax, runway, and vydra share byteplus's and xai's exact unguarded download call shape (confirmed by direct code reading of each file/line cited above), so the same divergence applies to them.
What was not tested: minimax, runway, and vydra were not driven through this same live harness (only byteplus and xai were, as two representative members of the affected set, contrasted against fal as the guarded sibling); no attempt was made to reach a real cloud-metadata service or any non-loopback private address, only a local loopback stand-in; the three related open PRs above were reviewed by reading their diffs only, not by executing them.

## Severity

Medium. CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery). Exploitation requires a compromised or malicious third-party provider API, a malicious custom base URL, or a man-in-the-middle position on the provider connection, not a remote chat-based actor, which is why this is filed as a normal issue rather than a GHSA advisory.

[Bug]: Hover, drag, and scroll can bypass browser SSRF enforcement
external_evidence.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

The managed Playwright `hover`, `drag`, and `scrollIntoView` actions do not receive the resolved browser SSRF policy and bypass the navigation guard used by neighboring DOM actions. If one of these interactions triggers a document navigation, the action can report success without applying the configured destination policy.

This is a browser destination-policy boundary, not an agent-to-agent authorization boundary. OpenClaw treats authenticated Gateway callers as trusted operators, but the model and page content are not trusted principals; the browser SSRF policy is intended to keep page-influenced automation from reaching private or internal network destinations that the operator did not allow.

## Affected surface

- `extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.interactions.ts`
  - `hoverViaPlaywright`
  - `dragViaPlaywright`
  - `scrollIntoViewViaPlaywright`
  - the corresponding `executeSingleAction` branches
- `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/agent.act.ts` supplies the resolved policy to `executeActViaPlaywright`, but the three branches above drop it.
- `assertInteractionNavigationCompletedSafely` is the existing canonical interaction guard used by click, coordinate click, type/submit, key press, select, fill, and evaluate.
- Chrome MCP existing-session actions already run post-interaction navigation checks for hover, drag, and scroll. The omission is in the Playwright-backed sibling path.

The affected Playwright path includes locally managed Chrome, extension-relay profiles, and remote CDP profiles. The bug is present at current `main` commit `9b4c7c0991dddb77295453259b433122e705bfb4` and in shipped `v2026.6.11` and `v2026.7.1-beta.3` code.

## Validation environment

- OpenClaw: source checkout at the commit above; shipped-state comparison against `v2026.6.11` and `v2026.7.1-beta.3`
- Host: macOS 26.5.2
- Browser: real Google Chrome over the managed CDP path
- Model/provider: behavior is model-independent; final live acceptance must use a real OpenAI-backed agent turn rather than direct route calls alone

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start a real Gateway with the default strict browser SSRF policy and a real Chrome profile.
2. Prepare an otherwise allowed page whose hover, drag/drop, or scroll handler performs a document navigation to a controlled destination denied by that policy.
3. Invoke each action through the browser tool.
4. Observe that the current Playwright path does not pass `ssrfPolicy` to those helpers and does not run the canonical interaction-navigation guard.

Keep any network target in this reproduction local and controlled. Do not attach credentials, internal service responses, or exploit-oriented payloads to this public issue.

## Expected behavior

- Every DOM interaction that can cause navigation receives the same resolved browser policy.
- A directly action-triggered, policy-denied document request is aborted before network dispatch.
- The browser action returns the policy error even if the underlying Playwright locator also resolves or rejects.
- Allowed and non-navigating hover, drag, and scroll behavior remains unchanged.
- A request blocked before dispatch does not unnecessarily close or quarantine the still-allowed source page. Existing quarantine behavior remains for post-navigation checks that prove a blocked URL actually loaded.

## Actual behavior

Hover, drag, and scroll omit the policy and canonical guard. A navigation caused by one of those actions can complete and the action can return success.

Adding only the existing post-action check would improve error reporting and quarantine behavior, but it would not be sufficient request prevention: the destination may already have received the request before the final URL is checked.

## Best bounded fix

1. Add optional `ssrfPolicy` input to `hoverViaPlaywright`, `dragViaPlaywright`, and `scrollIntoViewViaPlaywright`.
2. Forward it from every `executeSingleAction` branch, including nested batch execution.
3. Route all three through the existing canonical interaction guard so immediate, delayed, same-URL, and subframe observations use one implementation.
4. Extract/reuse the existing document-request classification beside `gotoPageWithNavigationGuard` in `pw-session.ts`.
5. For the full action plus delayed-navigation grace window, install an exact page-scoped Playwright route that:
   - checks only main-frame and subframe document/navigation requests;
   - aborts a denied direct request before dispatch;
   - records the first policy denial so it wins over a locator, abort, or navigation error;
   - uses `route.fallback()` for allowed and non-document requests so older page/context handlers remain reachable;
   - removes only its own route in `finally` and waits for already-running guard handlers before deciding the result.
6. Retain the current post-navigation checks as residual detection/quarantine defense.
7. Avoid a second grace delay: once these actions use the navigation-aware guard, `actionNeedsStandaloneDownloadGrace` should follow the same `!ssrfPolicy` rule as the other guarded actions.

No config migration or public API compatibility shim is needed. These helper options are internal and optional. The broad private-network opt-in remains `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true`; strict/default behavior should fail closed.

## Scope and Playwright limits

The bounded fix must make a precise claim: it prevents direct action-triggered document requests on the selected page before dispatch and retains best-effort post-navigation checking.

It must not claim complete browser SSRF prevention. OpenClaw currently pins `playwright-core` 1.61.1, whose documented routing contract has these gaps:

- `page.route` handles only the first URL when a response redirects;
- `page.route` does not intercept the first request of a popup;
- page and browser-context routes do not intercept requests handled by a Service Worker.

Using `browserContext.route` globally is not an acceptable shortcut: extension and remote-CDP contexts can contain unrelated user or agent tabs, so a context-wide transient route would violate the selected-page ownership boundary and still would not solve Service Worker traffic.

The existing final-URL and redirect-chain checks should remain, but they are detection/quarantine after dispatch for these residual cases.

## Complete enforcement follow-up

Complete network prevention is a separate architecture change, not part of this bounded repair.

external_evidence.title: [Bug]: Hover, drag, and scroll can bypass browser SSRF enforcement
external_evidence.description:
## Bug type

Behavior bug

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

The managed Playwright `hover`, `drag`, and `scrollIntoView` actions do not receive the resolved browser SSRF policy and bypass the navigation guard used by neighboring DOM actions. If one of these interactions triggers a document navigation, the action can report success without applying the configured destination policy.

This is a browser destination-policy boundary, not an agent-to-agent authorization boundary. OpenClaw treats authenticated Gateway callers as trusted operators, but the model and page content are not trusted principals; the browser SSRF policy is intended to keep page-influenced automation from reaching private or internal network destinations that the operator did not allow.

## Affected surface

- `extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.interactions.ts`
  - `hoverViaPlaywright`
  - `dragViaPlaywright`
  - `scrollIntoViewViaPlaywright`
  - the corresponding `executeSingleAction` branches
- `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/agent.act.ts` supplies the resolved policy to `executeActViaPlaywright`, but the three branches above drop it.
- `assertInteractionNavigationCompletedSafely` is the existing canonical interaction guard used by click, coordinate click, type/submit, key press, select, fill, and evaluate.
- Chrome MCP existing-session actions already run post-interaction navigation checks for hover, drag, and scroll. The omission is in the Playwright-backed sibling path.

The affected Playwright path includes locally managed Chrome, extension-relay profiles, and remote CDP profiles. The bug is present at current `main` commit `9b4c7c0991dddb77295453259b433122e705bfb4` and in shipped `v2026.6.11` and `v2026.7.1-beta.3` code.

## Validation environment

- OpenClaw: source checkout at the commit above; shipped-state comparison against `v2026.6.11` and `v2026.7.1-beta.3`
- Host: macOS 26.5.2
- Browser: real Google Chrome over the managed CDP path
- Model/provider: behavior is model-independent; final live acceptance must use a real OpenAI-backed agent turn rather than direct route calls alone

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start a real Gateway with the default strict browser SSRF policy and a real Chrome profile.
2. Prepare an otherwise allowed page whose hover, drag/drop, or scroll handler performs a document navigation to a controlled destination denied by that policy.
3. Invoke each action through the browser tool.
4. Observe that the current Playwright path does not pass `ssrfPolicy` to those helpers and does not run the canonical interaction-navigation guard.

Keep any network target in this reproduction local and controlled. Do not attach credentials, internal service responses, or exploit-oriented payloads to this public issue.

## Expected behavior

- Every DOM interaction that can cause navigation receives the same resolved browser policy.
- A directly action-triggered, policy-denied document request is aborted before network dispatch.
- The browser action returns the policy error even if the underlying Playwright locator also resolves or rejects.
- Allowed and non-navigating hover, drag, and scroll behavior remains unchanged.
- A request blocked before dispatch does not unnecessarily close or quarantine the still-allowed source page. Existing quarantine behavior remains for post-navigation checks that prove a blocked URL actually loaded.

## Actual behavior

Hover, drag, and scroll omit the policy and canonical guard. A navigation caused by one of those actions can complete and the action can return success.

Adding only the existing post-action check would improve error reporting and quarantine behavior, but it would not be sufficient request prevention: the destination may already have received the request before the final URL is checked.

## Best bounded fix

1. Add optional `ssrfPolicy` input to `hoverViaPlaywright`, `dragViaPlaywright`, and `scrollIntoViewViaPlaywright`.
2. Forward it from every `executeSingleAction` branch, including nested batch execution.
3. Route all three through the existing canonical interaction guard so immediate, delayed, same-URL, and subframe observations use one implementation.
4. Extract/reuse the existing document-request classification beside `gotoPageWithNavigationGuard` in `pw-session.ts`.
5. For the full action plus delayed-navigation grace window, install an exact page-scoped Playwright route that:
   - checks only main-frame and subframe document/navigation requests;
   - aborts a denied direct request before dispatch;
   - records the first policy denial so it wins over a locator, abort, or navigation error;
   - uses `route.fallback()` for allowed and non-document requests so older page/context handlers remain reachable;
   - removes only its own route in `finally` and waits for already-running guard handlers before deciding the result.
6. Retain the current post-navigation checks as residual detection/quarantine defense.
7. Avoid a second grace delay: once these actions use the navigation-aware guard, `actionNeedsStandaloneDownloadGrace` should follow the same `!ssrfPolicy` rule as the other guarded actions.

No config migration or public API compatibility shim is needed. These helper options are internal and optional. The broad private-network opt-in remains `browser.ssrfPolicy.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork: true`; strict/default behavior should fail closed.

## Scope and Playwright limits

The bounded fix must make a precise claim: it prevents direct action-triggered document requests on the selected page before dispatch and retains best-effort post-navigation checking.

It must not claim complete browser SSRF prevention. OpenClaw currently pins `playwright-core` 1.61.1, whose documented routing contract has these gaps:

- `page.route` handles only the first URL when a response redirects;
- `page.route` does not intercept the first request of a popup;
- page and browser-context routes do not intercept requests handled by a Service Worker.

Using `browserContext.route` globally is not an acceptable shortcut: extension and remote-CDP contexts can contain unrelated user or agent tabs, so a context-wide transient route would violate the selected-page ownership boundary and still would not solve Service Worker traffic.

The existing final-URL and redirect-chain checks should remain, but they are detection/quarantine after dispatch for these residual cases.

## Complete enforcement follow-up

Complete network prevention is a separate architecture change, not part of this bounded repair.

For locally managed Chrome, the complete boundary is a lifecycle-owned loopback HTTP/CONNECT egress proxy that Chrome is forced to use. That proxy must resolve each destination under `resolvePinnedHostnameWithPolicy`, connect to an approved pinned address, remove implicit loopback/QUIC bypasses, and enforce the policy for redirects, frames/OOPIFs, popups, downloads, workers/Service Workers, subresources, and DNS rebinding at connect time. HTTPS should remain end-to-end through CONNECT; no TLS interception is required.

Extension, existing-session, and remote-CDP profiles cannot be retrofitted with a launch-time proxy by this process. Complete enforcement for those profiles requires owner-side egress isolation or an explicitly proven filtering proxy. Until then, their navigation protection remains request-time where Playwright exposes it plus best-effort post-checking.

Track that work separately so this issue can land the missing action parity without overstating its guarantee or expanding into a browser-network product redesign.

## Regression tests

- Parameterized direct-helper tests for hover, drag, and scroll proving exact policy propagation and canonical post-check invocation.
- Parameterized one-action batch tests for all three so a forgotten `executeSingleAction` forwarding branch fails.
- Browser server contract assertions that `/act` carries the resolved policy to all three helpers.
- Request-guard tests covering:
  - direct top-level document denial and pre-dispatch abort;
  - direct subframe document denial;
  - allowed document and non-document `route.fallback()` behavior;
  - no route installation when no policy is supplied to an internal helper;
  - exact cleanup on success, action failure, and abort;
  - an in-flight route handler finishing before the final action result;
  - policy-denial precedence over locator/action errors;
  - a navigation beginning inside the existing delayed-action grace window.
- Existing click/type/press/select/fill/evaluate, download, dialog, and no-policy compatibility tests must remain green.

Focused proof:

```text
pnpm test extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.browser-ssrf-guard.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.interactions.navigation-guard.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-session.create-page.navigation-guard.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/server.agent-contract-core.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.clamps-timeoutms-scrollintoview.test.ts
```

Run through the repository Testbox path, plus the normal changed-surface checks and build before landing.

## Live acceptance proof

Use a real Chrome process, real Gateway, and real OpenAI-backed agent turn under strict/default browser policy:

1. Create three isolated `about:blank` tabs through raw CDP and inject one controlled hover, scroll, or drag trigger per tab. `about:blank` avoids pre-blocking the source page and is the explicitly supported non-network bootstrap URL.
2. Point each trigger at a controlled denied loopback canary that records request count without returning sensitive data.
3. Ask the agent to perform the exact three browser actions.
4. Require all three tool calls to return a browser navigation policy error.
5. Require the canary request count to remain zero for the direct-navigation cases.
6. Verify through raw CDP that each source target remains open at `about:blank`; quarantined targets, if any post-load guard fires, may intentionally be hidden from later OpenClaw tab listings.
7. Verify Chrome and Gateway health, the effective provider/model, and call-id-linked tool requests/results in the transcript.

The PR verification comment should report the exact focused commands, hosted run IDs, live artifact or log location, zero-request canary result, and the Playwright limitations above. It should explicitly avoid claiming popup, redirect-hop, Service Worker, or DNS-pinning coverage from `page.route`.

## Additional information

- The helper omission dates to the original Playwright interaction surface; later interaction-navigation hardening migrated neighboring actions but not these three.
- `src/config/types.browser.ts` currently says `dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork` defaults to `true`, while the runtime resolver and public browser docs correctly default to strict/private access off. Correct that stale comment to `Default: false` while touching this surface; it is documentation-only and does not change the config shape.

external_evidence.title: [Bug]: node approval can dispatch after caller timeout
external_evidence.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A pending plugin approval can outlive the `node.invoke` caller timeout/disconnect and dispatch dangerous node work after the caller has already observed failure.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Register a dangerous plugin-owned node command whose policy calls `ctx.approvals.request()` and then `ctx.invokeNode()` after approval.
2. Call `node.invoke` through an agent Gateway tool using the default 30-second Gateway request timeout.
3. Leave the approval pending until the caller times out or disconnects.
4. Resolve the still-pending approval before its default 120-second expiry.
5. Observe that the detached server handler continues into `nodeRegistry.invoke` even though the original caller has already received a timeout.

### Expected behavior

The Gateway owns one authoritative request lifetime. Timeout, cancellation, or connection close must expire a still-pending approval and make later node dispatch impossible. If node execution has already begun, cancellation must report that it is too late/indeterminate rather than claim success.

### Actual behavior

The TypeScript Gateway client removes its local waiter on timeout/abort, but no cancellation reaches the server request. The server method continues awaiting the plugin approval and can dispatch after a late allow decision.

### OpenClaw version

2026.6.11, current `main` at `b1e688c6577f2b12a3f3a77563a8cc5b4ed9fca4`

### Operating system

All Gateway/client platforms; source-confirmed on the TypeScript Gateway path

### Install method

Source checkout / any installation using Gateway `node.invoke`

### Model

N/A; Gateway request-lifecycle bug

### Provider / routing chain

agent tool -> local Gateway -> plugin node-invoke policy -> node transport

### Additional provider/model setup details

No provider-specific setup is required.

### Logs

```shell
Agent Gateway timeout: src/agents/tools/gateway.ts (30 seconds by default)
Plugin approval timeout: src/infra/plugin-approvals.ts (120 seconds by default, 600 seconds maximum)
Client local waiter cleanup: packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts
Server dispatch without request signal: src/gateway/server/ws-connection/message-handler.ts
Synchronous approval wait: src/gateway/node-invoke-plugin-policy.ts
Post-approval dispatch: extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/node-invoke-policy.ts
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Found while security-reviewing #98561 for #98560. The timeout and approval windows overlap deterministically, and the request handler currently has no caller-lifetime signal.

### Impact and severity

- Affected: dangerous plugin-owned node commands, currently including file-transfer policy paths.
- Severity: P1 security/expectation violation.
- Frequency: every request where approval arrives after caller timeout/disconnect but before approval expiry.
- Consequence: side effects can occur after the UI/tool reported timeout or cancellation.

### Additional information

Preferred owner boundary: an additive, negotiated Gateway request-cancellation capability. The server should own per-request pending/effecting/completed state; cancellation or disconnect may win only while pending. Pass the resulting `AbortSignal` through handler options to `node.invoke`/plugin policy, expire approval on abort, and atomically guard dispatch. Add cross-connection rejection, late-allow, disconnect, and allow-vs-cancel race tests. A two-phase node approval protocol is a larger follow-up, not the minimal repair.

This is a prerequisite for safely landing #98561.

Codex review: keeping this open for maintainer follow-up; there is still a little grit to resolve. _Reviewed July 10, 2026, 7:35 PM ET / 23:35 UTC._

**Summary**
Keep open: current main and v2026.6.11 retain a deterministic request-lifetime race that can dispatch dangerous node work after the caller reports timeout or cancellation. The issue is canonical, assigned, security-sensitive, and requires explicit Gateway/security owner approval for the cancellation authority contract.

Reproducibility: yes. Hold a dangerous plugin node approval beyond the ordinary 30-second Gateway client timeout, then allow it before the 120-second approval expiry; current main continues through the detached server handler into node dispatch.

**Root-cause cluster**
Relationship: `canonical`
Canonical: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/103980
Summary: This issue canonically tracks the request-lifetime race; the linked approval-routing work is related but does not implement cancellation or replace this tracker.

Members:
- `adjacent_distinct`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/98560 - It concerns preserving approval routes when no live approval client is connected, not expiring authority when the originating request ends.
- `partial_overlap`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/98561 - It makes node policy approvals remain pending for routed decisions and therefore depends on this issue for safe late-decision behavior.

Proposal only: this assessment does not dispatch repair, suppress jobs, mutate sibling items, close, or merge anything.

**Next step**
The bug is source-proven and bounded, but its security and maintainer protection plus the new cancellation-authority contract require explicit human approval before implementation.

**Maintainer decision needed**
- Question: Should Gateway request cancellation become an additive, connection-bound protocol capability with server-owned pending, effecting, and completed states?
- Rationale: The defect is proven, but cancellation authority, cross-connection rejection, allow-versus-cancel ordering, and post-dispatch semantics define a security-sensitive public protocol contract.
- Likely owner: steipete — The issue is assigned to steipete, and his Gateway lifecycle and approval-routing history makes him the clearest coordinator for the security-owner decision.
- Options:
  - **Add negotiated cancellation (recommended):** Advertise capability support, bind cancellation to the originating connection, expire pending approvals, and reject cancellation once dispatch begins.
  - **Use server deadline only:** Add a server-side deadline without fully representing explicit caller abort and connection-disconnect semantics.

**Security**
Needs attention: The issue identifies a concrete authorization-lifetime gap where dangerous node side effects can occur after caller authority appears to have ended.


<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Add an advertised Gateway cancellation capability, retain connection-owned request state on the server, propagate its AbortSignal through plugin approval handling, and atomically claim effecting state immediately before nodeRegistry.invoke.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

Yes. Hold a dangerous plugin node approval beyond the ordinary 30-second Gateway client timeout, then allow it before the 120-second approval expiry; current main continues through the detached server handler into node dispatch.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

Yes in architectural direction: generic, additive Gateway cancellation with one server-owned state machine is the narrowest maintainable fix. Client-only waiter cleanup or a file-transfer-specific abort check would preserve competing request lifetimes and leave sibling plugin policies exposed.

AGENTS.md: found and applied where relevant.

Remaining risk / open question:

- Cancellation must be bound to the originating connection so another client cannot cancel an unrelated request by guessing or observing its identifier.
- The allow-versus-cancel transition must be atomic; separate best-effort approval expiry and dispatch checks can still permit contradictory successful outcomes.
- Once node dispatch begins, cancellation must report too-late or indeterminate rather than claiming the side effect was prevented.
- The open approval-routing work at https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/98561 should not land without resolving this prerequisite or providing an explicitly reviewed narrower mitigation.

Codex review notes: model internal, reasoning high; reviewed against [2f9cb9200669](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2f9cb9200669fe5df86fd229b445685e9b1b81b1).

</details>

- `impact:security`: Approval authority can outlive the originating request whose identity and intent established it.
- `maturity:stable`: The issue affects the M4 Stable gateway-runtime feature across approvals, nodes, lifecycle, protocol compatibility, security controls, and WebSocket handling.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Evidence reviewed</summary>

Security concerns:

- [high] Bind approval authority to the originating request lifetime — `packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts:1614`
  Current timeout, abort, and disconnect paths do not revoke the server-side approval wait, allowing a later allow decision to reach dangerous node dispatch after the caller observed failure.
  Confidence: 0.99
- [high] Make cancellation and dispatch mutually exclusive — `src/gateway/node-invoke-plugin-policy.ts:184`
  The repair needs a single atomic pending-to-effecting transition so simultaneous cancellation and approval cannot both succeed or produce misleading cancellation results.
  Confidence: 0.96

Acceptance criteria:

- pnpm test packages/gateway-client/src/client.watchdog.test.ts
- pnpm test src/gateway/node-invoke-plugin-policy.test.ts
- pnpm test src/gateway/server/ws-connection/message-handler.suspension-admission.test.ts
- pnpm test src/gateway/exec-approval-manager.test.ts
- pnpm test extensions/file-transfer/src/shared/node-invoke-policy.test.ts

What I checked:

- **Client timeout is local only:** GatewayClient.request removes its local pending waiter and rejects on timeout without sending cancellation to the server. ([`packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts:1614`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2f9cb9200669/packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts#L1614), [2f9cb9200669](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2f9cb9200669))
- **Client abort is local only:** The caller AbortSignal likewise deletes only client pending state and rejects locally. ([`packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts:1628`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2f9cb9200669/packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts#L1628), [2f9cb9200669](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2f9cb9200669))
- **Server handler remains detached:** The WebSocket handler launches handleGatewayRequest in a detached promise without retaining a per-request cancellation controller. ([`src/gateway/server/ws-connection/message-handler.ts:2507`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2f9cb9200669/src/gateway/server/ws-connection/message-handler.ts#L2507), [2f9cb9200669](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2f9cb9200669))
- **Disconnect does not cancel requests:** WebSocket close cleanup releases subscriptions, terminals, presence, and node sessions but does not abort in-flight operator request handlers. ([`src/gateway/server/ws-connection.ts:496`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2f9cb9200669/src/gateway/server/ws-connection.ts#L496), [2f9cb9200669](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2f9cb9200669))
- **Approval window exceeds caller timeout:** Plugin approvals default to 120 seconds, while ordinary Gateway requests default to 30 seconds, creating a deterministic late-decision window. ([`src/infra/plugin-approvals.ts:50`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2f9cb9200669/src/infra/plugin-approvals.ts#L50), [2f9cb9200669](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2f9cb9200669))
- **Late approval reaches dispatch:** The plugin policy waits for the approval promise and then invokeNode calls nodeRegistry.invoke without any caller-lifetime signal. ([`src/gateway/node-invoke-plugin-policy.ts:117`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2f9cb9200669/src/gateway/node-invoke-plugin-policy.ts#L117), [2f9cb9200669](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2f9cb9200669))

- **steipete:** The live issue is assigned to steipete, and his merged history covers Gateway lifecycle plus same-chat approval routing behavior adjacent to this boundary. (role: adjacent owner and decision coordinator; confidence: high; commits: [1bcc4c5e7063](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/1bcc4c5e7063e2614208e7408be181ade80e0335), [574d3c521358](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/574d3c521358b00ca041982901cfafe44554c898), [3ec000b99554](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3ec000b99554f186c9ad9e5c6db0bfd5dcf6b3f4); files: `src/gateway/`, `src/infra/approval-turn-source.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/approval-shared.ts`)
- **pgondhi987:** Authored the merged requester-metadata binding work that touched the node policy, approval manager, request context, and WebSocket message handler. (role: introduced adjacent approval binding; confidence: high; commits: [386d321634b3](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/386d321634b3681b22d0f2cf027cdfef49de0049); files: `src/gateway/node-invoke-plugin-policy.ts`, `src/gateway/exec-approval-manager.ts`, `src/gateway/server/ws-connection/message-handler.ts`)

(role: recent approval-path contributor; confidence: high; commits: [c9e481ac48e5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c9e481ac48e5bb924833f44c65ceaca55a1992e3), [5adc681238c6](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/5adc681238c61cd292c67fbfe1817949d903bd8a); files: `src/gateway/server-methods/approval-shared.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/plugin-approval.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/exec-approval.ts`)
- **kevinslin:** Authored merged work extending shared approval routing and turn-source behavior, which is the sibling invariant near the linked routing issue. (role: adjacent approval-routing contributor; confidence: medium; commits: [5fbaf2a8a236](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/5fbaf2a8a2367508a12f4194a628ba326d524cf3); files: `src/gateway/server-methods/approval-shared.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/plugin-approval.ts`, `src/infra/approval-turn-source.ts`)

Host-side note from running unattended agent loops where caller timeout and node approval race:

1. Treat caller timeout as authoritative cancel for the *dispatch* path — once the waiter is gone, late approval must not enqueue work.
2. Keep an interrupted/aborted ledger keyed by request id; approval handlers check it before spawn.
3. Bound approval UI lifetime separately from tool timeout (approval can outlive tool budget, but must not restart the tool after cancel).
4. On late approval after timeout: ack as discarded, log structured `approval_after_timeout`, never side-effect.
5. Regression: approval arrives 1ms after cancel; CPU-spin tool still running; double-approval after first reject.

Happy to share more host-ops patterns if useful. No product pitch.

Host-side note from running unattended agent loops where caller timeout and node approval race:

1. Treat caller timeout as authoritative cancel for the *dispatch* path — once the waiter is gone, late approval must not enqueue work.
2. Keep an interrupted/aborted ledger keyed by request id; approval handlers check it before spawn.
3. Bound approval UI lifetime separately from tool timeout (approval can outlive tool budget, but must not restart the tool after cancel).
4. On late approval after timeout: ack as discarded, log structured `approval_after_timeout`, never side-effect.
5. Regression: approval arrives 1ms after cancel; CPU-spin tool still running; double-approval after first reject.

Happy to share more host-ops patterns if useful. No product pitch.

external_evidence.title: sessions.create worktreeBaseRef reaches git worktree add without a -- separator, allowing git flag injection
external_evidence.body:
## Summary
`sessions.create` accepts a `worktreeBaseRef` and hands it, unchanged, to `git worktree add` as the final positional argument with no `--` separator. A dash-prefixed value is therefore parsed by git as an option rather than a ref. A plain `operator.write` caller (a broader population than `operator.admin`) can inject `git worktree add` flags. No code-execution or arbitrary-file-write primitive was found after a full sweep of the flag surface, but `--lock` produces a worktree that the managed-worktree cleanup then refuses to reclaim, a real self-inflicted cleanup DoS, and `--orphan` silently creates an unborn worktree instead of failing.

## Environment
- Commit: 04865fe44b4c8521cdd1fa72fb26f08b6e201b4d (origin/main at time of filing)
- Surface: gateway `sessions.create` worktree creation, `git worktree add` invocation in the managed-worktree service
- git 2.43.0

## Steps to reproduce
1. Call `sessions.create` with `worktree: true` and `worktreeBaseRef: "--orphan"` (or `"--lock"`), which requires only `operator.write`.
2. The service runs `git worktree add <path> -b openclaw/<name> <worktreeBaseRef>` with the raw value as the last positional argument.
3. git parses the dash-prefixed value as an option. `--orphan` creates an unborn worktree and exits 0. `--lock` creates a locked worktree.

## Expected
An explicit base ref should be interpreted only as a ref. An option-like value should fail `git worktree add` before the worktree is created, exactly as the sibling git-plugin checkout path was fixed to do in #79928.

## Actual
The dash-prefixed value is consumed as a git flag. `--orphan` silently produces an unborn worktree (HEAD `0000000`, no commit) and returns success. `--lock` silently produces a locked worktree that the cleanup paths then skip.

## Root cause
`worktreeBaseRef` reaches `git worktree add` with no `--` guard:

- `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions.ts:1223,1347` reads `worktreeBaseRef` and passes it as `baseRef` to `managedWorktrees.create`.
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/sessions.ts:260-264` validates `worktreeBaseRef` with `minLength: 1` only, no leading-dash rejection.
- `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:127-150` (`resolveBase`) returns the caller value unchanged: `if (baseRef) return { base: baseRef, remote: false };`.
- `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:418-427` places that value (`usedBase`) as the final positional argument with no `--` separator:

```
let usedBase = base.base;
let added = await runGit(repository.repoRoot, [
  "worktree",
  "add",
  worktreePath,
  "-b",
  branch,
  usedBase,
]);
```

The sharpest reachable consequence is `--lock`. The injected lock reason `added with --lock` does not match `OPENCLAW_LOCK_PATTERN`, so `lockState` (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:318-330`) classifies the worktree as `foreign`. The idle garbage collector then skips it (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:773-775`, `if (state.kind === "live" || state.kind === "foreign") continue;`), and non-force `remove()` refuses it (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:628-634`). The automatic hourly cleanup never reclaims the worktree.

The write/admin scope split for `worktreeBaseRef` is intentional and documented (`docs/concepts/managed-worktrees.md`: "both stay at `operator.write`"; `src/gateway/method-scopes.ts:101-109` returns the write scope for `sessions.create` without `cwd`/`execNode`), so this is reachable by the broader `operator.write` population, not just admins.

Scope honesty: a full adversarial sweep of the `git worktree add` flag surface (`-f`, `-b`/`-B`, `--orphan`, `-d`/`--detach`, `--checkout`/`--no-checkout`, `--lock`/`--reason`, `-q`, `--track`, `--guess-remote`) found no code-execution or arbitrary-file-write primitive, and the `execFile` argv path (no shell) blocks multi-flag smuggling through embedded spaces. The concrete impact is the `--lock` cleanup DoS plus the general flag-injection correctness defect.

## Sibling surfaces
Same bug class, already fixed in the sibling git-plugin checkout path: closed issue #79898 and its fix PR #79928 ("pass `--` before ref in git checkout to prevent flag injection") in `src/plugins/git-install.ts`. The `--` guard was not applied to `git worktree add` here. The restore path (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts` `worktree add --detach ... record.snapshotRef`) uses an internally generated snapshot ref, not caller input, so it is not reachable the same way.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: caller-supplied `worktreeBaseRef` is parsed as a `git worktree add` flag because it is the last positional with no `--` separator.
Real environment tested: real `git worktree add` invocation shape run by `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:418-427`, driven against a real git repository, at commit 04865fe44b4c8521cdd1fa72fb26f08b6e201b4d.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `git worktree add <path> -b <branch> <value>` with `value` set to the injected `worktreeBaseRef`, then the exact cleanup command `git worktree remove --force <path>` that `remove()`/`gc()` run.
Evidence after fix:
```
# OBSERVED (buggy, origin/main 04865fe) -- runtime shape: git worktree add <path> -b <branch> <usedBase>

$ git worktree add ../wt-inject -b openclaw/inject --orphan
Preparing worktree (new branch 'openclaw/inject')
$ echo exit=$?
exit=0
$ git worktree list
.../repo        0b951ac [main]
.../wt-inject   0000000 [openclaw/inject]     <- unborn HEAD, no commit checked out
$ git -C ../wt-inject log --oneline
fatal: your current branch 'openclaw/inject' does not have any commits yet

# --lock cleanup DoS: injected --lock, then the exact command remove()/gc() run
$ git worktree add ../wt-locked -b openclaw/locked --lock HEAD
Preparing worktree (new branch 'openclaw/locked')
HEAD is now at 0b951ac second     (add exit 0, worktree locked)
$ git worktree remove --force ../wt-locked
fatal: cannot remove a locked working tree, lock reason: added with --lock
use 'remove -f -f' to override or unlock first
exit=128     -> worktree STILL PRESENT, idle gc skips it as foreign-locked

# EXPECTED (with -- separator, identical injected input)
$ git worktree add ../wt-fixed -b openclaw/fixed -- --orphan
fatal: invalid reference: --orphan
exit=128     -> the option-like value is rejected as a ref, no worktree created
```
Observed result after fix: on current main a dash-prefixed `worktreeBaseRef` is consumed as a git option (`--orphan` yields an unborn worktree at exit 0, `--lock` yields a worktree the cleanup path cannot reclaim), while the `--` guarded form rejects the same value as an invalid ref.
What was not tested: no code-execution or arbitrary-file-write primitive was found across the full flag surface, and none is claimed. The gateway auth stack and the `operator.write` scope check were read but not exercised end to end; the repro drives the real `git worktree add` argument shape directly against a real repository rather than through the gateway RPC.

Codex review: keeping this open for maintainer follow-up; there is still a little grit to resolve. _Reviewed July 10, 2026, 11:30 PM ET / July 11, 2026, 03:30 UTC._

**Summary**
The report is valid on current `main`: a write-scoped caller can supply an option-like base ref, Git accepts at least `--orphan` and `--lock`, and the latter produces a foreign-locked worktree that normal removal and idle cleanup preserve. The feature is newer than `v2026.6.11`, so this should remain open for a focused pre-release fix while security handling avoids further public exploit amplification.

Reproducibility: yes. Current `main` visibly constructs the vulnerable argv, and an independent real Git 2.54.0 repository reproduced the unborn worktree, persistent lock, failed cleanup, and guarded rejection.

**Root-cause cluster**
Relationship: `canonical`
Canonical: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/104105
Summary: This issue is the canonical report for the managed-worktree command path; the older plugin checkout issue and closed unmerged PR establish an adjacent option-like-ref bug class but neither owns or fixes this behavior.

Members:
- `adjacent_distinct`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/79898 - It concerns option-like refs in plugin checkout, with a different Git command, owner boundary, and wrong-install consequence.
- `adjacent_distinct`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/79928 - It proposed a plugin-checkout repair, was closed unmerged, and does not touch managed-worktree creation or cleanup.

Proposal only: this assessment does not dispatch repair, suppress jobs, mutate sibling items, close, or merge anything.

**Next step**
The repair is narrow and well-proven, but security-sensitive reports are excluded from automatic ClawSweeper fix-PR staging until maintainers approve the disclosure and landing path.

**Maintainer decision needed**
- Question: Should this valid but currently unreleased operator-triggered argument-injection bug be fixed through private security handling before the managed-worktree feature ships?
- Rationale: The code repair is mechanical, but the report is publicly disclosed and security-labeled, so maintainers must choose the disclosure and landing path rather than ClawSweeper automatically staging a patch.
- Likely owner: steipete — He introduced and most recently expanded the managed-worktree and session base-ref behavior, making him the strongest available owner for the pre-release handling choice.
- Options:
  - **Fix privately before release (recommended):** Move detailed handling to the security process, land the narrow separator and regression-test fix, and avoid amplifying the public reproduction.
  - **Treat as public hardening:** Keep the issue public, explicitly scope it to trusted-operator cleanup denial, and land the same focused fix through ordinary review.

**Security**
Needs attention: The issue demonstrates caller-controlled Git option interpretation and cleanup denial, but the documented trusted-operator model limits the supported security severity.


<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Before managed worktrees ship, add `--` before the explicit base ref in both `git worktree add` attempts and add service regression coverage proving valid refs still succeed while option-like refs leave no branch, worktree directory, or registry record.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

Yes. Current `main` visibly constructs the vulnerable argv, and an independent real Git 2.54.0 repository reproduced the unborn worktree, persistent lock, failed cleanup, and guarded rejection.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

Yes. Securing the owning Git argv boundary is narrower and more maintainable than changing authorization or broadly restricting valid ref syntax, and it preserves the documented `operator.write` behavior.

AGENTS.md: found and applied where relevant.

Remaining risk / open question:

- The public issue already contains a working security-sensitive reproduction despite `SECURITY.md` requesting private disclosure; further handling should avoid adding exploit detail and may need migration to the central security process.
- The demonstrated impact is argument injection, incorrect worktree state, and persistent cleanup denial inside the documented trusted-operator boundary; no code-execution, arbitrary-file-write, or cross-tenant privilege-bypass claim is supported.
- Because the feature is current-main-only, the fix should land before its first release rather than adding a runtime compatibility path or changing the documented `operator.write` contract.

Codex review notes: model internal, reasoning high; reviewed against [ffc8051cacb5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ffc8051cacb50d1f4b39cc2c6f822083caba1f2a).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Label changes</summary>

Label changes:

- add `issue-rating: 🦀 challenger crab`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.
- add `clawsweeper:current-main-repro`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.
- add `clawsweeper:no-new-fix-pr`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.
- add `clawsweeper:needs-security-review`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.

Label justifications:

- `P2`: The defect is deterministic and persistent but affects an unreleased, bounded managed-worktree path without demonstrated code execution or arbitrary file write.
- `impact:security`: A write-scoped caller-controlled ref crosses a subprocess boundary and is interpreted as Git command options.
- `impact:other`: The injected lock produces a managed worktree that ordinary removal and hourly garbage collection preserve indefinitely.
- `maturity:stable`: The affected Gateway RPC, permissions, and security-control surface maps to the M4 Stable `gateway-runtime` feature.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Evidence reviewed</summary>

Security concerns:

- [medium] Route the public reproduction through security handling — `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:420`
  The report contains a working argument-injection transcript for an unfixed current-main path even though repository policy requests private disclosure; maintainers should avoid expanding the public exploit details while landing the pre-release fix.
  Confidence: 0.98

What I checked:

- **Current vulnerable command boundary:** `resolveBase` returns an explicit caller value unchanged, and both managed-worktree creation attempts append that value after `-b <branch>` without an end-of-options separator. ([`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:420`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/ffc8051cacb5/src/agents/worktrees/service.ts#L420), [ffc8051cacb5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ffc8051cacb5))

([`src/agents/worktrees/service.test.ts:157`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/ffc8051cacb5/src/agents/worktrees/service.test.ts#L157), [ffc8051cacb5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/ffc8051cacb5))

`sessions.create` accepts a `worktreeBaseRef` and hands it, unchanged, to `git worktree add` as the final positional argument with no `--` separator. A dash-prefixed value is therefore parsed by git as an option rather than a ref. A plain `operator.write` caller (a broader population than `operator.admin`) can inject `git worktree add` flags. No code-execution or arbitrary-file-write primitive was found after a full sweep of the flag surface, but `--lock` produces a worktree that the managed-worktree cleanup then refuses to reclaim, a real self-inflicted cleanup DoS, and `--orphan` silently creates an unborn worktree instead of failing.

## Environment
- Commit: 04865fe44b4c8521cdd1fa72fb26f08b6e201b4d (origin/main at time of filing)
- Surface: gateway `sessions.create` worktree creation, `git worktree add` invocation in the managed-worktree service
- git 2.43.0

## Steps to reproduce
1. Call `sessions.create` with `worktree: true` and `worktreeBaseRef: "--orphan"` (or `"--lock"`), which requires only `operator.write`.
2. The service runs `git worktree add <path> -b openclaw/<name> <worktreeBaseRef>` with the raw value as the last positional argument.
3. git parses the dash-prefixed value as an option. `--orphan` creates an unborn worktree and exits 0. `--lock` creates a locked worktree.

## Expected
An explicit base ref should be interpreted only as a ref. An option-like value should fail `git worktree add` before the worktree is created, exactly as the sibling git-plugin checkout path was fixed to do in #79928.

## Actual
The dash-prefixed value is consumed as a git flag. `--orphan` silently produces an unborn worktree (HEAD `0000000`, no commit) and returns success. `--lock` silently produces a locked worktree that the cleanup paths then skip.

## Root cause
`worktreeBaseRef` reaches `git worktree add` with no `--` guard:

- `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions.ts:1223,1347` reads `worktreeBaseRef` and passes it as `baseRef` to `managedWorktrees.create`.
- `packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/sessions.ts:260-264` validates `worktreeBaseRef` with `minLength: 1` only, no leading-dash rejection.
- `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:127-150` (`resolveBase`) returns the caller value unchanged: `if (baseRef) return { base: baseRef, remote: false };`.
- `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:418-427` places that value (`usedBase`) as the final positional argument with no `--` separator:

```
let usedBase = base.base;
let added = await runGit(repository.repoRoot, [
  "worktree",
  "add",
  worktreePath,
  "-b",
  branch,
  usedBase,
]);
```

The sharpest reachable consequence is `--lock`. The injected lock reason `added with --lock` does not match `OPENCLAW_LOCK_PATTERN`, so `lockState` (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:318-330`) classifies the worktree as `foreign`. The idle garbage collector then skips it (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:773-775`, `if (state.kind === "live" || state.kind === "foreign") continue;`), and non-force `remove()` refuses it (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:628-634`). The automatic hourly cleanup never reclaims the worktree.

The write/admin scope split for `worktreeBaseRef` is intentional and documented (`docs/concepts/managed-worktrees.md`: "both stay at `operator.write`"; `src/gateway/method-scopes.ts:101-109` returns the write scope for `sessions.create` without `cwd`/`execNode`), so this is reachable by the broader `operator.write` population, not just admins.

Scope honesty: a full adversarial sweep of the `git worktree add` flag surface (`-f`, `-b`/`-B`, `--orphan`, `-d`/`--detach`, `--checkout`/`--no-checkout`, `--lock`/`--reason`, `-q`, `--track`, `--guess-remote`) found no code-execution or arbitrary-file-write primitive, and the `execFile` argv path (no shell) blocks multi-flag smuggling through embedded spaces. The concrete impact is the `--lock` cleanup DoS plus the general flag-injection correctness defect.

## Sibling surfaces
Same bug class, already fixed in the sibling git-plugin checkout path: closed issue #79898 and its fix PR #79928 ("pass `--` before ref in git checkout to prevent flag injection") in `src/plugins/git-install.ts`. The `--` guard was not applied to `git worktree add` here. The restore path (`src/agents/worktrees/service.ts` `worktree add --detach ... record.snapshotRef`) uses an internally generated snapshot ref, not caller input, so it is not reachable the same way.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: caller-supplied `worktreeBaseRef` is parsed as a `git worktree add` flag because it is the last positional with no `--` separator.
Real environment tested: real `git worktree add` invocation shape run by `src/agents/worktrees/service.ts:418-427`, driven against a real git repository, at commit 04865fe44b4c8521cdd1fa72fb26f08b6e201b4d.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `git worktree add <path> -b <branch> <value>` with `value` set to the injected `worktreeBaseRef`, then the exact cleanup command `git worktree remove --force <path>` that `remove()`/`gc()` run.
Evidence after fix:
```
# OBSERVED (buggy, origin/main 04865fe) -- runtime shape: git worktree add <path> -b <branch> <usedBase>

$ git worktree add ../wt-inject -b openclaw/inject --orphan
Preparing worktree (new branch 'openclaw/inject')
$ echo exit=$?
exit=0
$ git worktree list
.../repo        0b951ac [main]
.../wt-inject   0000000 [openclaw/inject]     <- unborn HEAD, no commit checked out
$ git -C ../wt-inject log --oneline
fatal: your current branch 'openclaw/inject' does not have any commits yet

# --lock cleanup DoS: injected --lock, then the exact command remove()/gc() run
$ git worktree add ../wt-locked -b openclaw/locked --lock HEAD
Preparing worktree (new branch 'openclaw/locked')
HEAD is now at 0b951ac second     (add exit 0, worktree locked)
$ git worktree remove --force ../wt-locked
fatal: cannot remove a locked working tree, lock reason: added with --lock
use 'remove -f -f' to override or unlock first
exit=128     -> worktree STILL PRESENT, idle gc skips it as foreign-locked

# EXPECTED (with -- separator, identical injected input)
$ git worktree add ../wt-fixed -b openclaw/fixed -- --orphan
fatal: invalid reference: --orphan
exit=128     -> the option-like value is rejected as a ref, no worktree created
```
Observed result after fix: on current main a dash-prefixed `worktreeBaseRef` is consumed as a git option (`--orphan` yields an unborn worktree at exit 0, `--lock` yields a worktree the cleanup path cannot reclaim), while the `--` guarded form rejects the same value as an invalid ref.
What was not tested: no code-execution or arbitrary-file-write primitive was found across the full flag surface, and none is claimed. The gateway auth stack and the `operator.write` scope check were read but not exercised end to end; the repro drives the real `git worktree add` argument shape directly against a real repository rather than through the gateway RPC.

external_evidence.title: [Security] Proxy Capture Hardening: Implement Content-Type Aware Payload Redaction and Restrict Database File Modes
external_evidence.body:
### Summary / Problem Statement
The debug proxy capture system logs request/response headers and payloads to an SQLite database for debugging. However, the implementation leaves several security gaps:
1. **Plaintext Body Logging:** Request and response bodies are captured and stored in the SQLite blob store as-is without passing through the credential redaction engine. If an API request contains keys or credentials in its JSON body (e.g. POST to auth endpoints), those keys are persisted in plaintext.
2. **Unredacted URLs:** Query parameters containing sensitive data (e.g., `?token=...` or `?code=...`) are captured and stored in the events table without sanitization.
3. **Transient WAL/SHM File Permissions:** While the database file is hardened using `0o600` permissions, the temporary WAL and SHM sidecars created by SQLite during runtime inherit default system permissions, leaving a window of exposure on multi-user hosts.
4. **Fragment-Based Header Redaction:** Redaction uses loose string fragments (e.g., matching "session"), which can cause over-redaction of non-sensitive custom headers while missing others.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Body Logging:** `captureHttpExchange` writes the raw body payload:
  ```typescript
  const requestPayload = runtime.persistEventPayload(store, {
    data: redactCapturePayload(requestBody), // only handles string/buffer checks, not credential values
    contentType: requestContentType,
  });
  ```
- **URL Storage:** `redactCaptureUrl` does not clean query parameters against known sensitive keys.

### Impact Analysis
- Exposure of raw LLM provider API keys, OAuth tokens, and session credentials in capture databases.
- Multi-user host environments can access sensitive SQLite WAL logs containing captured API payloads before hardening runs.
- Potential compliance or data privacy issues if users share capture databases for troubleshooting.

### Proposed Solution / Implementation Plan
1. **Body Content Redaction:** Pass all text-based capture payloads through the secret redaction engine (`src/logging/redact.ts`). For `application/json` payloads, parse and apply structured key-value redaction.
2. **URL Parameter Sanitization:** Update `redactCaptureUrl` to scan query parameters and redact values matching sensitive keys (e.g., `token`, `key`, `code`, `session`).
3. **Secure Sidecar Creation:** Configure the SQLite database initialization to enforce strict file modes or restrictive umask so that WAL and SHM files are created with `0o600` permissions by default.
4. **Structured Header Allowlist/Denylist:** Transition header redaction from fragment matching to an explicit allowlist/denylist for common HTTP headers.

### Affected File References
- [src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts)
- [src/proxy-capture/store.sqlite.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/proxy-capture/store.sqlite.ts)

### Additional Considerations
Redaction should be highly optimized to avoid adding performance overhead to the global fetch hook.

**Summary**
This issue remains necessary: current main masks registered secret values but does not generally redact sensitive JSON, form, or query keys before proxy-capture persistence. Shared database sidecar hardening already exists and should be verified rather than duplicated.

Reproducibility: yes. for the content-redaction gap: current main deterministically stores an unregistered sensitive JSON, form, or query value because capture only substitutes registered secret values. The WAL/SHM permission claim is not yet reproduced because shared owner-level hardening already exists.

**Next step**
This is security-sensitive work, so ClawSweeper should not automatically queue a repair PR even though the implementation boundary is reasonably narrow.

Use the shared structured and text redaction primitives at the proxy-capture serialization boundary, add focused JSON, form, query, and header regressions, and modify shared SQLite handling only if a filesystem-stat test proves WAL or SHM files are not private while open.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

Yes for the content-redaction gap: current main deterministically stores an unregistered sensitive JSON, form, or query value because capture only substitutes registered secret values. The WAL/SHM permission claim is not yet reproduced because shared owner-level hardening already exists.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

Partly. Content-aware redaction through existing shared helpers is the narrow maintainable fix, but a proxy-local umask or duplicate sidecar-hardening path is unjustified unless the shared database's current permission contract fails a focused real-filesystem test.

- The issue overstates the SQLite sidecar gap unless a real mode-stat check shows the shared state database's existing WAL/SHM hardening is ineffective or delayed.
- Replacing fragment-based header masking with a narrow allowlist could expose provider-specific credential headers; shared sensitive-key classification plus registered-value masking should remain defense in depth.

What I checked:

([`src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts:279`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c909a7e75d0c/src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts#L279), [c909a7e75d0c](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c909a7e75d0c))
- **URL redaction gap:** Query names and values receive registered-value substitution only, so a token, code, key, or session parameter remains stored when its exact value was not registered. ([`src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts:251`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c909a7e75d0c/src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts#L251), [c909a7e75d0c](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c909a7e75d0c))
- **Header policy:** Header redaction combines an explicit set with substring fragments including token, secret, password, credential, and session; this supports the over-redaction concern but intentionally covers provider-specific variants. ([`src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts:183`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c909a7e75d0c/src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts#L183), [c909a7e75d0c](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c909a7e75d0c))
- **Shared database permission owner:** Proxy capture writes to the shared OpenClaw state database, whose lifecycle owns private permissions and iterates the primary, WAL, and SHM paths with mode 0600 hardening. ([`src/state/openclaw-state-db.ts:184`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c909a7e75d0c/src/state/openclaw-state-db.ts#L184), [c909a7e75d0c](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c909a7e75d0c))
- **Coverage gap:** Current tests cover registered-secret and header redaction but lack regression cases for unregistered sensitive structured fields or query parameters and lack a proxy-capture sidecar mode assertion. ([`src/proxy-capture/runtime.test.ts:140`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c909a7e75d0c/src/proxy-capture/runtime.test.ts#L140), [c909a7e75d0c](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c909a7e75d0c))
- **Stable maturity match:** The maturity shortlist classifies gateway-runtime as M4 Stable, including HTTP APIs and Security Controls, which cover this core proxy-capture security surface. ([`qa/maturity-scores.yaml`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c909a7e75d0c/qa/maturity-scores.yaml), [c909a7e75d0c](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c909a7e75d0c))

external_evidence.title: [Security] Proxy Capture Hardening: Implement Content-Type Aware Payload Redaction and Restrict Database File Modes
external_evidence.description:
### Summary / Problem Statement
The debug proxy capture system logs request/response headers and payloads to an SQLite database for debugging. However, the implementation leaves several security gaps:
1. **Plaintext Body Logging:** Request and response bodies are captured and stored in the SQLite blob store as-is without passing through the credential redaction engine. If an API request contains keys or credentials in its JSON body (e.g. POST to auth endpoints), those keys are persisted in plaintext.
2. **Unredacted URLs:** Query parameters containing sensitive data (e.g., `?token=...` or `?code=...`) are captured and stored in the events table without sanitization.
3. **Transient WAL/SHM File Permissions:** While the database file is hardened using `0o600` permissions, the temporary WAL and SHM sidecars created by SQLite during runtime inherit default system permissions, leaving a window of exposure on multi-user hosts.
4. **Fragment-Based Header Redaction:** Redaction uses loose string fragments (e.g., matching "session"), which can cause over-redaction of non-sensitive custom headers while missing others.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Body Logging:** `captureHttpExchange` writes the raw body payload:
  ```typescript
  const requestPayload = runtime.persistEventPayload(store, {
    data: redactCapturePayload(requestBody), // only handles string/buffer checks, not credential values
    contentType: requestContentType,
  });
  ```
- **URL Storage:** `redactCaptureUrl` does not clean query parameters against known sensitive keys.

### Impact Analysis
- Exposure of raw LLM provider API keys, OAuth tokens, and session credentials in capture databases.
- Multi-user host environments can access sensitive SQLite WAL logs containing captured API payloads before hardening runs.
- Potential compliance or data privacy issues if users share capture databases for troubleshooting.

### Proposed Solution / Implementation Plan
1. **Body Content Redaction:** Pass all text-based capture payloads through the secret redaction engine (`src/logging/redact.ts`). For `application/json` payloads, parse and apply structured key-value redaction.
2. **URL Parameter Sanitization:** Update `redactCaptureUrl` to scan query parameters and redact values matching sensitive keys (e.g., `token`, `key`, `code`, `session`).
3. **Secure Sidecar Creation:** Configure the SQLite database initialization to enforce strict file modes or restrictive umask so that WAL and SHM files are created with `0o600` permissions by default.
4. **Structured Header Allowlist/Denylist:** Transition header redaction from fragment matching to an explicit allowlist/denylist for common HTTP headers.

- [src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/proxy-capture/runtime.ts)
- [src/proxy-capture/store.sqlite.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/proxy-capture/store.sqlite.ts)

### Additional Considerations
Redaction should be highly optimized to avoid adding performance overhead to the global fetch hook.

external_evidence.title: [Security] Telegram Bot Token Leak in Diagnostic Timeout Logs
external_evidence.body:
### Summary / Problem Statement
In `extensions/telegram/src/api-fetch.ts`, `fetchTelegramChatId` passes the full request URL (which contains the raw Telegram bot API token) to `buildTimeoutAbortSignal`. If the request times out or throws an error, the logging helper logs the URL string directly, leaking the bot credentials into plain diagnostics/timeout logs.

### Detailed Technical Context
- **Vulnerable Code Location:** [extensions/telegram/src/api-fetch.ts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/extensions/telegram/src/api-fetch.ts#L58-L63)
- **Mechanics:**
  ```typescript
  const url = `${apiBase}/bot${params.token}/getChat?chat_id=${encodeURIComponent(params.chatId)}`;
  const timeout = buildTimeoutAbortSignal({
    signal: params.signal,
    timeoutMs: resolveTelegramRequestTimeoutMs("getchat", params.timeoutSeconds),
    operation: "telegram-getchat-lookup",
    url, // Token exposed in the URL property!
  });
  ```
- If log files or console streams are exported or read by non-privileged operators, the secret token is exposed.

### Impact Analysis
- Security credential exposure: Telegram Bot API tokens leaked in log archives.
- Violation of credential safety policies.

### Proposed Solution
1. Redact the token from the URL before passing it to diagnostic logging helpers:
   ```typescript
   const redactedUrl = url.replace(params.token, "<REDACTED_TELEGRAM_TOKEN>");
   ```

### Affected File References
- [api-fetch.ts:L58-L63](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/extensions/telegram/src/api-fetch.ts#L58-L63)
