[Bug]: apply_patch tool allows arbitrary file write via path traversal when sandbox is disabled
external_evidence.description:
## Summary

The `apply_patch` agent tool resolves file paths without any containment check when `sandboxRoot` is `undefined` (gateway/non-sandboxed mode). An attacker who can influence agent tool calls can write to arbitrary filesystem locations using `../` traversal or absolute paths.

## Executive Risk Snapshot

- CVSS v3.1: 8.5 (High)
- CVSS v4.0: 8.4 (High)
- Primary risk: The `apply_patch` agent tool resolves file paths without any containment check when `sandboxRoot` is `undefined` (gateway/non-sandboxed mode).

## Technical Analysis

`resolvePatchPath()` in `src/agents/apply-patch.ts` has two code paths. When `sandboxRoot` is set, it calls `assertSandboxPath()` which validates containment within the sandbox directory and rejects `..` sequences. When `sandboxRoot` is `undefined`, it falls through to `resolvePathFromCwd()` which accepts absolute paths and normalizes `../` sequences via `path.normalize()` / `path.resolve()` with zero containment checks.

The `sandboxRoot` becomes `undefined` when the gateway runs without Docker sandboxing, as shown in `pi-tools.ts` line 312: `sandboxRoot: sandboxRoot && allowWorkspaceWrites ? sandboxRoot : undefined`. This means any gateway deployment without sandbox isolation exposes this vulnerability.

The `expandPath()` helper (line 242) also resolves `~` to the user's home directory, further broadening the write surface.

## Affected Code

**File:** `src/agents/apply-patch.ts:215-236`
```typescript
async function resolvePatchPath(
  filePath: string,
  options: ApplyPatchOptions,
): Promise<{ resolved: string; display: string }> {
  if (options.sandboxRoot) {
    const resolved = await assertSandboxPath({
      filePath,
      cwd: options.cwd,
      root: options.sandboxRoot,
    });
    return {
      resolved: resolved.resolved,
      display: resolved.relative || resolved.resolved,
    };
  }

  // NO containment check when sandboxRoot is absent:
  const resolved = resolvePathFromCwd(filePath, options.cwd);
  return {
    resolved,
    display: toDisplayPath(resolved, options.cwd),
  };
}
```

**File:** `src/agents/apply-patch.ts:253-259`
```typescript
function resolvePathFromCwd(filePath: string, cwd: string): string {
  const expanded = expandPath(filePath);
  if (path.isAbsolute(expanded)) {
    return path.normalize(expanded);
  }
  return path.resolve(cwd, expanded);
}
```

**File:** `src/agents/pi-tools.ts:307-313`
```typescript
const applyPatchTool =
  !applyPatchEnabled || (sandboxRoot && !allowWorkspaceWrites)
    ? null
    : createApplyPatchTool({
        cwd: sandboxRoot ?? workspaceRoot,
        sandboxRoot: sandboxRoot && allowWorkspaceWrites ? sandboxRoot : undefined,
      });
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy OpenClaw gateway without Docker sandbox (e.g., bare-metal or VM deployment where `sandboxRoot` is not configured)
2. Connect an agent that can issue `apply_patch` tool calls
3. Issue an `apply_patch` call with a file path containing traversal sequences, e.g., `../../../etc/cron.d/malicious-job` or an absolute path like `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`
4. Observe that `resolvePathFromCwd` resolves the path without any containment check and the patch is applied to the traversed location

## Recommended Fix

Add a containment check in the non-sandboxed branch of `resolvePatchPath`. Verify that the resolved path stays within `options.cwd` (the workspace root). Alternatively, always require a `sandboxRoot` when the `apply_patch` tool is enabled, or add a deny-list for sensitive system directories.

## Detailed Risk Analysis

### CVSS Assessment

| Metric | v3.1 | v4.0 |
|--------|------|------|
| **Score** | 8.5 / 10.0 | 8.4 / 10.0 |
| **Severity** | High | High |
| **Vector** | CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:N | CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:H/SA:N |
| **Calculator** | [CVSS v3.1 Calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:N) | [CVSS v4.0 Calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/4.0#CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:H/VA:N/SC:L/SI:H/SA:N) |

### Attack Surface
- **Entry point:** Agent tool call interface (`apply_patch` tool)
- **Privilege boundary:** Gateway process runs as a system user with filesystem access; agent tool calls are mediated by the gateway but path resolution has no containment
- **Trust boundary:** The agent is partially trusted (can issue tool calls) but should be constrained to the workspace directory

### Exploit Conditions
- Gateway must be running without Docker sandbox (`sandboxRoot` is `undefined`)
- Attacker must be able to influence agent tool calls (via prompt injection, compromised agent, or malicious plugin)
- Gateway process must have write permissions to the target path

### Impact Assessment
- **Confidentiality:** Low — file write primitive can be leveraged for information disclosure (e.g., writing a script that exfiltrates data)
- **Integrity:** High — arbitrary file overwrites can modify system configuration, inject cron jobs, or plant SSH keys
- **Availability:** None directly, though overwriting critical files could cause service disruption

## References

- **CWE:** [CWE-22](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html) - Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
- **Related:** `src/agents/sandbox-paths.ts` — the containment logic that is bypassed in non-sandboxed mode

external_evidence.title: Codex approval bridge executes mutated script: exec approvals are not operand-bound (approval TOCTOU)
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

The Codex app-server approval path executes the **mutated** script, not the approved one. An operator who reviews and approves one payload can have a different payload run.

Since `codex` is the default harness, every exec approval in a default configuration goes through this unbound path.

## Reproduction (verified live, 2026-08-16, `66dc9d1`)

1. Create `script.sh` that writes `BENIGN-ORIGINAL`.
2. Ask the agent to execute it; an approval goes pending with summary `Command: sh …/script.sh`.
3. While the approval is pending, rewrite `script.sh` to write `MUTATED-PAYLOAD-EXECUTED`.
4. Resolve the approval with `allow-once`.
5. Result file contains `MUTATED-PAYLOAD-EXECUTED`.

## Root cause

This is an owner-boundary gap, not a missing check in general — the correct defense already exists on the sibling path:

- `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.ts:880-893` revalidates `approvalPlan.mutableFileOperand` at use time and denies with `APPROVAL_SCRIPT_OPERAND_DRIFT_DENIED_MESSAGE`.
- `src/infra/system-run-approval-binding.ts` carries the sha256 file-operand snapshot.

`extensions/codex/src/app-server/approval-bridge.ts` has no `sha256`, `digest`, `mutableFileOperand`, or drift concept at all — its approvals are text-summary only. The binding machinery exists; this surface never populates or revalidates it.

This matches the repository invariant that delegated run authority is closure-bound rather than bearer-bound: a pending approval's summary text is correlation, not authorization, and privileged use must revalidate the authoritative operand at use time.

## Impact

An approval dialog that shows one command can execute different bytes. On multi-user or agent-driven workspaces, any writer to an operand path can substitute the payload during the approval window (default expiry 120s).

## Suggested fix

Populate and revalidate the existing `mutableFileOperand` binding in the codex approval bridge — reusing `src/infra/system-run-approval-binding.ts`, not a parallel implementation — and deny on drift with the existing message semantics. Fail closed when an operand cannot be snapshotted. Sibling approval surfaces should be audited in the same change.

Found during an end-to-end QA campaign (scenario APPR-131).

Codex review: keeping this open for maintainer follow-up; there is still a little grit to resolve. _Reviewed August 16, 2026, 2:35 PM ET / 18:35 UTC._

**Summary**
Keep open for maintainer security-boundary triage. Current source shows a Codex approval cycle with no operand snapshot, but the reported same-path rewrite lacks an untrusted OpenClaw write primitive and is expressly out of scope as a vulnerability under the documented trust model.

Reproducibility: no. The missing snapshot is source-visible, but no live run was performed and the required sibling Codex source was unavailable for independent protocol verification.

**Ways to help us reproduce this**
- Add a screenshot or short recording showing the behavior.
- Add expected vs actual behavior.
- Include redacted logs or terminal output.

**Maintainer decision needed**
| Question | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Does this report demonstrate an untrusted OpenClaw path that can rewrite an approved operand, or should it be handled only as optional approval-integrity hardening? | **Treat as defense-in-depth:** Keep any follow-up as optional hardening unless a concrete untrusted OpenClaw writer path is demonstrated. |

Why: SECURITY.md expressly excludes same-path rewrite without an untrusted write primitive, while the plugin boundary also prevents directly reusing core-private system-run helpers.

**Next step**
Protected security item: require a maintainer security-boundary decision before any repair dispatch.

**Security**
Needs attention: The bridge lacks a direct operand binding, but the report needs a documented-boundary decision before it can be treated as a vulnerability.


<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Have security owners decide whether an untrusted writer path exists; otherwise treat this as optional defense-in-depth, and if implemented, expose any shared binding through a typed SDK seam rather than importing core internals into the plugin.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

No. The missing snapshot is source-visible, but no live run was performed and the required sibling Codex source was unavailable for independent protocol verification.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

Unclear. Directly reusing the core helper would violate the plugin boundary; a typed SDK seam is the maintainable route only if maintainers decide this hardening is in scope.

AGENTS.md: found and applied where relevant.

Remaining risk / open question:

- The report does not establish an untrusted OpenClaw-controlled writer for the approved path, and the exact Codex app-server execution contract could not be independently inspected.

Codex review notes: model internal, reasoning high; reviewed against [1bcec211d9ef](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/1bcec211d9efa3e6f68dbf0cdf8826da1be94f7a).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Label changes</summary>

Label changes:

- add `P3`: Without an untrusted writer primitive, the documented trust model classifies the reported behavior as defense-in-depth rather than an urgent boundary bypass.
- add `impact:security`: The report concerns integrity of an operator approval before host command execution.
- add `issue-rating: 🦪 silver shellfish`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.
- add `clawsweeper:no-new-fix-pr`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.
- add `clawsweeper:needs-security-review`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.

Label justifications:

- `P3`: Without an untrusted writer primitive, the documented trust model classifies the reported behavior as defense-in-depth rather than an urgent boundary bypass.
- `impact:security`: The report concerns integrity of an operator approval before host command execution.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Evidence reviewed</summary>

Security concerns:

- [medium] Resolve the approval-integrity boundary — `extensions/codex/src/app-server/approval-bridge.ts:131`
  The bridge waits on a human approval and returns an accept response without carrying a direct file snapshot; determine whether an untrusted OpenClaw writer can exploit that gap before assigning vulnerability severity.
  Confidence: 0.86

What I checked:

- **Current Codex bridge:** The bridge waits for a plugin approval and returns an app-server accept/decline response, while explicitly stating it has no enforceable resolved executable; it records no mutable-file snapshot in this path. ([`extensions/codex/src/app-server/approval-bridge.ts:131`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/1bcec211d9ef/extensions/codex/src/app-server/approval-bridge.ts#L131), [1bcec211d9ef](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/1bcec211d9ef))
- **Approval request caller:** The active Codex run routes command-approval server requests directly into that bridge for the current thread and turn. external_evidence.title: Codex approval bridge executes mutated script: exec approvals are not operand-bound (approval TOCTOU)
external_evidence.description:
## Summary

The Codex app-server approval path executes the **mutated** script, not the approved one. An operator who reviews and approves one payload can have a different payload run.

Since `codex` is the default harness, every exec approval in a default configuration goes through this unbound path.

## Reproduction (verified live, 2026-08-16, `66dc9d1`)

1. Create `script.sh` that writes `BENIGN-ORIGINAL`.
2. Ask the agent to execute it; an approval goes pending with summary `Command: sh …/script.sh`.
3. While the approval is pending, rewrite `script.sh` to write `MUTATED-PAYLOAD-EXECUTED`.
4. Resolve the approval with `allow-once`.
5. Result file contains `MUTATED-PAYLOAD-EXECUTED`.

## Root cause

This is an owner-boundary gap, not a missing check in general — the correct defense already exists on the sibling path:

- `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.ts:880-893` revalidates `approvalPlan.mutableFileOperand` at use time and denies with `APPROVAL_SCRIPT_OPERAND_DRIFT_DENIED_MESSAGE`.
- `src/infra/system-run-approval-binding.ts` carries the sha256 file-operand snapshot.

`extensions/codex/src/app-server/approval-bridge.ts` has no `sha256`, `digest`, `mutableFileOperand`, or drift concept at all — its approvals are text-summary only. The binding machinery exists; this surface never populates or revalidates it.

This matches the repository invariant that delegated run authority is closure-bound rather than bearer-bound: a pending approval's summary text is correlation, not authorization, and privileged use must revalidate the authoritative operand at use time.

## Impact

An approval dialog that shows one command can execute different bytes. On multi-user or agent-driven workspaces, any writer to an operand path can substitute the payload during the approval window (default expiry 120s).

## Suggested fix

Populate and revalidate the existing `mutableFileOperand` binding in the codex approval bridge — reusing `src/infra/system-run-approval-binding.ts`, not a parallel implementation — and deny on drift with the existing message semantics. Fail closed when an operand cannot be snapshotted. Sibling approval surfaces should be audited in the same change.

Found during an end-to-end QA campaign (scenario APPR-131).

external_evidence.title: Exec approval revalidation is not atomic with runtime spawn
external_evidence.body:
## Context

PR #124858 bound exec approvals to a SHA-256 snapshot of their mutable operands and revalidates at the last OpenClaw-owned boundary before returning `allow`. That closed the reproduced TOCTOU (#124738): rewriting a script while its approval sits pending now fails closed with `SYSTEM_RUN_DENIED: approval script operand changed before execution`.

## The residual gap

OpenClaw does not spawn the process. Codex (and the other external runtimes) spawn only *after* we return `allow`, so revalidation and `execve` are not atomic. The window shrank from the entire approval wait — default 120s of operator think-time, trivially winnable — to the microseconds between our final check and the runtime's spawn. Small, but not zero, and not closable from inside OpenClaw as currently structured.

Accepted deliberately when #124858 landed; this issue exists so the gap has an owner rather than living only in a PR body.

## Possible directions

1. **Upstream digest enforcement.** The Codex app-server protocol carries command and cwd but no digest (`../codex/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/item.rs`), and decisions correlate only by approval ID (`core/src/session/mod.rs`). If the protocol carried an operand digest that the runtime verified at spawn, the check would move to the process that actually execs.
2. **OpenClaw-owned file descriptors.** Validate, hold the fd, and hand *that* to the runtime rather than a path. Removes the re-resolution entirely, at the cost of a substantially different execution handoff.

## Out of contract either way

Recursive shebang-interpreter and dynamic-dependency attestation: we bind the named executable/script operands, not everything they subsequently load.

external_evidence.title: Exec approval revalidation is not atomic with runtime spawn
external_evidence.description:
## Context

PR #124858 bound exec approvals to a SHA-256 snapshot of their mutable operands and revalidates at the last OpenClaw-owned boundary before returning `allow`. That closed the reproduced TOCTOU (#124738): rewriting a script while its approval sits pending now fails closed with `SYSTEM_RUN_DENIED: approval script operand changed before execution`.

## The residual gap

OpenClaw does not spawn the process. Codex (and the other external runtimes) spawn only *after* we return `allow`, so revalidation and `execve` are not atomic. The window shrank from the entire approval wait — default 120s of operator think-time, trivially winnable — to the microseconds between our final check and the runtime's spawn. Small, but not zero, and not closable from inside OpenClaw as currently structured.

Accepted deliberately when #124858 landed; this issue exists so the gap has an owner rather than living only in a PR body.

## Possible directions

1. **Upstream digest enforcement.** The Codex app-server protocol carries command and cwd but no digest (`../codex/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/item.rs`), and decisions correlate only by approval ID (`core/src/session/mod.rs`). If the protocol carried an operand digest that the runtime verified at spawn, the check would move to the process that actually execs.
2. **OpenClaw-owned file descriptors.** Validate, hold the fd, and hand *that* to the runtime rather than a path. Removes the re-resolution entirely, at the cost of a substantially different execution handoff.

## Out of contract either way

Recursive shebang-interpreter and dynamic-dependency attestation: we bind the named executable/script operands, not everything they subsequently load.

external_evidence.title: terminal tool bypasses exec policy and approvals on both runtimes
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

The `terminal` tool bypasses exec policy entirely, on both the embedded and Codex runtimes. With exec denied, the agent opened a shell on the gateway host and reported success.

## Reproduction (verified live, 2026-08-16)

1. Configure `tools.exec.mode: "deny"` (global — verified honored for the exec tool itself).
2. Ask the agent to run a command.
3. The agent invokes `openclaw:core:terminal`, receives a `/bin/zsh` on the gateway host without any approval prompt, runs the command, and reports a confident `SAFE`.

## Root cause

`terminal-tool.ts:167-337` gates only on: terminal-enabled, launch policy, and task status. It never consults exec security or the approvals system. The launch policy itself checks only `sandbox.mode === "all"`.

So the operator-facing exec policy — the surface documented and understood as "what commands may this agent run" — governs one tool and not its sibling that provides equivalent capability.

## Why this matters

An operator who sets `tools.exec.mode: "deny"` reasonably believes shell execution is off for that agent. It isn't. The model does not need to do anything adversarial to reach it; it routed there on its own when the exec tool refused, and then reported success. That combination — capability reachable through an ungated sibling, plus a confident success message — is the failure shape this repo treats as worst-class.

## Not a harness divergence

Both runtimes behave identically here, so this is a product gap rather than an instance of the embedded-vs-Codex conformance problem tracked elsewhere.

## Suggested direction

Route terminal launches through the same policy owner as exec (security mode + approvals), so a denied exec policy denies terminal capability, and an `ask` policy prompts. Sandbox mode should remain an additional constraint, not the only one.

Found during an end-to-end QA campaign (scenario harness-173 sibling probe).

One concrete way to make the maintainer decision falsifiable is to model the interactive PTY as a **separate host-execution capability**, not as an implementation detail of `exec`.

We're building a provider-neutral evidence contract in [AgentCI](https://github.com/jinngimk-lang/agentci), and this issue is a good example of the failure class we call an **alternate authority channel**: one operator-facing capability is denied, but a sibling path reaches equivalent authority.

For this issue specifically, I'd suggest pinning the repair with a small matrix rather than only a code-path assertion:

| exec policy | agent terminal authority | expected |
|---|---|---|
| deny | none | terminal open denied before PTY creation |
| ask | no approval | no PTY / no shell process |
| ask | bounded approval for session X | only session X may open; grant has explicit subject + host resource + expiry/revocation |
| allow | explicit agent-terminal capability | PTY may open, with provenance tying the open to the decision |
| deny | administrator/operator terminal | preserve the separately-authorized admin path; do not union it into agent authority |

Two regressions seem especially worth keeping permanently:

1. **Sibling substitution:** make `exec` deny, then let the agent choose any other registered tool capable of host command execution. No sibling should turn deny into success.
2. **Approval lifetime/replay:** obtain one bounded PTY approval, close/revoke/expire it, then attempt a second open or later input under the old decision. It must not inherit indefinite shell authority.

Evidence-wise, I'd also keep `requested principal / action / resource / context -> decision -> PTY-open receipt` distinct. A successful command outcome is behavioral evidence; it should not itself prove that the authority decision was valid.

This is not a claim that AgentCI currently certifies OpenClaw or either runtime; I'm linking it only because the contract/tests may be reusable for this exact authority-confusion class. The current AgentCI 0.2 launch/context is here: https://github.com/jinngimk-lang/agentci/issues/118

Fixed on `main` in #129604 ([merge commit](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3626a8e18e2c18708398d166565927ea4b29a596)).

The implemented behavior is:

- Terminal creation is operator-owned through the Control UI; the agent-facing terminal tool no longer has an `open` action and cannot spawn its own shell.
- Agents can `list`, `read`, `resize`, and `close` only an operator-opened terminal belonging to their exact admitted session and terminal incarnation.
- Full/YOLO sessions can send terminal input immediately without an approval prompt, but only while the exact admitted run and Gateway owner remain active.
- Guarded/Guardian, Workspace/accept-only, and allowlist execution require a fresh explicit operator `allow-once` decision for every individual input; the approval displays the exact escaped input bytes and never offers `allow-always`.
- Read-only sessions and denied execution policy cannot write.
- Every permitted write, including Full mode, passes the same final synchronous live-run, receipt-authority, Gateway-instance, and terminal-owner check immediately before PTY I/O. Missing, released, replaced, canceled, or aborted runs; stale sessions; unavailable approval delivery; and denied approvals all fail closed without writing.
- Effective session and execution permissions now propagate through CLI/MCP grants and partition Gateway tool reuse; obsolete agent-created-terminal and task-terminal ownership paths were removed.

Verified with the complete application/Control UI build, 61 external plugin builds, 754 validated UI sidecars, 598 focused owner/sibling tests plus the final stale-run regressions, the complete repository security/type/lint/architecture gate, clean exact-head hosted CI, and an isolated real Gateway with five native shell PTYs, four real approval events, and 28 passing live security checks.

Route terminal launches through the same policy owner as exec (security mode + approvals), so a denied exec policy denies terminal capability, and an `ask` policy prompts. Sandbox mode should remain an additional constraint, not the only one.

One concrete way to make the maintainer decision falsifiable is to model the interactive PTY as a **separate host-execution capability**, not as an implementation detail of `exec`.

We're building a provider-neutral evidence contract in [AgentCI](https://github.com/jinngimk-lang/agentci), and this issue is a good example of the failure class we call an **alternate authority channel**: one operator-facing capability is denied, but a sibling path reaches equivalent authority.

For this issue specifically, I'd suggest pinning the repair with a small matrix rather than only a code-path assertion:

| exec policy | agent terminal authority | expected |
|---|---|---|
| deny | none | terminal open denied before PTY creation |
| ask | no approval | no PTY / no shell process |
| ask | bounded approval for session X | only session X may open; grant has explicit subject + host resource + expiry/revocation |
| allow | explicit agent-terminal capability | PTY may open, with provenance tying the open to the decision |
| deny | administrator/operator terminal | preserve the separately-authorized admin path; do not union it into agent authority |

Two regressions seem especially worth keeping permanently:

1. **Sibling substitution:** make `exec` deny, then let the agent choose any other registered tool capable of host command execution. No sibling should turn deny into success.
2. **Approval lifetime/replay:** obtain one bounded PTY approval, close/revoke/expire it, then attempt a second open or later input under the old decision. It must not inherit indefinite shell authority.

Evidence-wise, I'd also keep `requested principal / action / resource / context -> decision -> PTY-open receipt` distinct. A successful command outcome is behavioral evidence; it should not itself prove that the authority decision was valid.

This is not a claim that AgentCI currently certifies OpenClaw or either runtime; I'm linking it only because the contract/tests may be reusable for this exact authority-confusion class. The current AgentCI 0.2 launch/context is here: https://github.com/jinngimk-lang/agentci/issues/118

Fixed on `main` in #129604 ([merge commit](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3626a8e18e2c18708398d166565927ea4b29a596)).

The implemented behavior is:

- Terminal creation is operator-owned through the Control UI; the agent-facing terminal tool no longer has an `open` action and cannot spawn its own shell.
- Agents can `list`, `read`, `resize`, and `close` only an operator-opened terminal belonging to their exact admitted session and terminal incarnation.
- Full/YOLO sessions can send terminal input immediately without an approval prompt, but only while the exact admitted run and Gateway owner remain active.
- Guarded/Guardian, Workspace/accept-only, and allowlist execution require a fresh explicit operator `allow-once` decision for every individual input; the approval displays the exact escaped input bytes and never offers `allow-always`.
- Read-only sessions and denied execution policy cannot write.
- Every permitted write, including Full mode, passes the same final synchronous live-run, receipt-authority, Gateway-instance, and terminal-owner check immediately before PTY I/O. Missing, released, replaced, canceled, or aborted runs; stale sessions; unavailable approval delivery; and denied approvals all fail closed without writing.
- Effective session and execution permissions now propagate through CLI/MCP grants and partition Gateway tool reuse; obsolete agent-created-terminal and task-terminal ownership paths were removed.

Verified with the complete application/Control UI build, 61 external plugin builds, 754 validated UI sidecars, 598 focused owner/sibling tests plus the final stale-run regressions, the complete repository security/type/lint/architecture gate, clean exact-head hosted CI, and an isolated real Gateway with five native shell PTYs, four real approval events, and 28 passing live security checks.

external_evidence.title: [Security][Third-Party] skill-flow: Function Constructor Template RCE
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Community NPM Packages
**Category**: third-party-risk
**Priority**: Critical

## Summary

The Skill-Flow template engine's `interpolate()` function uses the JavaScript `Function` constructor to dynamically evaluate user-controlled template expressions. An attacker who can influence template content (via prompt injection or direct skill authoring) can execute arbitrary Node.js code on the host system. This grants full access to `process.env` (all credentials), filesystem operations, and network capabilities. CVSS 10.0 — unauthenticated remote code execution.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 10.0 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` |
| **CWE** | CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code |
| **STRIDE** | Tampering, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege |
| **Priority** | P0 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Community NPM Packages runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

| Step | File | Function/Line | Description |
|------|------|--------------|-------------|
| 1 | `skill-flow/src/interpolate.ts` | Line 42 | Function constructor dynamically executes user-supplied template expression strings |
| 2 | `skill-flow/src/interpolate.ts` | Line 58 | Template variables passed directly into Function constructor execution context without sandboxing |


## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `skill-flow/src/interpolate.ts` | 42 | Function constructor dynamically executes user-supplied template expression strings |
| `skill-flow/src/interpolate.ts` | 58 | Template variables passed directly into Function constructor execution context without sandboxing |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: The `interpolate()` function in Skill-Flow engine uses the JavaScript `Function` constructor to evaluate user-controlled template expressions without sandboxing.
**Underlying Cause**: No safe template evaluation alternative is provided. Template variables are passed directly into the Function constructor's execution context.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Host operating system, all plugins
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Full system access, all credentials, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-002, ECO-009, ECO-012, CSD-001

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Add input validation and sanitization
- Implement parameterized queries/commands
- Escape special characters in user input

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) headers
- Implement output encoding for all user-facing content
- Add prompt injection detection layer

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Implement instruction-data separation architecture
- Deploy defense-in-depth with multiple validation layers
- Add behavioral monitoring for anomalous patterns

Thanks for the report.

External dependency risks are managed via Dependabot and GitHub Security advisories. We currently do not have an active advisory for this package in this repository, and this report appears to be either previously resolved or focused on a third-party package that is not part of this repo’s maintained code.

Please review SECURITY.md and report concerns through the appropriate security channels:
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/SECURITY.md

external_evidence.title: [Security] Coding Agent Skill: Unsandboxed RCE via --yolo Flag
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Bundled Skills
**Category**: security
**Priority**: Critical

## Summary

The `coding-agent` bundled skill supports a `--yolo` flag that disables all execution confirmation prompts, enabling unsandboxed command execution. When combined with prompt injection, an attacker can cause the AI agent to invoke the coding agent with `--yolo`, executing arbitrary system commands without user confirmation. No audit logging captures executed commands.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 9.8 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` |
| **CWE** | CWE-250: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges |
| **STRIDE** | Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege, Repudiation, Spoofing |
| **Priority** | P0 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Bundled Skills runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

```
  Attacker embeds malicious instructions in user input
  AI Agent processes input and is influenced by injected instructions
  Agent invokes the coding_agent tool
  Coding agent launches in --yolo mode (no confirmation required)
  Arbitrary system commands are executed
```

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

See entry points and detailed analysis for affected files.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: The `--yolo` flag in the coding agent skill disables all sandboxing and user confirmation prompts.
**Underlying Cause**: SKILL.md recommends using `--yolo` for efficiency, and no audit logging captures commands executed through this mode.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Host operating system, all plugins
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Full system access, all credentials, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-010, ECO-005, CSD-001, CSD-008

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Disable `--yolo` flag by default
- Add input sanitization on all user-controlled parameters
- Block shell metacharacters in command arguments

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Implement command allowlisting for subprocess execution
- Add sandboxed execution environment for user-triggered code
- Implement mandatory confirmation for destructive operations

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Deploy process-level isolation (bubblewrap/gVisor) per plugin
- Implement capability-based security model
- Add comprehensive audit logging for all command execution

@steipete 

Good plan. Security shouldn't wait.

**Quick wins:**
- Disable `--yolo` by default
- Validate all user inputs
- Block shell metacharacters

**Architecture:**
- Process-level isolation (bubblewrap/gVisor)

external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Community NPM Packages
**Category**: third-party-risk
**Priority**: Critical

## Summary

The `sandbox:/` URL handler lacks path normalization, allowing `../` path traversal sequences to escape the sandbox directory and access arbitrary files on the filesystem. An attacker can read sensitive files including SSH keys, wallet credentials, and configuration files containing secrets.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 9.3 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory |
| **STRIDE** | Tampering, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service |
| **Priority** | P0 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Community NPM Packages runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

| Step | File | Function/Line | Description |
|------|------|--------------|-------------|
| 1 | `clawd/sandbox.js` | Line 32 | handleSandboxUrl function concatenates user-supplied paths without calling path.resolve for normalization |
| 2 | `clawd/sandbox.js` | Line 48 | File read operations do not verify final path stays within sandbox directory bounds |


## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `clawd/sandbox.js` | 32 | handleSandboxUrl function concatenates user-supplied paths without calling path.resolve for normalization |
| `clawd/sandbox.js` | 48 | File read operations do not verify final path stays within sandbox directory bounds |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: The `sandbox:/` URL handler directly concatenates user-supplied path components without calling `path.resolve()` or validating the final path stays within the sandbox directory.
**Underlying Cause**: Path normalization and sandbox boundary verification are completely absent.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Community NPM Packages
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-001, ECO-012

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Add input validation and sanitization
- Implement parameterized queries/commands
- Escape special characters in user input

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) headers
- Implement output encoding for all user-facing content
- Add prompt injection detection layer

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Implement instruction-data separation architecture
- Deploy defense-in-depth with multiple validation layers
- Add behavioral monitoring for anomalous patterns

### Mitigation note: Docker sandbox filesystem isolation

For deployments using Docker sandbox mode, this path traversal vulnerability has negligible impact because the `sandbox:/` URL handler operates within the container's filesystem namespace, not the host's.

**Why container isolation neutralizes this:**
- `../` traversal can only reach files within the container's own filesystem
- The container has a read-only root filesystem — no host-sensitive files (`~/.ssh/`, wallet credentials, `/etc/shadow`) are present
- The sandbox container mounts only the agent's workspace directory (at the configured `workdir`), not the host home directory or the config directory containing tokens/API keys
- Even if traversal escapes the workspace mount, the agent reaches base image OS files, not user secrets
- No extra bind mounts are added unless explicitly configured via the `docker.binds` sandbox option

The application-layer bug in `clawd/sandbox.js` (missing `path.resolve()` and boundary check) still exists and should be fixed — defense in depth matters. But for deployments already running Docker sandbox mode, the CVSS 9.3 score reflects a host-execution scenario that doesn't apply when the container's filesystem namespace prevents access to host-sensitive paths.

---
*Analysis assisted by Claude.*

Thanks for the report.

Closing as out-of-scope for `openclaw/openclaw`: this issue references `clawd/sandbox.js`, which is not part of this repository, and the report does not include a reproducible PoC against code in this repo.

Per our security policy, please report vulnerabilities to the repository where the affected code lives, or use the channels listed in `SECURITY.md`:
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/SECURITY.md

If you believe this is incorrect, please reply with a minimal repro against this repository and we can reopen.

**What's happening:** sandbox:/ URL handler resolves paths with ../ sequences without canonicalizing or validating that the resolved path remains within the sandbox root directory

**What worked for us:**

Resolve the requested path to its canonical absolute form (e.g. path.resolve), then verify it starts with the sandbox root prefix. Reject any path that escapes the sandbox boundary. Do NOT rely on container isolation as a fix — that is defense-in-depth, not remediation.

```typescript
const path = require('path');

function safeSandboxPath(sandboxRoot, requestedPath) {
  const resolved = path.resolve(sandboxRoot, requestedPath);
  const normalizedRoot = path.resolve(sandboxRoot) + path.sep;
  if (resolved !== path.resolve(sandboxRoot) && !resolved.startsWith(normalizedRoot)) {
    throw new Error('Path traversal blocked: ' + requestedPath);
  }
  return resolved;
}
```

Hope this helps! Let me know if it doesn't match your case — happy to dig deeper. 🦞

external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
**Category**: security
**Priority**: Critical

## Summary

The memory system has a complete injection chain: (1) auto-capture via `agent_end` hook stores conversation content without filtering, (2) `memory_store` tool allows direct memory insertion, (3) `before_agent_start` hook retrieves memories and injects into `<relevant-memories>`, (4) no sanitization separates instructions from data. This enables persistent prompt injection surviving across conversations.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 9.1 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:L` |
| **CWE** | CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code |
| **STRIDE** | Tampering |
| **Priority** | P0 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

`P-400`, `P-401`, `P-402`, `DS-002`, `DF-002` (Trust Boundary: `TB-002`)

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `memory/memory-lancedb/index.ts` | - | See detailed analysis |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: No instruction-data separation in the memory system. Content stored as memories is later injected as part of the agent's context without sanitization or classification.
**Underlying Cause**: The auto-capture hook (`agent_end`) stores all conversation content without distinguishing between data and instructions.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-008, ECO-019, CSD-008

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Disable `--yolo` flag by default
- Add input sanitization on all user-controlled parameters
- Block shell metacharacters in command arguments

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Implement command allowlisting for subprocess execution
- Add sandboxed execution environment for user-triggered code
- Implement mandatory confirmation for destructive operations

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Deploy process-level isolation (bubblewrap/gVisor) per plugin
- Implement capability-based security model
- Add comprehensive audit logging for all command execution

Thanks for reporting this. Revalidated on current `main` and landed hardening for the memory-lancedb path.

Merged:
- `61725fb37` `fix (memory/lancedb): harden memory recall and auto-capture`
- `3ca74f8e6` `chore (changelog): note memory-lancedb injection hardening`

What changed:
- Treat recalled memories as untrusted context when injected (explicit non-instruction framing).
- Escape recalled memory text before prompt injection so memory payloads cannot break context markup.
- Skip likely prompt-injection payloads during auto-capture.
- Restrict auto-capture to `user` messages (avoid model self-poisoning via assistant output).
- Added regression coverage in `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts`.

Validation run:
- `pnpm vitest extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts`

Closing as fixed on `main`.

external_evidence.title: [Security][Third-Party] x402_pay: SSRF Internal Network Scanning
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Community NPM Packages
**Category**: third-party-risk
**Priority**: Critical

## Summary

The x402_pay tool accepts arbitrary URL parameters which can be exploited to perform Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks. An attacker can scan internal network resources and access cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., 169.254.169.254) through the payment request mechanism.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 9.0 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery |
| **STRIDE** | Elevation of Privilege |
| **Priority** | P0 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Community NPM Packages runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

| Step | File | Function/Line | Description |
|------|------|--------------|-------------|
| 1 | `clawdbot/packages/x402/src/x402_pay.ts` | Line 28 | pay function URL parameter lacks protocol allowlist and internal network address filtering |
| 2 | `clawdbot/packages/x402/src/x402_pay.ts` | Line 35 | HTTP requests have no proxy or DNS resolution restrictions; can access metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254 |


## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `clawdbot/packages/x402/src/x402_pay.ts` | 28 | pay function URL parameter lacks protocol allowlist and internal network address filtering |
| `clawdbot/packages/x402/src/x402_pay.ts` | 35 | HTTP requests have no proxy or DNS resolution restrictions; can access metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254 |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: The `x402_pay` URL parameter has no protocol whitelist and no internal network address filtering.
**Underlying Cause**: HTTP requests can target any address including RFC 1918 ranges and cloud metadata endpoints.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Community NPM Packages
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-007, ECO-009

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Add input validation and sanitization
- Implement parameterized queries/commands
- Escape special characters in user input

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) headers
- Implement output encoding for all user-facing content
- Add prompt injection detection layer

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Implement instruction-data separation architecture
- Deploy defense-in-depth with multiple validation layers
- Add behavioral monitoring for anomalous patterns
Closing as duplicate of #12520. If this is incorrect, please contact us.

external_evidence.title: [Security] Nostr Channel: Unauthenticated Config Modification Leading to System Takeover
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

The Nostr plugin exposes an HTTP handler that calls `runtime.config.writeConfigFile()` without any authentication. This allows unauthenticated remote callers to modify the configuration of ALL 31 plugins — injecting attacker-controlled OAuth credentials, redirecting API endpoints, and enabling/disabling plugins at will. CVSS 10.0.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 8.5 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:L` |
| **CWE** | CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function |
| **STRIDE** | Tampering, Elevation of Privilege |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

`DS-001`, `DF-011` (Trust Boundary: `TB-001`)

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `channels/nostr/src/nostr-relay.ts` | - | See detailed analysis |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: Missing authentication on an administrative HTTP endpoint. The Nostr HTTP handler was designed for local relay configuration but exposed to the network without access control.
**Underlying Cause**: The endpoint calls `runtime.config.writeConfigFile()` which modifies configuration for ALL plugins.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component

- Set restrictive file permissions on config files

### Medium-term (Sprint)

- Add credential rotation automation

- Implement per-plugin credential isolation
- Deploy hardware security modules for key management

@steipete 

#12533 was fixed — thank you. 

This one (#12534) is still open. Same severity: unauthenticated config modification leading to full system takeover.

CVSS 8.5, P1 priority. Should be fixed together with the other security issues from February.

Related: #12515, #12517, #12518, #12539, #12540, #12543.

Closing this as implemented after Codex review.

Current main already protects the Nostr profile mutation surface behind gateway auth, trusted-operator runtime scope, explicit `operator.admin` checks, and loopback-only mutation guards. The changelog records this exact security issue as fixed in release `v2026.2.12`.

What I checked:

- **Nostr route is not unauthenticated:** The Nostr profile HTTP route is registered with `auth: "gateway"` and `gatewayRuntimeScopeSurface: "trusted-operator"`, so it is not exposed as a plugin-managed public endpoint. ([`extensions/nostr/index.ts:86`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/extensions/nostr/index.ts#L86), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Mutation handlers require admin scope and loopback-only access:** Before any profile update/import path can reach the config write path, the handler rejects callers missing `operator.admin`, rejects non-loopback remote addresses, rejects forwarded non-loopback client IPs, and rejects cross-site Origin/Referer requests. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.ts:267`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.ts#L267), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Gateway blocks protected plugin routes without auth:** Gateway dispatch fails closed when a matched plugin route requires gateway auth and the request is unauthenticated, before invoking the plugin handler at all. ([`src/gateway/server/plugins-http.ts:85`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/src/gateway/server/plugins-http.ts#L85), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Regression tests cover unauthenticated and remote mutation attempts:** Nostr tests explicitly reject non-loopback mutation requests and reject callers missing `operator.admin` for both PUT `/profile` and POST `/profile/import`. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.test.ts:351`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.test.ts#L351), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Gateway auth coverage includes the Nostr profile path:** Gateway auth tests verify `/api/channels/nostr/default/profile` returns unauthorized without bearer auth and only passes through when authenticated. ([`src/gateway/server.plugin-http-auth.test.ts:230`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/src/gateway/server.plugin-http-auth.test.ts#L230), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Release notes record this exact fix:** The `v2026.2.12` changelog includes: `Security: fix unauthenticated Nostr profile API remote config tampering. (#13719)`. (`CHANGELOG.md:5039`)

So I’m closing this as already implemented rather than keeping a duplicate issue open.

Review notes: reviewed against [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e295e9bb1f55cbfb38861ea9413e45); fix evidence: release [v2026.2.12](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/releases/tag/v2026.2.12).

Current main already protects the Nostr profile mutation surface behind gateway auth, trusted-operator runtime scope, explicit `operator.admin` checks, and loopback-only mutation guards. The changelog records this exact security issue as fixed in release `v2026.2.12`.

What I checked:

- **Nostr route is not unauthenticated:** The Nostr profile HTTP route is registered with `auth: "gateway"` and `gatewayRuntimeScopeSurface: "trusted-operator"`, so it is not exposed as a plugin-managed public endpoint. ([`extensions/nostr/index.ts:86`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/extensions/nostr/index.ts#L86), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Mutation handlers require admin scope and loopback-only access:** Before any profile update/import path can reach the config write path, the handler rejects callers missing `operator.admin`, rejects non-loopback remote addresses, rejects forwarded non-loopback client IPs, and rejects cross-site Origin/Referer requests. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.ts:267`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.ts#L267), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Gateway blocks protected plugin routes without auth:** Gateway dispatch fails closed when a matched plugin route requires gateway auth and the request is unauthenticated, before invoking the plugin handler at all. ([`src/gateway/server/plugins-http.ts:85`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/src/gateway/server/plugins-http.ts#L85), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Regression tests cover unauthenticated and remote mutation attempts:** Nostr tests explicitly reject non-loopback mutation requests and reject callers missing `operator.admin` for both PUT `/profile` and POST `/profile/import`. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.test.ts:351`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-profile-http.test.ts#L351), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))

external_evidence.title: [Security] Skill Loader: .skill Package Zip Slip and Supply Chain Attack
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Bundled Skills
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

The `package_skill.py` script uses `rglob()` which follows symbolic links, allowing sensitive files (e.g., `/etc/passwd`, `~/.ssh/id_rsa`) to be included in `.skill` packages. Additionally, a malicious SKILL.md within a `.skill` package can inject arbitrary agent instructions on installation.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 7.7 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-426: Untrusted Search Path |
| **STRIDE** | Elevation of Privilege, Tampering |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Bundled Skills runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

```
  Create symbolic link in skill directory pointing to /etc/passwd
  Run package_skill.py to package the skill
  rglob() follows symbolic links
  Sensitive files are included in the .skill package
```

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

See entry points and detailed analysis for affected files.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: The `package_skill.py` script uses `rglob()` which follows symlinks without restriction. No path validation prevents inclusion of files outside the skill directory.
**Underlying Cause**: The packaging tool was designed for convenience without considering adversarial input.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Bundled Skills
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-003, CSD-001, CSD-003

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Pin all dependency versions
- Audit existing dependencies for known vulnerabilities
- Disable postinstall scripts from untrusted packages

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Implement SCA scanning in CI/CD
- Deploy package integrity verification (checksums/signatures)
- Add dependency allowlisting

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Implement code signing for all artifacts
- Deploy SBOM generation and monitoring
- Establish vendor security assessment program
Fix in #16959 — adds symlink detection and path traversal checks in the skill packager. Prevents zip slip via directory traversal and symlink-based escapes.

external_evidence.title: [Security] Google-Maps Skill: SSRF via place_id URL Path Manipulation
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Bundled Skills
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

The Places API proxy constructs URLs using user-supplied `place_id` values without path normalization. Path traversal characters in the `place_id` can redirect the upstream HTTP request to different API endpoints, potentially triggering unintended operations or accessing restricted resources.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 7.5 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery |
| **STRIDE** | Tampering |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Bundled Skills runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

```
  Craft a place_id containing path traversal sequences
  Send GET /places/{malicious_place_id} request
  Server constructs URL: {base_url}/places/{malicious_id}
  httpx request is sent to the manipulated URL
```

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

See entry points and detailed analysis for affected files.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: URL path construction using user-supplied `place_id` without path normalization or input validation.
**Underlying Cause**: The Places API proxy trusts the format of incoming place_id parameters.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Bundled Skills
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-026

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Add input validation and sanitization
- Implement parameterized queries/commands
- Escape special characters in user input

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) headers
- Implement output encoding for all user-facing content
- Add prompt injection detection layer

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Implement instruction-data separation architecture
- Deploy defense-in-depth with multiple validation layers
- Add behavioral monitoring for anomalous patterns
Closing as duplicate of #9007. If this is incorrect, please contact us.

external_evidence.title: [Security] HTML-Gallery Skill: Stored XSS in Image Gallery
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Bundled Skills
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

The image generation tool's `write_gallery()` function embeds user-provided prompt text directly into HTML output without escaping. An attacker can include `<script>` tags in image prompts, resulting in stored XSS that executes when any user opens the generated gallery HTML file.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 7.5 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation |
| **STRIDE** | Tampering |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Bundled Skills runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

```
  Provide prompt text containing HTML/JavaScript
  gen.py calls OpenAI API to generate image
  write_gallery() embeds unescaped prompt into HTML
  Victim opens gallery.html
  Browser executes the injected JavaScript
```

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

See entry points and detailed analysis for affected files.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: The `write_gallery()` function embeds user-provided prompt text into HTML without calling `html.escape()`.
**Underlying Cause**: Output encoding was not applied to user-controlled content in HTML generation.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Bundled Skills
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

> Omitted

> Omitted

> Omitted

### Short-term (Immediate)

- Escape special characters in user input

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) headers

- Add behavioral monitoring for anomalous patterns

external_evidence.title: [Security] Bundled Skills: Unauthenticated API Access Enabling Quota Exhaustion
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Bundled Skills
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

The Places API server binds to 0.0.0.0 on port 8000 without any authentication requirement. All four API endpoints accept unauthenticated requests. An attacker can send concurrent requests to exhaust the Google Places API quota, causing denial of service for legitimate users.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 7.5 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` |
| **CWE** | CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function |
| **STRIDE** | Denial of Service, Repudiation, Spoofing |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Verified |

## Entry Points

Via Bundled Skills runtime

## Data Flow Analysis

```
  Discover target API (port 8000, bound to 0.0.0.0)
  Send large volume of concurrent search requests
  Exhaust Google Places API quota
  Legitimate users are denied service
```

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

See entry points and detailed analysis for affected files.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: No authentication requirement and no rate limiting on the Places API server. Server binds to 0.0.0.0 exposing all endpoints to the network.
**Underlying Cause**: The API was designed for local development use but deployed without network-appropriate security controls.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Bundled Skills
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-023, ECO-030

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Add authentication to all exposed endpoints
- Implement webhook signature verification
- Add rate limiting on authentication endpoints

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Deploy RBAC with least-privilege principle
- Implement multi-factor authentication
- Add constant-time token comparison

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Migrate to OAuth 2.0/OIDC with PKCE
- Implement API gateway with centralized auth
- Deploy mutual TLS for service-to-service auth

Closing this as implemented after Codex review.

Current main does not ship the reported unauthenticated Google Places API server. Bundled skills are instruction-only `SKILL.md` entries, and the only Google Places bundled skill is the external-CLI-based `goplaces` skill; the older `local-places` skill/proxy is no longer present.

What I checked:

- **Bundled skills are loaded from `SKILL.md` files:** The bundled skills resolver only looks for a `skills/` directory containing markdown skill files or subdirectories with `SKILL.md`; it does not wire up a bundled HTTP service. ([`src/agents/skills/bundled-dir.ts:6`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/src/agents/skills/bundled-dir.ts#L6), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Skill loading reads `SKILL.md` metadata/instructions:** `loadSingleSkillDirectory` reads `SKILL.md`, parses frontmatter, and returns a `Skill` record with name/description/file paths. Current bundled skill loading is file-based, not a server runtime. ([`src/agents/skills/local-loader.ts:44`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/src/agents/skills/local-loader.ts#L44), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Docs describe bundled skills as AgentSkills folders:** The skills docs say each bundled skill is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` with frontmatter and instructions, and describe load-time filtering via metadata. Public docs: [`docs/tools/skills.md`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/skills). ([`docs/tools/skills.md:9`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/skills), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Current Google Places bundle is CLI-based only:** The only Google Places bundled skill is [`skills/goplaces/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/skills/goplaces/SKILL.md), which requires an external `goplaces` binary and `GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY`. Its instructions show CLI commands only; there is no host/port/auth server configuration. ([`skills/goplaces/SKILL.md:1`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/skills/goplaces/SKILL.md#L1), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **`local-places` is gone on current main:** A tree scan of `HEAD` for Google Places skill names returns only [`skills/goplaces/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/skills/goplaces/SKILL.md); there is no `local-places` path in the current checkout. ([3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Changelog records removal of the old proxy path:** The changelog explicitly says: remove duplicate `local-places` Google Places skill/proxy and keep `goplaces` as the single supported Google Places path. ([`CHANGELOG.md:4985`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/CHANGELOG.md#L4985), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))

So I’m closing this as already implemented rather than keeping a duplicate issue open.

Review notes: reviewed against [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e295e9bb1f55cbfb38861ea9413e45).

external_evidence.title: [Security] Google Auth Extensions: Hardcoded OAuth Credentials in Source Code
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

OAuth CLIENT_SECRET values are hardcoded in source code (google-antigravity, google-gemini-cli-auth). The gemini-cli-auth plugin explicitly parses another tool's source code to extract CLIENT_ID and CLIENT_SECRET via regex, creating a cross-dependency credential extraction pattern.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 7.5 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials |
| **STRIDE** | Spoofing |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Theoretical |

## Entry Points

`P-100`, `EI-022`, `DS-010`

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `auth/google-antigravity/src/index.ts` | - | See detailed analysis |
| `auth/google-gemini-cli-auth/src/index.ts` | - | See detailed analysis |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: OAuth credentials embedded in source code rather than using secure credential management.
**Underlying Cause**: CLIENT_SECRET values are hardcoded as string literals and extractable from published packages.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Host operating system, all plugins
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Full system access, all credentials, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-025, ECO-046

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Disable `--yolo` flag by default
- Add input sanitization on all user-controlled parameters
- Block shell metacharacters in command arguments

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Implement command allowlisting for subprocess execution
- Add sandboxed execution environment for user-triggered code
- Implement mandatory confirmation for destructive operations

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Deploy process-level isolation (bubblewrap/gVisor) per plugin
- Implement capability-based security model
- Add comprehensive audit logging for all command execution

@steipete 

#12549 was fixed — thank you.

This one (#12543) is still open: hardcoded OAuth secrets in source code (CVSS 7.5). 

Along with #12515, #12517, #12518, #12534, #12539, #12540 — all security issues from February. Most are still open.

These should be prioritized together.

Closing this as implemented after Codex review.

The reported hardcoded Google OAuth secret issue is no longer present on current `main`, and the latest shipped tag already uses an externalized Google OAuth flow instead of embedding Google OAuth client secrets in OpenClaw source. The specific bundled plugins named in the report are also no longer shipped.

What I checked:

- **Reported plugin IDs are retired:** Current config treats `google-antigravity-auth` and `google-gemini-cli-auth` as legacy removed plugin IDs, which matches the report's cited components no longer being shipped. ([`src/config/validation.ts:43`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/src/config/validation.ts#L43), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Current Google OAuth flow does not embed a client secret:** `resolveOAuthClientConfig()` first reads `OPENCLAW_GEMINI_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` / `_SECRET` (or `GEMINI_CLI_*`) from env, then falls back to extracting the locally installed Gemini CLI credentials; there is no hardcoded Google OAuth client secret literal in OpenClaw production code here. ([`extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts:258`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3361593442e2/extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts#L258), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Docs describe external credential sources:** User-facing docs for the shipped Google OAuth flow require a local `gemini` install and document env vars for the OAuth client id/secret rather than any bundled OpenClaw secret. Public docs: [`docs/providers/google.md`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/providers/google). ([`docs/providers/google.md:65`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/providers/google), [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **No non-test hardcoded Google OAuth literals in current Google plugin:** A production-code search under `extensions/google` found no `GOCSPX-...` or `.apps.googleusercontent.com` literals outside tests; the only remaining matches are test fixtures and regex parsing helpers. ([3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e2))
- **Latest shipped release already contains the non-hardcoded implementation:** Release tag `v2026.4.22` (`00bd2cf7a376f1fba26291c6c4766f1f15cbdfa5`) contains the same [`extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/00bd2cf7a376/extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts) implementation that sources credentials from env or the installed Gemini CLI rather than embedding them in OpenClaw source. ([`extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts:258`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/00bd2cf7a376/extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts#L258), [00bd2cf7a376](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/00bd2cf7a376))

So I’m closing this as already implemented rather than keeping a duplicate issue open.

Review notes: reviewed against [3361593442e2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3361593442e295e9bb1f55cbfb38861ea9413e45); fix evidence: commit [00bd2cf7a376](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/00bd2cf7a376f1fba26291c6c4766f1f15cbdfa5).

([`extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts:258`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/00bd2cf7a376/extensions/google/oauth.credentials.ts#L258), [00bd2cf7a376](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/00bd2cf7a376))
