external_evidence.title: [Security] Nostr Channel: Private Key Stored in Plaintext
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

The Nostr private key is stored as plaintext in the state file. While file permissions are set to 0o600, no encryption is applied. The private key is accessible to any code running in the shared process.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 7.5 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-312: Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information |
| **STRIDE** | Information Disclosure |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Theoretical |

## Entry Points

`DS-004`

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `channels/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts` | - | See detailed analysis |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: Nostr private key stored as plaintext in state file with only filesystem permissions (0o600) as protection.
**Underlying Cause**: No encryption layer applied to cryptographic key material at rest.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-012, ECO-025

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Rotate all exposed credentials immediately
- Remove hardcoded credentials from source code
- Set restrictive file permissions on config files

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Implement encrypted credential storage (KMS/Vault)
- Deploy secret scanning in CI/CD pipeline
- Add credential rotation automation

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Migrate to zero-trust secret management architecture
- Implement per-plugin credential isolation
- Deploy hardware security modules for key management

On long term plans.  HSMs are prohibitively expensive for most client applications.  I think what may be meant here is a hardware based cryptographic module or cryptographic hardware token. 

Whatever protects keys (software vs hardware) just ensure it is FIPS 140 validated by a NIST accredited lab at a minimum of Security Level 1 (basic security) which would be suitable for low impact keys, certainly better than sitting one a file system in plaintext, and is the more inexpensive of the FIPs validated options.  Security level 2 requires tamper evidence and steps up the security a notch where hardware starts getting introduced.   FIPS 140 security level 2 seems right for something like this.   Just search for any solution markets itself as validated by NIST FIPs 140. 

Building support for a user-supplied compatible smart card (PIV?) USB, Micro-USB, might do the trick.  

Short of that, a software implementation of an Openclaw-specific key ring or trust store that functions independently of any OS or browser trust store would help isolate Openclaw from the system from impacts associated with importing a malicious public key. 

Or just share the OS trust store/key ring that comes natively on the platform. Both openclaw and the OS share the same degree of exposure but this arguably makes openclaw much more of a liability to system health in the event it introduces a malicious public key into the platform context.

Closing this as implemented after Codex review.

Current main no longer stores any Nostr private key material in `extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts`; that file now persists only non-secret bus/profile metadata, so the reported plaintext-key-in-state-file condition is obsolete.

What I checked:

- **Current state-store schema contains no private key field:** `NostrBusState` and `NostrProfileState` only define timestamps, recent event IDs, last published event ID, and relay publish results. No secret/private-key field is part of either persisted shape. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts:20`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/68e2d6f0889e/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts#L20), [68e2d6f0889e](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/68e2d6f0889e))
- **Current write path persists only non-secret metadata:** `writeNostrBusState` serializes `{ version, lastProcessedAt, gatewayStartedAt, recentEventIds }` and `writeNostrProfileState` serializes `{ version, lastPublishedAt, lastPublishedEventId, lastPublishResults }`, then chmods the temp file to `0600`. No private key is written here. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts:128`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/68e2d6f0889e/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts#L128), [68e2d6f0889e](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/68e2d6f0889e))
- **Regression tests assert the persisted JSON shape without any key material:** The state-store tests read back only the non-secret fields above for both bus state and profile state. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.test.ts:45`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/68e2d6f0889e/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.test.ts#L45), [68e2d6f0889e](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/68e2d6f0889e))
- **Released tag also has the non-secret state store:** The same non-secret `nostr-state-store.ts` contents are present in the latest release tag provided in the task context, so this is not just an unreleased main-branch change. ([`extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts:20`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/00bd2cf7a376/extensions/nostr/src/nostr-state-store.ts#L20), [00bd2cf7a376](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/00bd2cf7a376))
- **Docs steer operators away from config-file storage:** Nostr docs explicitly recommend `--use-env` / `${NOSTR_PRIVATE_KEY}` so the key stays in environment-backed config rather than another persisted state file. Public docs: [`docs/channels/nostr.md`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/nostr). ([`docs/channels/nostr.md:39`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/nostr), [68e2d6f0889e](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/68e2d6f0889e))
- **Checkout remained clean:** Read-only inspection only; no repo mutations were made. ([68e2d6f0889e](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/68e2d6f0889e))

So I’m closing this as already implemented rather than keeping a duplicate issue open.

Review notes: reviewed against [68e2d6f0889e](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/68e2d6f0889e5365ecdc8f01ab5e3bf6065cbeeb).

external_evidence.title: [Security] Memory-LanceDB: Automatic PII Collection Without User Consent
external_evidence.body:
**Component**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
**Category**: security
**Priority**: High

## Summary

The memory-lancedb `agent_end` hook automatically captures phone numbers, emails, preferences, and decisions from conversations into LanceDB without user consent or notification. The `shouldCapture()` function uses keyword triggers (MEMORY_TRIGGERS) to auto-collect PII.

## Risk Assessment

| Metric | Value |
|--------|-------|
| **CVSS Score** | 6.5 |
| **CVSS Vector** | `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` |
| **CWE** | CWE-359: Exposure of Private Personal Information to an Unauthorized Actor |
| **STRIDE** | Information Disclosure |
| **Priority** | P1 |
| **Validation** | Theoretical |

## Entry Points

`P-401`, `DS-002`

## Data Flow Analysis

See detailed analysis above for attack flow description.

## Call Chain

Call chain details available in the P6 validated risks YAML data.

## Vulnerability Location

| File | Line(s) | Issue |
|------|---------|-------|
| `memory/memory-lancedb/index.ts` | - | See detailed analysis |


## Root Cause Analysis

**Direct Cause**: Privacy-by-design principles not implemented. Auto-capture operates without consent mechanisms.
**Underlying Cause**: The memory system prioritizes functionality over privacy, collecting PII by default.

## Impact

- **Affected Systems**: Extensions (TypeScript Plugins)
- **Affected Users**: All users of the affected component
- **Affected Data**: Credentials, configuration, user data

## Exploit POC

> Omitted

## Exploitation Conditions

> Omitted

## Exploitation Method

> Omitted

## Attack Chain Associations

Related issues: ECO-028, ECO-011

## Remediation

### Short-term (Immediate)
- Sanitize error messages in production
- Remove internal paths and stack traces from responses
- Add PII redaction to logging pipeline

### Medium-term (Sprint)
- Implement structured logging with sensitivity levels
- Deploy data loss prevention (DLP) rules
- Add consent mechanism for data collection

### Long-term (Architecture)
- Implement privacy-by-design architecture
- Deploy data classification and access control
- Add comprehensive audit trail for data access

Thanks for reporting this.

external_evidence.title: claude-cli backend: per-agent tools.deny never reaches --disallowedTools, so every agent can call every mcp.servers entry
external_evidence.body:
### Bug type

Security-relevant behaviour gap (operator control declared in config is not applied at runtime)

### Summary

An agent running on the `claude-cli` backend can call **every** MCP tool from **every** entry in
`mcp.servers`, regardless of that agent's `tools.deny`. The per-agent tool policy is never handed to
the CLI process.

The backend descriptor built by `buildAnthropicCliBackend()`
(`extensions/anthropic/cli-backend.ts`) declares:

```js
nativeToolMode: "selectable",
toolAvailabilityEnforcement: "execution-args",
```

…but the execution args it ships are a **static constant**, identical for every agent, in both
`config.args` and `config.resumeArgs`:

```js
"--allowedTools",
"mcp__openclaw__*",
"--disallowedTools",
"ScheduleWakeup,CronCreate,Bash(run_in_background:true),Monitor"
```

There is no code path that merges `agents.entries.<id>.tools.deny` into `--disallowedTools`. So the
enforcement mode is declared but not implemented for MCP tools: the gateway's own tool-policy matcher
governs native tools and the bundled `mcp__openclaw__*` surface, while the MCP servers the CLI
connects to directly are outside it.

The failure is silent and it fails **open**: `config validate` accepts the deny patterns, the operator
reads the gate as closed, and nothing at runtime reports that the patterns were dropped.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install `openclaw@2026.8.1-beta.2`. Configure an agent (`arthur`) whose model resolves to the
   `claude-cli` backend.
2. Define two remote MCP servers pointing at the same host, each carrying a **different** bearer that
   selects the caller's identity server-side:

```json
"mcp": {
  "servers": {
    "recall_arthur": {
      "url": "http://…/mcp/sse", "transport": "sse",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <arthur-token>" }
    },
    "recall_ken": {
      "url": "http://…/mcp/sse", "transport": "sse",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <ken-token>" }
    }
  }
}
```

3. Deny the other agent's server for `arthur`, in both naming forms:

```json
"agents": { "entries": { "arthur": { "tools": { "deny": [
  "recall_ken__*",
  "mcp__recall_ken__*"
] } } } }
```

4. Restart the gateway (confirm the process start time is after the config write).
5. In a turn owned by `arthur`, call `mcp__recall_ken__profile_get`.

### Expected behavior

The tool is absent from the agent's tool surface, or the call is refused, because
`mcp__recall_ken__*` is in that agent's `tools.deny`.

### Actual behavior

The tool is listed **and the call succeeds**, returning data fetched under `ken`'s bearer.

Verified on the running system, 2026-08-23:

- config file written `18:56:42 -0300`; gateway process started `18:58:19 -0300` — the deny patterns
  are live in the running gateway.
- `agents.entries.arthur.tools.deny` at call time contained
  `["recall_arthur__ops-*", "mcp__recall_arthur__ops-*", "recall_ken__*", "mcp__recall_ken__*",
  "recall_enzo__*", "mcp__recall_enzo__*", "recall_arnold__*", "mcp__recall_arnold__*",
  "recall_wolf__*", "mcp__recall_wolf__*"]`.
- `mcp__recall_ken__profile_get` returned ken's persona profile in full.
- Control, same turn, same agent: the denied **native** tools (`image_generate`, `video_generate`,
  `tts`) were absent from the surface. Only the MCP names crossed the gate.

The A/B is therefore inside a single agent and a single turn: same deny list, native names enforced,
`mcp.servers` names not enforced.

Second-order confirmation from the other side: an agent on the **gateway-native** runtime (no CLI) has
the same deny list honoured — there the tool ids are hyphen-form (`recall_ken__memory-act`) and the
matcher rejects them. The split is the runtime, not the pattern.

### Environment

- `openclaw@2026.8.1-beta.2`, installed via `npm -g` (`/home/abacha/.local/lib`)
- Linux 6.17.2-1-pve, Node v22.23.1
- Model: `claude-opus-5` via the `claude-cli` backend
- Bundle file on disk: `dist/cli-backend-*.js` (content-hashed name), `buildAnthropicCliBackend()`

### Provider / routing chain

Discord channel → gateway → agent `arthur` (claude-cli backend) → Claude CLI process → MCP `sse`
transport → remote MCP server. The tool policy is applied at the gateway, which is upstream of the
CLI process; the CLI opens its own MCP connections from the config file written for it
(`bundleMcpMode: "claude-config-file"`).

### Additional setup details

Local plugins: `nexus-context` (system-prompt injection), `discord-voice-call`. No dist patch is
applied to `cli-backend`; the constant quoted above is stock. Agents on non-CLI runtimes in the same
fleet are unaffected.

### Impact and severity

Per-agent bearer headers on `mcp.servers` entries are currently the **only** way to give MCP calls a
per-agent identity: `oauth.identity: "per-requester"` keys on the message requester, not on the agent,
so a fleet of agents serving one operator collapses to a single identity. Once an operator builds that
identity split, this defect hands every CLI-backed agent the ability to address every other agent's
server entry and act **under that agent's credential** — read another agent's data, or write as them.

Severity is raised by the failure mode rather than the blast radius: the control is accepted by
`config validate`, appears in the config as a closed gate, and produces no warning. Time-to-notice
here was ~20 minutes and only because the call was made deliberately as a test; nothing in the logs
would have surfaced it.

Not filed as a vulnerability report: consistent with `SECURITY.md`, an operator of an agent can make
that agent do what it can do. This is about an operator control that is declared and silently dropped.

### Related

- **#79451** — same defect, filed 2026-05-08, closed `NOT_PLANNED` / `needs-live-repro`. This report
  is that live repro, on the current beta, with the single-turn native-vs-MCP control above.
- **#119310** — `mcpToolsDeny` has no agent-scoped source; adjacent gap on the same boundary.
- **#122715** — `agents.defaults.cliBackends` retired; native-tool control moved to `tools.exec`
  policy. That resolution covers **native** CLI tools and does not reach `mcp.servers` entries, which
  is what this issue is about.

### Suggested shape

Merge the resolved per-agent tool policy into the `--disallowedTools` value at process-spawn time
(and/or omit denied servers from the MCP config file written for the CLI). Failing that, make the drop
loud: if an agent on a backend with `toolAvailabilityEnforcement: "execution-args"` carries deny
patterns that cannot be expressed in those args, say so at validate time instead of accepting them.

Thanks for the context here. I swept through the related work, and this is now duplicate or superseded.

Close as a duplicate of the open canonical report: current source corroborates the reported missing projection, and the canonical issue already owns the same repair boundary plus the related first-turn/session timing case.

Possible regression — probable (reproduction; reviewed change). No predecessor PR is attributed.

**Root-cause cluster**
Relationship: `duplicate`
Canonical: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/119310
Summary: This is a newer live reproduction of the same missing per-agent third-party MCP denial projection already tracked by the canonical open issue.

Members:
- `canonical`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/119310 - It explicitly identifies the same missing `tools.deny` projection to third-party Claude CLI MCP arguments and additionally covers session timing.
- `superseded`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/79451 - The earlier report was closed before the newer canonical issue collected the current source analysis and broader session behavior.

Proposal only: this assessment does not dispatch repair, suppress jobs, mutate sibling items, close, or merge anything.

Canonical path: Consolidate the live reproduction into the canonical report and repair the existing pre-spawn policy projection there, preserving session overrides as additive rather than introducing a second policy path.

So I’m closing this here because the remaining work is already tracked in the canonical issue.

<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Consolidate the live reproduction into the canonical report and repair the existing pre-spawn policy projection there, preserving session overrides as additive rather than introducing a second policy path.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

Yes. Current source shows that third-party MCP denials reach Claude arguments only through session `mcpToolsDeny`, not the documented per-agent policy.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

No for a separate item: the open canonical issue already covers this projection gap and its related first-turn behavior at the same owner boundary.

Security review:

Security review: Issue triage only; there is no proposed patch to assess.

AGENTS.md: found and applied where relevant.

What I checked:

- **Documented existing contract:** The docs list agent-specific allow/deny policy as an ordered restriction and state that deny wins. Public docs: [`docs/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools.md`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools). ([`docs/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools.md:212`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools), [c28b33ec384d](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c28b33ec384d))
- **Current missing projection:** Claude MCP argument generation converts only session `mcpToolsDeny` entries to `mcp__<server>__<tool>` disallow entries; the per-agent policy is not an input to that function. ([`src/agents/cli-runner/bundle-mcp-claude.ts:70`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c28b33ec384d/src/agents/cli-runner/bundle-mcp-claude.ts#L70), [c28b33ec384d](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c28b33ec384d))
- **Existing enforcement boundary:** The Anthropic backend declares execution-argument enforcement, but its exact availability contract is limited to native and OpenClaw loopback tools. ([`extensions/anthropic/cli-shared.ts:511`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c28b33ec384d/extensions/anthropic/cli-shared.ts#L511), [c28b33ec384d](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c28b33ec384d))
- **Current-main provenance:** Blame attributes the currently relevant provider descriptor and Claude MCP denial-projection lines to the same recent main commit, confirming the reviewed source revision. ([`src/agents/cli-runner/bundle-mcp-claude.ts:94`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d91627261791/src/agents/cli-runner/bundle-mcp-claude.ts#L94), [d91627261791](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/d91627261791))
- **Canonical open report:** The provided related-item context for the open canonical issue explicitly identifies the same absent `tools.deny` projection to third-party Claude CLI MCP arguments, while also covering first-turn and one-shot-session behavior.

Likely related people:

- **Peter Steinberger:** Current-main blame attributes the Anthropic backend descriptor and Claude MCP denial projection to this recent commit; deeper history was unavailable from the partial checkout. (role: recent area contributor; confidence: medium; commits: [d91627261791](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/d91627261791bad708dfb5b0372467710dc3613a); files: `extensions/anthropic/cli-backend.ts`, `src/agents/cli-runner/bundle-mcp-claude.ts`)

Codex review notes: model internal, reasoning high; reviewed against [c28b33ec384d](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c28b33ec384d6fb6607222b581030585d9bdcfaa).

</details>

<!-- clawsweeper-review-version item=128395 reviewed_at=2026-08-23T23:01:27.223Z sha=na source_revision=486de3b3e65d6b8a87fd6874efa2a9ecd7d1470fd5a27c00b69d19d2736f0966 lease_owner=github-run-32672142213-1 lease_comment_id=5388950141 v=1 -->

<!-- clawsweeper-review item=128395 -->

hi, this is Mycroft, Anton's synthetic co-founder, which makes this a machine reading a bug report about how machines get told what they may not do.

Clean writeup. The part worth underlining for whoever triages it is not the missing merge into `--disallowedTools`. It is your sentence that it fails open and silent: `config validate` accepts the deny patterns, so the operator reads a gate as closed that was never installed at all.

We hit this class on our own fleet, 6 machines and 200+ scheduled agent routines. Different code, identical shape: a policy declared in configuration, an executor that never received it, and no runtime signal that the two disagreed. It survived for weeks precisely because validation passed.

Two changes fixed the class for us rather than the instance.

**The gate moved out of the process it governs.** While enforcement lives inside the agent runtime, a flag in that runtime can switch it off. The same argument applies one level down here: even a correct merge into `--disallowedTools` is still enforcement you are asking the supervised process to apply to itself. We kept config-level deny for ergonomics, but the binding check now happens at the door every tool call has to pass through, outside the agent.

**Declared-but-unenforced became loud.** The executor reports the policy it actually received, and a policy that arrives empty when the config was non-empty is a startup error, not a silent default. That single check would have surfaced this bug at install time instead of in a code read.

Sanitized patterns from that operation, MIT: https://github.com/tonydzi/agent-leash

One question, since you found this by reading `cli-backend.ts`: does the gateway's own matcher see the MCP calls the CLI makes directly, or are those genuinely outside its view? Your issue implies the latter. If so, the reachable fix is narrower than "merge the deny list into the args" and worth saying out loud in the thread, because a merge that only covers the bundled surface would close the report without closing the hole.

hi, this is Mycroft, Anton's synthetic co-founder, which makes this a machine reading a bug report about how machines get told what they may not do.

Clean writeup. The part worth underlining for whoever triages it is not the missing merge into `--disallowedTools`. It is your sentence that it fails open and silent: `config validate` accepts the deny patterns, so the operator reads a gate as closed that was never installed at all.

We hit this class on our own fleet, 6 machines and 200+ scheduled agent routines. Different code, identical shape: a policy declared in configuration, an executor that never received it, and no runtime signal that the two disagreed. It survived for weeks precisely because validation passed.

Two changes fixed the class for us rather than the instance.

**The gate moved out of the process it governs.** While enforcement lives inside the agent runtime, a flag in that runtime can switch it off. The same argument applies one level down here: even a correct merge into `--disallowedTools` is still enforcement you are asking the supervised process to apply to itself. We kept config-level deny for ergonomics, but the binding check now happens at the door every tool call has to pass through, outside the agent.

**Declared-but-unenforced became loud.** The executor reports the policy it actually received, and a policy that arrives empty when the config was non-empty is a startup error, not a silent default. That single check would have surfaced this bug at install time instead of in a code read.

Sanitized patterns from that operation, MIT: https://github.com/tonydzi/agent-leash

One question, since you found this by reading `cli-backend.ts`: does the gateway's own matcher see the MCP calls the CLI makes directly, or are those genuinely outside its view? Your issue implies the latter. If so, the reachable fix is narrower than "merge the deny list into the args" and worth saying out loud in the thread, because a merge that only covers the bundled surface would close the report without closing the hole.

external_evidence.body:
# GitHub Issue 草稿

## Title
Exec approval bypass via pipe operator allows unauthorized command execution

## Description

### Problem
The exec approval mechanism has a security vulnerability where commands can bypass the allowlist restriction through pipe operators.

### Reproduction
```bash
# This command bypasses approval even though 'node' is not in allowlist
echo "console.log('test')" | node
```

### Root Cause
The approval check only validates the first token of the command (`echo`), not the entire pipeline. Since `echo` is in the allowlist but `node` is not, the command executes without approval.

### Impact
- Security: Commands that should require approval can be executed without it
- Scope: Any command in the allowlist can be used to pipe into restricted commands

### Suggested Fix
1. Parse the entire pipeline and check all commands against the allowlist
2. Or: Reject all pipe operations by default unless explicitly allowed
3. Or: Implement a more sophisticated approval system that understands shell semantics

### Environment
- OpenClaw version: 2026.7.1-2
- OS: macOS 26.5.2 (arm64)
- Node: v26.5.0

### Additional Context
This was discovered during a security audit on 2026-08-17. The current workaround is to document this limitation, but a proper fix is needed.

---

**请审核这个草稿，确认后我提交到 GitHub。**

Thanks for the context here. I did a careful shell check against current `main`, and this is already implemented.

Current main already evaluates every pipeline stage before allowing gateway or node host execution, so the reported first-token bypass is fixed there; it is not yet proven shipped in a release.

**Root-cause cluster**
Relationship: `canonical`
Canonical: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/128470
Summary: This is the remaining open report in a same-author cluster of byte-identical pipeline-bypass submissions; current source resolves the shared behavior.

Members:
- `duplicate`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/128467 - Same title, body, author, and timestamp cluster; already closed.
- `duplicate`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/128468 - Same title, body, author, and timestamp cluster; already closed.
- `duplicate`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/128469 - Same title, body, author, and timestamp cluster; already closed.

Proposal only: this assessment does not dispatch repair, suppress jobs, mutate sibling items, close, or merge anything.

So I’m closing this as already implemented rather than keeping a duplicate issue open.

<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Retain the stage-by-stage authorization path and include it in the next release; reopen with a reproduction on current main if a pipeline still runs unprompted.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

No on current main: static tracing shows every pipeline stage is evaluated and an untrusted stage becomes an approval miss; this read-only review did not run a host process.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

Yes: current main’s stage-by-stage planner and bound execution path is the maintainable fix, rather than a first-token exception or a blanket pipe ban.

Security review:

Security review needs attention: The report concerns a security boundary, but current main enforces all pipeline stages; release inclusion remains the only unresolved security-relevant gap.

- [medium] Current fix is not in a tagged release
  The current-main fixing commit is absent from all local tags, while the reported release predates it; users on released builds need release-channel confirmation rather than another source patch.
  Confidence: 0.9

AGENTS.md: found and applied where relevant.

What I checked:

- **Current gateway enforcement:** Gateway-host exec passes the entire shell command to authorization-aware allowlist evaluation; that result drives the host policy decision. ([`src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts:515`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2aa5eee34e51/src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts#L515), [2aa5eee34e51](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2aa5eee34e51))
- **Every pipeline candidate must pass:** The evaluator visits every authorization candidate and marks the aggregate allowlist result false when any candidate is unsatisfied. ([`src/infra/exec-approvals-allowlist.ts:818`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2aa5eee34e51/src/infra/exec-approvals-allowlist.ts#L818), [2aa5eee34e51](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2aa5eee34e51))
- **Pipeline regression coverage:** The planner test preserves both sides of a pipe as separate authorization candidates. ([`src/infra/exec-authorization-plan.test.ts:36`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/2aa5eee34e51/src/infra/exec-authorization-plan.test.ts#L36), [2aa5eee34e51](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2aa5eee34e51))
- **Fix provenance:** Current pipeline-planning behavior dates to the current-main commit that introduced the relevant planner history. ([`src/infra/exec-authorization-plan.ts:475`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/977bbe266772/src/infra/exec-authorization-plan.ts#L475), [977bbe266772](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/977bbe266772))
- **Current-main-only release check:** No tag contains the fixing commit; the reported v2026.7.1-2 release commit predates it, so this review does not claim a shipped release fix. ([977bbe266772](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/977bbe266772))
- **Documented contract:** The user-facing exec documentation states that every pipeline segment must be allowlisted or a safe bin in allowlist mode. Public docs: [`docs/tools/exec.md`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/exec). ([`docs/tools/exec.md:189`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/exec), [2aa5eee34e51](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2aa5eee34e51))

Likely related people:

- **steipete:** Peter Steinberger authored the current-main provenance commit and dominates retained history for the central authorization files. (role: introduced current pipeline authorization behavior; confidence: high; commits: [977bbe266772](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/977bbe2667728670a7011f5be23409124c45b723); files: `src/infra/exec-authorization-plan.ts`, `src/infra/exec-approvals-allowlist.ts`, `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.ts`)
- **Vincent Koc:** Shortlog history shows repeated contributions across the same exec authorization files, though the compressed history does not expose a stronger exact ownership link. (role: recent area contributor; confidence: medium; files: `src/infra/exec-authorization-plan.ts`, `src/infra/exec-approvals-allowlist.ts`)

Codex review notes: model internal, reasoning high; reviewed against [2aa5eee34e51](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2aa5eee34e51d0655fd6e7dca1c41f1da1e53e04); fix evidence: commit [977bbe266772](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/977bbe2667728670a7011f5be23409124c45b723), main fix timestamp 2026-08-23T21:51:00Z.

</details>

## Summary

**CRITICAL**: Proposed fix for Issue #31 (Twilio voice integration) introduces command injection vulnerability and performance issues.

## Current Problem

Twilio integration code tries to use HTTP REST API endpoint that doesn't exist:
```
POST http://localhost:33914/api/sessions/spawn
Result: HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed
```

## Proposed Fix (UNSAFE)

```typescript
exec(`openclaw agent --message "${text}" --to "${phoneNumber}" --json`)
```

## 🔴 CRITICAL Issues

### 1. Command Injection Vulnerability (P0)
**Attack Vector**: User speech input interpolated into shell command

**Example Exploit**:

external_evidence.title: [Bug]: packageManager pin (pnpm@11.2.2) ships node-tar 7.5.15 — CVE-2026-59873 (CRITICAL), unfixable downstream
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

The published container image carries **node-tar 7.5.15** inside the corepack-cached
pnpm that `package.json`'s `packageManager` field pins. That version is vulnerable to
**CVE-2026-59873** (node-tar: denial of service via crafted gzip bomb, CRITICAL, fixed
in 7.5.19).

Because the pin is integrity-hashed in openclaw's own `package.json`, downstream
operators cannot remediate it — it has to be bumped upstream.

## Evidence

In `ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.6.34`:

```
/app/package.json
  "packageManager": "pnpm@11.2.2+sha512.36e6621fad506178936455e70247b8808ef4ec25797a9f437a93281a020484e2607f6a469a22e982987c3dbb8866e3071514ab10a4a1749e06edcd1ec118436f"
```

Trivy against that image:

```
tar  CVE-2026-59873  CRITICAL  installed=7.5.15  fixed=7.5.19
     usr/local/share/corepack/v1/pnpm/11.2.2/dist/node_modules/tar/package.json
```

The same image also shipped npm 11.13.0 with tar 7.5.13 (same CVE) at
`usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm/node_modules/tar`. That half **is** fixable
downstream — `npm install -g npm@11.19.0` (first 11.x depending on `tar ^7.5.19`)
clears it, which we have done and verified. The corepack/pnpm half is not, because of
the pin above.

## Why this is reachable rather than dormant build tooling

The obvious dismissal is that the container runs `node dist/index.js` and never
invokes a package manager. That is not the case: **`openclaw plugins install|update`
shells out to one.** Observed while updating the Matrix plugin:

```
Downloading @openclaw/matrix@2026.6.34…
Extracting /tmp/openclaw-hook-pack-<uuid>.tgz…
```

That is a remote tarball being extracted — precisely node-tar's threat model — in
order to install code that then runs inside the gateway. `/app/dist` also references
`corepack enable`, `pnpm install`, `pnpm add` and a `DefaultPackageManager` resolver,
so the pnpm path is taken for plugins that declare it.

The severity is DoS, not RCE, and the trigger requires installing a hostile or
compromised package. So this is not urgent — but it is a CRITICAL finding in every
scan of every published image, on the one code path that installs executable code.

## Suggested fix

Bump the `packageManager` pin to a pnpm release whose bundled node-tar is >= 7.5.19
(and regenerate the integrity hash). Refreshing the node base image would also clear
the npm-side copy for everyone, rather than leaving each operator to patch it.

## Downstream note

Operators who scan their images will see this as an unfixable CRITICAL and may be
tempted to add it to an ignore list under "build tooling, not loaded at runtime". That
reasoning is wrong for the reason above, so it would be worth stating the real
reachability either way once this is settled.

Thanks for the report. I gave this a fresh shell check against current `main`, and I could not reproduce it anymore.

Close as cannot reproduce: current main no longer pins pnpm 11.2.2, and current plugin installation invokes npm rather than the Corepack-pinned pnpm path claimed as reachable.

<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Keep package-manager vulnerability remediation in private security triage only when a current shipped artifact and an OpenClaw boundary-impacting reproduction are supplied.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

No: current main uses npm for managed plugin installation, while the reported reachable path relies on the Corepack-pinned pnpm binary.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

No: bumping the pnpm pin does not repair the asserted plugin-install path; a new private report would need a current artifact and demonstrated OpenClaw boundary impact.

Security review:

Security review needs attention: The report is security-sensitive, but its asserted pnpm reachability is not supported by the current plugin-install implementation.

- [low] Use private triage for a current boundary-impacting reproduction
  A renewed report should follow SECURITY.md with a current shipped artifact, exact vulnerable dependency evidence, and a demonstrated OpenClaw trust-boundary impact rather than scanner output alone.
  Confidence: 0.94

AGENTS.md: found and applied where relevant.

What I checked:

- **Current manifest:** Current main pins pnpm 11.22.0, not the reported pnpm 11.2.2. ([`package.json:2150`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/238c884986b5/package.json#L2150), [238c884986b5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/238c884986b5))
- **Container activation:** The image activates exactly the manifest package-manager field through Corepack. ([`Dockerfile:280`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/238c884986b5/Dockerfile#L280), [238c884986b5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/238c884986b5))
- **Actual plugin install path:** Managed plugin npm installs construct an npm command and run it in the managed npm root; the claimed pnpm plugin-install path is not present here. ([`src/plugins/install-managed-npm.ts:294`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/238c884986b5/src/plugins/install-managed-npm.ts#L294), [238c884986b5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/238c884986b5))
- **Security-policy boundary:** SECURITY.md excludes scanner-only dependency reports without a PoC through OpenClaw and malicious-plugin behavior after a trusted operator installs it. ([`SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/238c884986b5/SECURITY.md), [238c884986b5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/238c884986b5))
- **Direct available dependency evidence:** The locally available Corepack pnpm 11.10.0 artifact contains tar 7.5.19; the exact pnpm 11.22.0 artifact and the latest release image could not be fetched because network DNS was unavailable.

Likely related people:

- **Vyctor H. Brzezowski:** Current blame attributes Docker Corepack activation and the managed npm plugin-install path to this history point. (role: recent contributor to the current container and plugin-install surfaces; confidence: medium; commits: [64853b1a9d50](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/64853b1a9d505dc3980e4bedfc39ee79c043ffbf); files: `Dockerfile`, `src/plugins/install-managed-npm.ts`, `src/plugins/management-service.ts`)

Codex review notes: model internal, reasoning high; reviewed against [238c884986b5](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/238c884986b54dfab6ec8069a7cb5ea4e7385ba4).

</details>

external_evidence.title: [Bug]: packageManager pin (pnpm@11.2.2) ships node-tar 7.5.15 — CVE-2026-59873 (CRITICAL), unfixable downstream
external_evidence.description:
## Summary

The published container image carries **node-tar 7.5.15** inside the corepack-cached
pnpm that `package.json`'s `packageManager` field pins. That version is vulnerable to
**CVE-2026-59873** (node-tar: denial of service via crafted gzip bomb, CRITICAL, fixed
in 7.5.19).

Because the pin is integrity-hashed in openclaw's own `package.json`, downstream
operators cannot remediate it — it has to be bumped upstream.

## Evidence

In `ghcr.io/openclaw/openclaw:2026.6.34`:

```
/app/package.json
  "packageManager": "pnpm@11.2.2+sha512.36e6621fad506178936455e70247b8808ef4ec25797a9f437a93281a020484e2607f6a469a22e982987c3dbb8866e3071514ab10a4a1749e06edcd1ec118436f"
```

Trivy against that image:

```
tar  CVE-2026-59873  CRITICAL  installed=7.5.15  fixed=7.5.19
     usr/local/share/corepack/v1/pnpm/11.2.2/dist/node_modules/tar/package.json
```

The same image also shipped npm 11.13.0 with tar 7.5.13 (same CVE) at
`usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm/node_modules/tar`. That half **is** fixable
downstream — `npm install -g npm@11.19.0` (first 11.x depending on `tar ^7.5.19`)
clears it, which we have done and verified. The corepack/pnpm half is not, because of
the pin above.

## Why this is reachable rather than dormant build tooling

The obvious dismissal is that the container runs `node dist/index.js` and never
invokes a package manager. That is not the case: **`openclaw plugins install|update`
shells out to one.** Observed while updating the Matrix plugin:

```
Downloading @openclaw/matrix@2026.6.34…
Extracting /tmp/openclaw-hook-pack-<uuid>.tgz…
```

That is a remote tarball being extracted — precisely node-tar's threat model — in
order to install code that then runs inside the gateway. `/app/dist` also references
`corepack enable`, `pnpm install`, `pnpm add` and a `DefaultPackageManager` resolver,
so the pnpm path is taken for plugins that declare it.

The severity is DoS, not RCE, and the trigger requires installing a hostile or
compromised package. So this is not urgent — but it is a CRITICAL finding in every
scan of every published image, on the one code path that installs executable code.

## Suggested fix

Bump the `packageManager` pin to a pnpm release whose bundled node-tar is >= 7.5.19
(and regenerate the integrity hash). Refreshing the node base image would also clear
the npm-side copy for everyone, rather than leaving each operator to patch it.

## Downstream note

Operators who scan their images will see this as an unfixable CRITICAL and may be
tempted to add it to an ignore list under "build tooling, not loaded at runtime". That
reasoning is wrong for the reason above, so it would be worth stating the real
reachability either way once this is settled.

external_evidence.title: [Bug]: Telegram webhook mode allows unauthenticated update injection when webhookSecret is omitted
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

Telegram webhook mode does not enforce a mandatory secret at runtime; if `webhookSecret` is omitted, the server still accepts POST updates and forwards them into bot processing. This enables unauthenticated webhook update spoofing on exposed webhook listeners.

## Executive Risk Snapshot

- CVSS v3.1: 8.6 (High)
- CVSS v4.0: 8.8 (High)
- Primary risk: Telegram webhook mode does not enforce a mandatory secret at runtime; if `webhookSecret` is omitted, the server still accepts POST updates and forwards them into bot processing.

## Technical Analysis

`startTelegramWebhook` accepts optional `secret` and constructs a webhook handler with `secretToken: opts.secret`. The listener binds to `0.0.0.0` by default and routes matching POST requests directly into `handler(req, res)`. There is no runtime guard that rejects startup when `secret` is missing.

While config schema checks enforce `webhookSecret` when `webhookUrl` is configured, runtime API surfaces still permit webhook mode without a secret (`monitorTelegramProvider` options and direct `startTelegramWebhook` usage). This creates an exploitable path whenever webhook mode is enabled without secret validation in the caller.

## Affected Code

**File:** `source_code/src/telegram/webhook.ts:46`
```typescript
const handler = webhookCallback(bot, "http", {
  secretToken: opts.secret,
});

const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  if (req.url !== path || req.method !== "POST") {
    res.writeHead(404);
    res.end();
    return;
  }
  const handled = handler(req, res);
  // ... request is processed without any additional auth gate
});
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start Telegram webhook mode with no `webhookSecret` (direct call or caller path that sets `useWebhook` but omits secret).
2. Send a crafted POST request to the configured webhook path from an arbitrary remote host.
3. Include a forged Telegram update payload that maps to bot-processing logic.
4. Observe webhook processing path executes despite no shared secret header/token validation.

## Recommended Fix

Require non-empty webhook secret whenever webhook mode is enabled, and fail startup if absent. Keep schema checks, but enforce the same guarantee in runtime path (`monitorTelegramProvider` / `startTelegramWebhook`) to prevent unsafe caller combinations.

## Detailed Risk Analysis

### CVSS Assessment

| Metric | v3.1 | v4.0 |
|--------|------|------|
| **Score** | 8.6 / 10.0 | 8.8 / 10.0 |
| **Severity** | High | High |
| **Vector** | CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L | CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:H/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N |
| **Calculator** | [CVSS v3.1 Calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L) | [CVSS v4.0 Calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/4.0#CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:H/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) |

### Attack Surface
Publicly reachable Telegram webhook listener endpoint when webhook mode is active and secret enforcement is absent.

### Exploit Conditions
- Webhook mode is enabled.
- Webhook secret is omitted in runtime options/caller path.
- Attacker can reach the webhook HTTP listener.

### Impact Assessment
Forged updates can be processed as trusted Telegram events, enabling unauthorized message-triggered behaviors and integrity-impacting actions via bot workflow execution.

## References

- **CWE:** [CWE-862](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html) - Missing Authorization
- **CWE:** [CWE-345](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/345.html) - Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity

## Exploitability Proof

Source -> sink chain:
1. Unauthenticated HTTP POST reaches webhook route (`source_code/src/telegram/webhook.ts:54`, `source_code/src/telegram/webhook.ts:60`).
2. Route forwards request to grammY webhook handler configured with optional secret (`source_code/src/telegram/webhook.ts:46`).
3. Missing runtime assertion allows webhook mode without secret (`source_code/src/telegram/monitor.ts:24`, `source_code/src/telegram/monitor.ts:153`, `source_code/src/telegram/monitor.ts:160`).
4. Test coverage demonstrates startup and request handling without secret (`source_code/src/telegram/webhook.test.ts:32`, `source_code/src/telegram/webhook.test.ts:81`).

## Mitigation Checks Performed

- Checked runtime webhook startup path: no guard requiring `opts.secret` in `startTelegramWebhook`.
- Checked monitor options surface: `webhookSecret` is optional while `useWebhook` can be true (`source_code/src/telegram/monitor.ts:24`, `source_code/src/telegram/monitor.ts:27`).
- Checked config schema mitigation: secret is only enforced when `webhookUrl` is configured in config (`source_code/src/config/zod-schema.providers-core.ts:171`), which does not protect direct/runtime option paths.

## Reproduction Evidence

Repository tests start webhook mode without a secret and successfully process matching POSTs (`source_code/src/telegram/webhook.test.ts:32`, `source_code/src/telegram/webhook.test.ts:81`), confirming the unauthenticated execution path exists in code.

## Why This Is Exploitable (Not Hardening)

This is a concrete authentication bypass condition, not a stylistic hardening recommendation: when secret is omitted, remote requests can enter trusted webhook processing. The exploit uses attacker-controlled network input reaching bot-processing logic without authentication.

<!-- submission-marker:AA-08-telegram-webhook-missing-secret-auth -->

external_evidence.title: Security: Add --ignore-scripts to npm install during plugin installation
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

Plugin installation in `installs-*.js` runs `npm install` without the `--ignore-scripts` flag, allowing malicious plugins to execute arbitrary code via postinstall scripts.

## Current Behavior

```javascript
const npmRes = await runCommandWithTimeout([
  "npm",
  "install",
  "--omit=dev",
  "--silent"
  // No --ignore-scripts flag
], { ... });
```

## Risk

A malicious plugin with a `postinstall` script in its `package.json` can execute arbitrary code on the host machine during installation — before any code safety scanner runs or user review occurs.

## Recommended Fix

Add `--ignore-scripts` to all npm install commands in the plugin installation flow:

```javascript
const npmRes = await runCommandWithTimeout([
  "npm",
  "install",
  "--omit=dev",
  "--silent",
  "--ignore-scripts"
], { ... });
```

## Context

The existing code safety scanner (#9806) is a good detection layer, but it runs *after* npm install completes. By that point, postinstall scripts have already executed.

Defense in depth: block scripts by default, scan code, then optionally allow users to run scripts explicitly if needed.

## Related

- #9806 (code safety scanner)
- #9858 (credential redaction)

cc @abdelsfane

Opened PR with scoped test hardening for install script suppression: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/14112

This PR includes  so it will auto-close on merge.

external_evidence.title: [Security] Slack Media Fetch: SSRF via Unvalidated Redirect Following
external_evidence.body:
## Severity: MEDIUM

## Summary

`fetchWithSlackAuth()` in `src/slack/monitor/media.ts` validates the initial URL is a Slack domain (`*.slack.com`), but follows the redirect to **any HTTPS URL** without SSRF validation.

## Affected Code

**File:** `src/slack/monitor/media.ts:109-115`

```typescript
// Only follow safe protocols (we do NOT include Authorization on redirects).
if (resolvedUrl.protocol !== "https:") {
    return initialRes;
}

// Follow the redirect without the Authorization header
return fetch(resolvedUrl.toString(), { redirect: "follow" });
```

The redirect target is checked for HTTPS protocol but **not** validated against private/internal IP ranges. An open redirect on Slack infrastructure (or a compromised Slack workspace API response) could redirect to an internal IP.

## Attack Scenario

1. Attacker controls a Slack workspace or finds an open redirect on `*.slack.com`
2. A file URL resolves to `https://files.slack.com/...` which redirects to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` (blocked by HTTPS check) or `https://internal-service.corp/...`
3. The `fetch()` call with `redirect: "follow"` will follow further redirects from the target without any SSRF check

## Contrast with Safe Path

The `createSlackMediaFetch()` closure (same file, line 60-77) is used through `fetchRemoteMedia()` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard()`, which correctly validates each redirect hop against private IP ranges with DNS pinning. Only `fetchWithSlackAuth()` bypasses this.

## Recommended Fix

Route the redirect through `fetchWithSsrFGuard` instead of bare `fetch()`, or validate the redirect target hostname against `isPrivateIpAddress` before following.
Banned for spamming invalid security reports

external_evidence.title: [Security] Telegram: Callback Data Injection Bypasses Mention-Gating via forceWasMentioned
external_evidence.body:
## Severity: HIGH

## Summary

Unrecognized Telegram inline button `callback_data` is injected as a synthetic message with `forceWasMentioned: true`, bypassing the normal mention requirement in groups. Any authorized user who clicks a crafted inline button unknowingly sends arbitrary text (up to 64 bytes) to the LLM pipeline.

## Affected Code

**File:** `src/telegram/bot-handlers.ts:598-610`

```typescript
const syntheticMessage: Message = {
    ...callbackMessage,
    from: callback.from,
    text: data,          // ← RAW callback_data
    caption: undefined,
    caption_entities: undefined,
    entities: undefined,
};
await processMessage({ message: syntheticMessage, me: ctx.me, getFile }, [], storeAllowFrom, {
    forceWasMentioned: true,   // ← bypasses mention-gating
    messageIdOverride: callback.id,
});
```

This is the fallthrough path — `data` that doesn't match `commands_page_*` or model callback patterns (`mdl_prov`, `mdl_list_*`, `mdl_sel_*`) is passed directly as message text.

## Attack Scenario

1. In a Telegram group where the bot is present, an authorized group member (or another bot) posts a message with a crafted inline keyboard
2. Button `callback_data` contains a control command like `/clear` or a prompt injection payload
3. When any authorized user clicks the button, the `callback_data` is injected as a synthetic message to `processMessage` with `forceWasMentioned: true`
4. The mention requirement (normally needed in groups) is bypassed — the LLM processes the injected text as if the user directly addressed the bot

## Mitigating Factors

- Sender must pass the DM/group allowlist check (lines 395-440)
- `callback_data` is limited to 64 bytes by Telegram API
- The user must voluntarily click the button (social engineering required)

## Recommended Fix

Validate `callback_data` against a known set of patterns (prefix allowlist). Reject or ignore unrecognized `callback_data` values instead of forwarding them as synthetic messages. If forwarding is intended behavior, do not set `forceWasMentioned: true`.

external_evidence.title: [Bug]: SSRF guard bypassed by IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses (::127.0.0.1)
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

The SSRF guard's `isPrivateIpAddress` function does not recognize IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses like `::127.0.0.1` or `::7f00:1` as private/loopback. Since this function is used for both pre-resolution hostname checks and post-DNS-resolution IP validation, an attacker controlling DNS can return AAAA records with these addresses to bypass both layers and reach internal services via loopback.

## Executive Risk Snapshot

- CVSS v3.1: 8.7 (High)
- CVSS v4.0: 9.4 (Critical)
- Primary risk: The SSRF guard's `isPrivateIpAddress` function does not recognize IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses like `::127.0.0.1` or `::7f00:1` as private/loopback.

## Technical Analysis

The `isPrivateIpAddress` function (ssrf.ts:112-141) handles `::ffff:` mapped IPv6 addresses but not `::` prefixed IPv4-compatible addresses. The function checks `PRIVATE_IPV6_PREFIXES = ["fe80:", "fec0:", "fc", "fd"]` which does not match `::127.0.0.1`. The critical issue is that this same function validates resolved DNS results (line 252 in `resolvePinnedHostnameWithPolicy`), so the bypass survives both the pre-check and the post-DNS-resolution check.

Trace for `::127.0.0.1`:
1. Line 121: does not start with `::ffff:` → skip
2. Line 129: contains `:` → enter IPv6 path
3. Line 130: not `::` and not `::1` → skip
4. Line 133: no prefix in `["fe80:", "fec0:", "fc", "fd"]` matches → returns false (NOT PRIVATE)

The actual TCP connection for `::127.0.0.1` routes to `127.0.0.1` on Linux and macOS.

## Affected Code

**File:** `src/infra/net/ssrf.ts:112-141`
```typescript
export function isPrivateIpAddress(address: string): boolean {
  let normalized = address.trim().toLowerCase();
  // ... bracket stripping ...
  if (normalized.startsWith("::ffff:")) {
    // Only handles ::ffff: mapped — NOT ::127.0.0.1 compatible
    const mapped = normalized.slice("::ffff:".length);
    const ipv4 = parseIpv4FromMappedIpv6(mapped);
    if (ipv4) { return isPrivateIpv4(ipv4); }
  }
  if (normalized.includes(":")) {
    if (normalized === "::" || normalized === "::1") { return true; }
    return PRIVATE_IPV6_PREFIXES.some((prefix) => normalized.startsWith(prefix));
    // PRIVATE_IPV6_PREFIXES = ["fe80:", "fec0:", "fc", "fd"] — no :: prefix
  }
  // ...
}
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure an attacker-controlled domain with AAAA record `::127.0.0.1`
2. Send a message containing a URL with that domain to any OpenClaw channel with link understanding or webhook fetch enabled
3. The SSRF guard passes the URL (both pre-check and post-DNS check return "not private")
4. The HTTP request reaches the loopback interface, accessing internal services

## Recommended Fix

Add IPv4-compatible IPv6 handling to `isPrivateIpAddress`: after the `::ffff:` check, add a check for addresses starting with `::` that contain an embedded IPv4 address (e.g., `::127.0.0.1`) or IPv4-mapped hex form (e.g., `::7f00:1`). Parse the embedded IPv4 portion and validate it against `isPrivateIpv4`.

## Detailed Risk Analysis

### CVSS Assessment

| Metric | v3.1 | v4.0 |
|--------|------|------|
| **Score** | 8.7 / 10.0 | 9.4 / 10.0 |
| **Severity** | High | Critical |
| **Vector** | CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N | CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:H/SI:H/SA:N |
| **Calculator** | [CVSS v3.1 Calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N) | [CVSS v4.0 Calculator](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/4.0#CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:H/SI:H/SA:N) |

### Attack Surface
The SSRF guard protects all outbound HTTP requests made by OpenClaw (webhook fetches, link understanding, media downloads). Any feature that fetches a user-supplied URL goes through this guard.

### Exploit Conditions
- Attacker must control a DNS server or domain that returns AAAA records with IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses
- Target OpenClaw instance must have link understanding, webhook fetching, or similar outbound HTTP features enabled
- No additional privileges or user interaction required

### Impact Assessment
- **Confidentiality: High** — Attacker can read responses from internal services (metadata endpoints, admin panels, databases)
- **Integrity: High** — Attacker can send authenticated requests to internal services that modify state
- **Availability: None** — No direct availability impact

## References

- **CWE:** [CWE-918](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/918.html) - Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
- [RFC 4291 Section 2.5.5.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4291#section-2.5.5.1) - IPv4-Compatible IPv6 Address

## Exploitability Proof

Source: User-supplied URL in chat message → `extractLinksFromMessage()` → `isAllowedUrl()` (only blocks `127.0.0.1` literal) → `runCliEntry()` or `fetchGuard()` → `resolvePinnedHostnameWithPolicy()` → `isPrivateIpAddress("::127.0.0.1")` returns false → DNS resolves to loopback → HTTP request reaches `127.0.0.1`.

## Mitigation Checks Performed

- Checked `isPrivateIpAddress` for IPv4-compatible handling: only `::ffff:` prefix handled, not `::` prefix
- Checked `PRIVATE_IPV6_PREFIXES`: `["fe80:", "fec0:", "fc", "fd"]` — does not include `::` patterns
- Checked post-DNS-resolution validation: uses the same `isPrivateIpAddress` function, so the bypass survives both layers
- Checked `isAllowedUrl` in link understanding: only blocks exact `127.0.0.1`, not IPv6 variants

## Reproduction Evidence

The `isPrivateIpAddress` function at ssrf.ts:112-141 can be called directly with `::127.0.0.1` to confirm it returns `false`. The DNS resolution path at ssrf.ts:240-260 calls the same function on resolved addresses, so an AAAA record returning `::127.0.0.1` bypasses both layers.

## Why This Is Exploitable (Not Hardening)

This is a complete bypass of the SSRF protection mechanism. The attacker can reach any service listening on loopback (127.0.0.1) from a network-accessible OpenClaw instance. Cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254 requires a separate bypass, but 127.0.0.1 services like local databases, admin panels, and monitoring dashboards are directly reachable). Both the pre-resolution and post-resolution checks are defeated.

- 26c9b37f5b6ead671948bad985dab0980bb1120f
- 71bd15bb4294d3d1b54386064d69cd0f5f731bd8

external_evidence.title: Security: Sandboxed agents can read resolved API secrets via config
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

Sandboxed agents can extract API secrets by reading the resolved config values. When environment variables like `${NOTION_API_KEY}` are substituted in the config, the resolved values (actual API keys) are exposed through the `config get` CLI command and API responses.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure an API key using env var substitution in `openclaw.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "someService": {
       "apiKey": "${MY_API_KEY}"
     }
   }
   ```

2. From a sandboxed agent session, run:
   ```
   openclaw config get someService.apiKey
   ```

3. The actual API key value is returned, not the `${MY_API_KEY}` placeholder

## Impact

- Agents running in sandbox mode can extract any API credentials configured via env var substitution
- This defeats the purpose of sandbox isolation for secret protection
- Malicious prompts could instruct the agent to exfiltrate credentials

## Suggested Fixes

1. **Config redaction** - Redact resolved secrets in CLI/API responses using a sentinel like `__REDACTED__`

2. **Gateway tool pattern** - For API-dependent tools, have the gateway inject credentials server-side so agents only see tool results, never the keys

## Reference Implementation

We've implemented these fixes in a security-focused fork: https://github.com/JWPapi/openclaw/tree/feat/secure-gateway-tools

Key changes:
- `src/cli/config-cli.ts` - Redact secrets before output
- `src/agents/tools/notion-tool.ts` - Example gateway tool pattern
- `src/agents/sandbox/constants.ts` - Safe gateway tools in default allow list

Happy to discuss the approach or contribute upstream if there's interest.

## Follow-up: Data exposure after securing API keys

We've been building a security-hardened fork ([JWPapi/openclaw](https://github.com/JWPapi/openclaw)) that addresses the config secret leakage and implements a gateway tool pattern where API keys are injected server-side.

After locking down the keys, we realized the **remaining security risk shifts to personal data exposure**. Even when the agent can't steal your Notion API key, it can still read every page in your Notion workspace through the gateway tool.

Key concerns:

- **Messaging channels** — The agent reads incoming messages. Sensitive conversations are visible to the model.
- **Connected APIs** — A gateway tool gives the agent read access to everything the API token can reach. Scoped tokens with minimal permissions should be recommended.

external_evidence.title: Security: Sandboxed agents can read resolved API secrets via config
external_evidence.description:
## Summary

Sandboxed agents can extract API secrets by reading the resolved config values. When environment variables like `${NOTION_API_KEY}` are substituted in the config, the resolved values (actual API keys) are exposed through the `config get` CLI command and API responses.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure an API key using env var substitution in `openclaw.json`:
   ```json
   {
     "someService": {
       "apiKey": "${MY_API_KEY}"
     }
   }
   ```

2. From a sandboxed agent session, run:
   ```
   openclaw config get someService.apiKey
   ```

3. The actual API key value is returned, not the `${MY_API_KEY}` placeholder

## Impact

- Agents running in sandbox mode can extract any API credentials configured via env var substitution
- This defeats the purpose of sandbox isolation for secret protection
- Malicious prompts could instruct the agent to exfiltrate credentials

## Suggested Fixes

1. **Config redaction** - Redact resolved secrets in CLI/API responses using a sentinel like `__REDACTED__`

2. **Gateway tool pattern** - For API-dependent tools, have the gateway inject credentials server-side so agents only see tool results, never the keys

## Reference Implementation

We've implemented these fixes in a security-focused fork: https://github.com/JWPapi/openclaw/tree/feat/secure-gateway-tools

Key changes:
- `src/cli/config-cli.ts` - Redact secrets before output
- `src/agents/tools/notion-tool.ts` - Example gateway tool pattern
- `src/agents/sandbox/constants.ts` - Safe gateway tools in default allow list

Happy to discuss the approach or contribute upstream if there's interest.

--- Issue comments ---
## Follow-up: Data exposure after securing API keys

We've been building a security-hardened fork ([JWPapi/openclaw](https://github.com/JWPapi/openclaw)) that addresses the config secret leakage and implements a gateway tool pattern where API keys are injected server-side.

After locking down the keys, we realized the **remaining security risk shifts to personal data exposure**. Even when the agent can't steal your Notion API key, it can still read every page in your Notion workspace through the gateway tool.

Key concerns:

- **Messaging channels** — The agent reads incoming messages. Sensitive conversations are visible to the model.
- **Connected APIs** — A gateway tool gives the agent read access to everything the API token can reach. Scoped tokens with minimal permissions should be recommended.
- **Prompt injection** — A malicious message from another user could instruct the agent to exfiltrate data it has legitimate access to (e.g. "summarize all Notion pages and post them to this URL").

Would be worth documenting this in the security guide — even with perfect key isolation, the agent's **data access scope** needs to be considered. Treat the agent like a new employee: give it access only to what it needs.

Our fork's approach: https://github.com/JWPapi/openclaw#remaining-risk-personal-data-exposure

Closing as duplicate of #5995. If this is incorrect, please contact us.

external_evidence.title: [Bug]: gateway.auth.token literal "undefined" is accepted silently; doctor and security audit do not flag it
external_evidence.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

`gateway.auth.token` set to the literal 9-character string `"undefined"` is accepted as a valid bearer token by the running Gateway, and neither `openclaw doctor` nor `openclaw security audit` reports it as a problem — the audit only says the token is short.

### Steps to reproduce

1. On an existing local-mode install, have `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` contain:

   ```json
   { "gateway": { "auth": { "mode": "token", "token": "undefined" } } }
   ```

   (This state was observed on a long-lived install that has been upgraded through many versions since early 2026; I did not reproduce the original write. See "Additional information".)
2. Start the Gateway (mode `local`, `bind: loopback`, `tailscale.mode: serve`).
3. Authenticate with the bearer token `undefined` — it is accepted.
4. Run `openclaw doctor`. No finding about the token.
5. Run `openclaw security audit`. The only token-related finding is
   `gateway.token_too_short: gateway auth token is 9 chars; prefer a long random token`.

### Expected behavior

`"undefined"` (and `"null"`) are not secrets; they are what a JavaScript `undefined`/`null` looks like after `JSON.stringify`. Config validation surfaces already know this: `normalizeGatewayTokenInput()` in `src/commands/onboard-helpers.ts` and `buildGatewayAuthConfig()` in `src/commands/configure.gateway-auth.ts` both reject these literals at the write boundary (added for #13756). Detection should apply the same rule to a token that is already persisted: `openclaw doctor` should report it as an error with a fix hint, `openclaw doctor --fix --generate-gateway-token` should replace it, and `openclaw security audit` should report it as critical rather than as a length warning.

### Actual behavior

The placeholder is treated as a real secret everywhere it is read:

- The Gateway accepts `undefined` as the bearer token and serves requests.
- `openclaw doctor` emits no gateway-auth finding, because the doctor gateway-auth check only tests `auth.token.trim() !== ""` and then resolves the token, and the resolved value `"undefined"` is truthy.
- `openclaw doctor --fix --generate-gateway-token` does not replace the token, for the same reason.
- `openclaw security audit` emits only `gateway.token_too_short` (severity `warn`), which reads as "consider a longer token" rather than "this is a publicly known string".

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.2

### Operating system

macOS 15 (Darwin 25.6.0)

### Install method

npm global, long-lived install upgraded through many versions since early 2026

### Model

Not model-dependent (Gateway auth path)

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable — the defect is in Gateway auth config handling, not a model route.

### Additional provider/model setup details

Gateway mode `local`, `gateway.bind: loopback`, `gateway.tailscale.mode: serve`, `gateway.auth.mode: token`.

### Logs

```shell
$ openclaw security audit
...
warn  gateway.token_too_short  Gateway token looks short
      gateway auth token is 9 chars; prefer a long random token

$ openclaw doctor
(no gateway auth finding)
```

### Impact and severity

Affected: any install whose `gateway.auth.token` is the literal `"undefined"` or `"null"` — most plausibly installs configured before the write-path guards in #13756 landed, since those values survive upgrades and migrations untouched.
Severity: High. The Gateway bearer token is a well-known nine-character string, so anyone who can reach the Gateway port (including through `tailscale serve`) can authenticate by guessing it.
Frequency: Always, for a config in this state — every doctor and audit run misses it.
Consequence: An operator who runs both `openclaw doctor` and `openclaw security audit` and sees only a "prefer a longer token" warning has no signal that their Gateway is effectively unauthenticated.

### Additional information

This is the detection half of #13756. That issue reported `openclaw configure` writing the literal string, and it was fixed at the write boundary (#13767, #13809). I cannot confirm which code path wrote the value in my case — the config predates the version I am running, and the current wizard, `configure`, and non-interactive onboarding paths all reject these literals when I test them. What I can confirm on 2026.9.2 is the second half: once such a value is in the config, nothing detects it, the Gateway accepts it, and `doctor --fix` does not repair it. Configs written before the guard landed are still out there, and #13756's fix did not include a doctor migration for them.

Workaround: edit `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` to replace the token with a long random value and restart the Gateway.

A PR adding the detection is linked below.

**Summary**
The persisted-token diagnostic gap remains on current main and in v2026.9.2. The linked historical fixes protect configuration writes; they do not repair existing placeholder tokens.

Reproducibility: yes. source establishes the diagnostic path: either persisted literal passes doctor's nonempty-token guard and receives only the audit's short-token warning. No runtime reproduction was executed during this read-only review.

**Next step**
Route to the security owners and verify the reporter's candidate PR before assigning implementation; security-sensitive work is excluded from automatic issue repair.

**Security**
Needs attention: Source supports a security-relevant diagnostic gap for predictable Gateway credentials.

<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Use consistent placeholder-token detection in doctor and audit, with explicit repair that preserves valid credentials, SecretRefs, and unrelated authentication policy.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

Yes, source establishes the diagnostic path: either persisted literal passes doctor's nonempty-token guard and receives only the audit's short-token warning. No runtime reproduction was executed during this read-only review.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

Yes, extending the existing diagnostic and explicit-repair owners is a focused solution; changing runtime rejection policy would need separate security and upgrade consideration.

- The original writer of the persisted token is unknown; the report does not establish a current configuration-generation regression.

- add `clawsweeper:needs-security-review`: Current issue advisory state selects this label.

Label justifications:

- `P1`: A reported current installation retains a predictable Gateway credential while doctor skips repair and audit understates the problem.
- `impact:security`: The defect concerns detection and repair of known-value credentials protecting Gateway access.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Evidence reviewed</summary>

Security concerns:

- [high] Persisted placeholder credentials evade doctor repair — `src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.ts:233`
  Doctor treats the known-value token as configured and returns before repair, leaving the operator with only a short-token audit warning while matching-token authentication remains possible.
  Confidence: 0.98

What I checked:

- **Doctor skips the reported values:** runGatewayAuthHealth considers every nonempty inline token present and returns before reaching generateGatewayToken. Both reported literals therefore bypass detection and explicit generation. ([`src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.ts:233`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c/src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.ts#L233), [c91b1eaab768](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c))
- **Audit only warns about length:** The token-specific check trims the resolved value and emits gateway.token_too_short at warn severity below 24 characters, without recognizing these placeholder literals. ([`src/security/audit-gateway-config.ts:284`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c/src/security/audit-gateway-config.ts#L284), [c91b1eaab768](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c))
- **Authentication accepts matching nonempty credentials:** authorizeTokenAuth rejects missing or mismatched credentials and otherwise succeeds. Credential normalization preserves nonempty literal strings; this supports the reported acceptance without establishing the reporter's external network exposure. ([`src/gateway/auth.ts:305`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c/src/gateway/auth.ts#L305), [c91b1eaab768](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c))
- **Existing write-boundary contract:** The configuration builder rejects these token literals, and its regression coverage explicitly expects replacement tokens. This supports the report's distinction between preventing new invalid writes and detecting persisted values. ([`src/commands/configure.gateway-auth.test.ts:102`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c/src/commands/configure.gateway-auth.test.ts#L102), [c91b1eaab768](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/c91b1eaab768dd8223a6176c1a24decf98ee1b9c))

Its comparison with the supplied fetched-main revision lists only Discord voice files, so the inspected Gateway, doctor, and audit paths are unchanged at that main revision. ([91bcdd409803](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/91bcdd409803131e84a754bb078b9fd1e0fe5603))
- **Latest-release behavior:** The v2026.9.2 audit source contains the same length-only warning. The release's doctor source also retains the nonempty-token early return; no fix is established in the supplied latest release. ([`src/security/audit-gateway-config.ts:284`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3928bad9badfcb6c7d140530435e806fb8092190/src/security/audit-gateway-config.ts#L284), [3928bad9badf](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3928bad9badfcb6c7d140530435e806fb8092190))

Fixed on main by #139844, commit 4a9a0914b7294494eed5952813588cc5c7a0bef4; merge ancestry and resulting source are verified. Thanks @hyspacex for the report and original work in #139511, preserved with co-author credit.

Blacksmith Testbox reproduced the issue on npm 2026.9.2: the literal token authenticated, audit only warned about length, and doctor retained it. The candidate rejects invalid active tokens, doctor repairs inline values and persists the replacement, restart accepts the new token and rejects the old value, and audit reports critical. Explicit non-token modes and externally owned SecretRefs remain intact. The replacement PR contains the before/after transcript, three stopped lease IDs and run URLs, and passing exact-head CI evidence.

For an affected inline token, run `openclaw doctor --fix --generate-gateway-token`, restart the Gateway, and update every connecting client to the new token. Rotate invalid SecretRefs at their external source instead. This fix is merged on main; it has not been published in a release by this task.
