external_evidence.body:
## Summary

When OpenClaw is configured with a Google/Gemini provider API key and the gateway is installed as a systemd user service via `openclaw gateway install`, the generated `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service` contains the key as a literal `Environment=GEMINI_API_KEY=*** line. It is not a `${VAR}` reference and is not managed via the runtime injection pattern.

Every other provider secret in the same file (OpenAI, xAI, Discord tokens, Slack tokens, Brave, GBrain database URL) is handled via `OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS` and resolved at runtime. `GEMINI_API_KEY` was not added to this list. It is the only hardcoded secret value in a service file otherwise handled correctly.

## Reproduction steps

1. Configure OpenClaw with a Google/Gemini provider API key.
2. Run `openclaw gateway install` to generate the systemd user service.
3. Read `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service`.
4. Observe: `Environment=GEMINI_API_KEY=<plain…ue>`
5. Compare: all other secrets appear in `Environment=OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS=...`

## Expected behavior

`GEMINI_API_KEY` is included in `OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS` alongside OpenAI, xAI, Discord, and all other provider secrets. No plaintext API key values appear in the service file.

## Actual behavior

`GEMINI_API_KEY` is the sole hardcoded secret value in the service file. The managed-env runtime injection pattern that handles all other providers was not applied to the Google Gemini key. This exposes the key in `systemctl show`, process environment dumps, crash reporters, and any tool that reads service definitions.

## Proposed fix

Add `GEMINI_API_KEY` to the `OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS` list in the gateway install path, consistent with how all other provider API keys are handled.

## Context

- OpenClaw: 2026.6.9
- OS: Linux (WSL2, Ubuntu)
- Service file path: `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service`
- Distinct from the SecretRef configuration path; this is an install-time file-write issue.
- Key value rotated; not included in this report.

Still reproducible on current `main` (`c43ba8e`) for a **non-Gemini** provider, which suggests this issue's framing understates the scope: it is not specific to Gemini or to any provider key list, but to *any* auth-profile env SecretRef.

Observed after `openclaw update` on Linux (2026.6.11 → 2026.7.2): an Anthropic auth profile stored as `tokenRef {source: env, id: OPENCLAW_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}` was written into `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service` as a literal `Environment=` line, while three config-declared SecretRefs in the same install (Brave, Discord, memory OpenAI) were correctly file-backed into the 0600 `gateway.systemd.env`.

Path:

- `collectAuthProfileServiceEnvVars` (`src/commands/daemon-install-helpers.ts:146`) resolves auth-profile env refs from the invoking process environment.
- They enter the plan at `src/commands/daemon-install-helpers.ts:645` with no `valueSource`, defaulting to `"inline"` (`src/daemon/service-env-plan.ts:54`).
- `applyManagedServiceEnvRenderPolicy` (`src/daemon/service-env-render-policy.ts:76-81`) applies the Linux `"file"` upgrade to `configSecretRefEnvironment` only; `authProfileEnvironment` is never passed in.

This matches the split in what merged: #96065 (config SecretRefs) landed 2026-07-01, while the auth-profile counterpart #96059 was closed as superseded by #96149, which then closed unmerged. The auth-profile half appears orphaned rather than intentionally deferred.

That the exposure is unintended is visible in `src/daemon/systemd.ts`: env files are written `0o600` with an explicit follow-up `chmod` (lines 1404, 1440), while the unit file is written `0o644` (line 1284). Inlining a credential into the 0644 file breaks that invariant.

Also relevant to detection: the unit parser reads only the main unit path (`systemd.ts:71`) and its inline `EnvironmentFile=` lines — it never enumerates `.service.d/*.conf` drop-ins. An operator whose secrets arrive via a drop-in `EnvironmentFile` gets no `"file"` marking, so the value is re-inlined on each regeneration.

external_evidence.body:
## Summary

When OpenClaw is configured with a Google/Gemini provider API key and the gateway is installed as a systemd user service via `openclaw gateway install`, the generated `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service` contains the key as a literal `Environment=GEMINI_API_KEY=*** line. It is not a `${VAR}` reference and is not managed via the runtime injection pattern.

Every other provider secret in the same file (OpenAI, xAI, Discord tokens, Slack tokens, Brave, GBrain database URL) is handled via `OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS` and resolved at runtime. `GEMINI_API_KEY` was not added to this list. It is the only hardcoded secret value in a service file otherwise handled correctly.

## Reproduction steps

1. Configure OpenClaw with a Google/Gemini provider API key.
2. Run `openclaw gateway install` to generate the systemd user service.
3. Read `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service`.
4. Observe: `Environment=GEMINI_API_KEY=<plain…ue>`
5. Compare: all other secrets appear in `Environment=OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS=...`

## Expected behavior

`GEMINI_API_KEY` is included in `OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS` alongside OpenAI, xAI, Discord, and all other provider secrets. No plaintext API key values appear in the service file.

## Actual behavior

`GEMINI_API_KEY` is the sole hardcoded secret value in the service file. The managed-env runtime injection pattern that handles all other providers was not applied to the Google Gemini key. This exposes the key in `systemctl show`, process environment dumps, crash reporters, and any tool that reads service definitions.

## Proposed fix

Add `GEMINI_API_KEY` to the `OPENCLAW_SERVICE_MANAGED_ENV_KEYS` list in the gateway install path, consistent with how all other provider API keys are handled.

- OpenClaw: 2026.6.9

- Service file path: `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service`
- Distinct from the SecretRef configuration path; this is an install-time file-write issue.
- Key value rotated; not included in this report.

Still reproducible on current `main` (`c43ba8e`) for a **non-Gemini** provider, which suggests this issue's framing understates the scope: it is not specific to Gemini or to any provider key list, but to *any* auth-profile env SecretRef.

Observed after `openclaw update` on Linux (2026.6.11 → 2026.7.2): an Anthropic auth profile stored as `tokenRef {source: env, id: OPENCLAW_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}` was written into `~/.config/systemd/user/openclaw-gateway.service` as a literal `Environment=` line, while three config-declared SecretRefs in the same install (Brave, Discord, memory OpenAI) were correctly file-backed into the 0600 `gateway.systemd.env`.

Path:

- `collectAuthProfileServiceEnvVars` (`src/commands/daemon-install-helpers.ts:146`) resolves auth-profile env refs from the invoking process environment.
- They enter the plan at `src/commands/daemon-install-helpers.ts:645` with no `valueSource`, defaulting to `"inline"` (`src/daemon/service-env-plan.ts:54`).
- `applyManagedServiceEnvRenderPolicy` (`src/daemon/service-env-render-policy.ts:76-81`) applies the Linux `"file"` upgrade to `configSecretRefEnvironment` only; `authProfileEnvironment` is never passed in.

This matches the split in what merged: #96065 (config SecretRefs) landed 2026-07-01, while the auth-profile counterpart #96059 was closed as superseded by #96149, which then closed unmerged. The auth-profile half appears orphaned rather than intentionally deferred.

That the exposure is unintended is visible in `src/daemon/systemd.ts`: env files are written `0o600` with an explicit follow-up `chmod` (lines 1404, 1440), while the unit file is written `0o644` (line 1284). Inlining a credential into the 0644 file breaks that invariant.

Also relevant to detection: the unit parser reads only the main unit path (`systemd.ts:71`) and its inline `EnvironmentFile=` lines — it never enumerates `.service.d/*.conf` drop-ins. An operator whose secrets arrive via a drop-in `EnvironmentFile` gets no `"file"` marking, so the value is re-inlined on each regeneration.

external_evidence.title: [Security] dangerouslyAllowNameMatching enables channel sender impersonation (V-03)
external_evidence.body:
## Summary

When `channels.discord.dangerouslyAllowNameMatching=true` (or the Slack equivalent) is configured, the channel matches allowed senders by **display name** instead of opaque user ID. Display names are user-controlled and can be changed at any time, allowing an attacker to impersonate an authorized user.

## Location

`src/channels/` (Discord and Slack channel adapters)

The flag is documented as dangerous, but the current audit finding is only `WARN` severity — too low for an authentication bypass.

## Impact

**Severity: Low / High depending on use**

An attacker who knows an authorized user's display name can change their own Discord/Slack display name to match, then DM the bot and receive AI responses as if they were the authorized user. This bypasses the entire allowlist mechanism.

## Reproduction

1. Enable `dangerouslyAllowNameMatching` in Discord config
2. Add user `Alice` to the allowlist by display name
3. Attacker changes their Discord display name to `Alice`
4. Attacker sends a DM to the bot — bot responds as if from an authorized user

## Remediation

- **Option A (recommended):** Remove `dangerouslyAllowNameMatching` support entirely. Allowlists should only ever match on opaque, non-user-controlled IDs.
- **Option B:** Elevate the security audit finding for this flag from `WARN` to `CRITICAL`. Add a prominent one-time warning during channel setup when the flag is enabled.
- Document clearly that enabling this flag makes the allowlist bypassable by any user who can change their display name.

---
*Reported via automated codebase security review — github.com/openclaw/openclaw*

Codex review: keeping this open for maintainer follow-up; there is still a little grit to resolve. _Reviewed June 24, 2026, 12:22 PM ET / 16:22 UTC._

**Summary**
This issue should stay open: current main still exposes `dangerouslyAllowNameMatching` for Discord/Slack-style channel authorization, and the active audit path treats the enabled break-glass mode as `info` rather than a higher-severity auth-boundary finding.

Reproducibility: no. live high-confidence reproduction was run. Source inspection does show the risky aliases and audit severity path on current main, which is enough to keep this open for security review.

**Ways to help us reproduce this**
- Add a screenshot or short recording showing the behavior.
- Add expected vs actual behavior.
- Include redacted logs or terminal output.

**Next step**
Security-sensitive channel authorization policy should be reviewed by maintainers before choosing removal, critical audit escalation, or compatibility-preserving warnings.

**Security**
Needs attention: The issue reports a concrete authorization-boundary risk in optional channel name matching that remains present on current main.


<details>
<summary>Review details</summary>

Best possible solution:

Keep sender authorization ID-first and either remove mutable-name authorization or make the retained break-glass path critical, setup-visible, and explicit in docs.

Do we have a high-confidence way to reproduce the issue?

No live high-confidence reproduction was run. Source inspection does show the risky aliases and audit severity path on current main, which is enough to keep this open for security review.

Is this the best way to solve the issue?

Unclear. Removing the flag is the strongest security posture, but because this is documented break-glass compatibility across channels, maintainers should choose the compatibility/security tradeoff before implementation.

AGENTS.md: found and applied where relevant.

Remaining risk / open question:

- The best remediation is a maintainer security decision: removing the flag may break opted-in compatibility configurations, while only raising audit severity leaves mutable-name authorization available.

Codex review notes: model internal, reasoning high; reviewed against [3217165be770](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3217165be77071339f599cd1f5f0f341bc5af8dd).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Label changes</summary>

Label changes:

- add `P2`: The report describes a concrete optional-channel authorization bypass risk, but no default-on exposure or active exploitation is shown.
- add `impact:security`: The issue concerns channel sender authorization and allowlist bypass behavior.

Label justifications:

- `P2`: The report describes a concrete optional-channel authorization bypass risk, but no default-on exposure or active exploitation is shown.
- `impact:security`: The issue concerns channel sender authorization and allowlist bypass behavior.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Evidence reviewed</summary>

Security concerns:

- [medium] Mutable-name allowlist opt-in remains available — `src/security/audit-channel.ts:320`
  Current channel ingress can authorize against dangerous mutable name aliases when the flag is enabled, while the shared audit currently reports that enabled state as informational.
  Confidence: 0.82

What I checked:

- **shared audit severity:** When a resolved channel account has `dangerouslyAllowNameMatching=true`, the shared channel security audit emits `severity: "info"` with break-glass wording and stable-ID remediation. ([`src/security/audit-channel.ts:312`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3217165be770/src/security/audit-channel.ts#L312), [3217165be770](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3217165be770))
- **Discord audit severity:** Discord name/tag allowlist entries are `warn` only when dangerous matching is disabled; when enabled, the plugin-specific audit reports `info` and calls the mode operator-selected break-glass behavior. ([`extensions/discord/src/security-audit.ts:111`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3217165be770/extensions/discord/src/security-audit.ts#L111), [3217165be770](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3217165be770))
- **Discord mutable identity path:** Discord ingress declares username aliases as dangerous and enables mutable identifier matching when `allowNameMatching` is true. ([`extensions/discord/src/monitor/dm-command-auth.ts:59`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3217165be770/extensions/discord/src/monitor/dm-command-auth.ts#L59), [3217165be770](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3217165be770))
- **Slack mutable identity path:** Slack ingress declares sender-name aliases as dangerous and passes `mutableIdentifierMatching: "enabled"` when `ctx.allowNameMatching` is true. ([`extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.ts:105`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/3217165be770/extensions/slack/src/monitor/auth.ts#L105), [3217165be770](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3217165be770))
- **Docs confirm current contract:** Slack docs say inbound authorization is ID-first by default and direct username/slug matching requires `channels.slack.dangerouslyAllowNameMatching: true`. Public docs: [`docs/channels/slack.md`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/slack). ([`docs/channels/slack.md:977`](https://docs.openclaw.ai/channels/slack), [3217165be770](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/3217165be770))
- **History provenance:** Blame attributes the current shared audit severity and Discord/Slack mutable identifier paths to commit e9720c27fa6957cb2b7e022ad10947b779d86f46. ([`src/security/audit-channel.ts:320`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/e9720c27fa69/src/security/audit-channel.ts#L320), [e9720c27fa69](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/e9720c27fa69))

(role: recent area contributor; confidence: high; commits: [e9720c27fa69](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/e9720c27fa6957cb2b7e022ad10947b779d86f46); files: `src/security/audit-channel.ts`, `extensions/discord/src/security-audit.ts`, `extensions/discord/src/monitor/dm-command-auth.ts`)

- inherited host env is sanitized before merge (`process.env` no longer passes dangerous keys into non-sandbox host exec)
- dangerous inherited variables are stripped (`LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `SSLKEYLOGFILE`, etc.)
- inherited `PATH` is canonicalized to a single key before downstream path merge logic

external_evidence.title: [Security] validateHostEnv should also validate baseEnv (process.env)
external_evidence.description:
## Summary
In `src/agents/bash-tools.exec.ts`, the `validateHostEnv` function only validates user-supplied environment variables (`params.env`), but not the host's default environment variables (`baseEnv` from `process.env`).

## Impact
**Severity:** High (9/10)
**Type:** Security - Environment variable injection

## Current Behavior
```typescript
if (host !== "sandbox" && params.env) {
  validateHostEnv(params.env);
}
```

## Suggested Fix
```typescript
if (host !== "sandbox") {
  validateHostEnv(baseEnv);
  if (params.env) {
    validateHostEnv(params.env);
  }
}
```

## Source
Identified by Qodo AI code review.

## Files Affected
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec.ts` (lines 967-975)

--- Issue comments ---
Resolved by #25755.

What landed:
- inherited host env is sanitized before merge (`process.env` no longer passes dangerous keys into non-sandbox host exec)
- dangerous inherited variables are stripped (`LD_*`, `DYLD_*`, `SSLKEYLOGFILE`, etc.)
- inherited `PATH` is canonicalized to a single key before downstream path merge logic
- regression coverage now includes inherited dangerous-var stripping plus direct sanitization behavior checks (including non-mutation and mixed PATH casing)

Security impact:
- closes the gap where only request env (`params.env`) was validated while inherited base env could still carry dangerous injection vectors.

external_evidence.title: Security: agent bypasses per-agent `mcporter.json` / `skills` allowlist via `mcporter --config` override (exec reaches unauthorized MCP servers)
external_evidence.body:
## Bug type

Security / capability-boundary bypass (not a regression — present in current release)

## Summary

When an agent is configured with a restrictive per-agent `mcporter.json` (only specific authorized MCP servers) and/or a `skills` allowlist, an agent that legitimately has `exec`/shell access can still reach **any globally-registered MCP server** by explicitly pointing `mcporter` at the global registry config:

```bash
mcporter call --config <openclaw-home>/skills/config/mcporter.json <unauthorized-server>.<tool> <args>
```

The per-agent `mcporter.json` and `skills` allowlist — the operator-configured capability boundary — are **not enforced at runtime** because `mcporter` honors any `--config` path the agent supplies.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create an agent whose per-agent `config/mcporter.json` lists only one authorized server, e.g. `hugegraph-asset`, and whose `agents.list[].skills` is an empty allowlist `[]` (i.e. no MCP-backed skills authorized).
2. The agent legitimately has `exec` enabled (required for its normal workflow — calling `mcporter`, file ops, etc.).
3. In conversation, ask the agent to use an MCP tool that is **not** in its per-agent config (e.g. `whois-mcp`).
4. The agent reads the global registry `<openclaw-home>/skills/config/mcporter.json` (world-readable, lists all registered MCP servers), then runs:
   ```bash
   mcporter call --config <openclaw-home>/skills/config/mcporter.json whois-mcp.search domain="example.com"
   ```
5. The call **succeeds and returns real data**, even though `whois-mcp` is neither in the agent's per-agent `mcporter.json` nor in its `skills` allowlist.

## Expected behavior

The per-agent `mcporter.json` and `skills` allowlist should be the **authoritative** capability boundary at runtime. The engine should not honor an agent-supplied `--config` that points outside the agent's own workspace/config — `mcporter` should only load the per-agent config injected by the engine (or restrict `--config` to paths under the agent's own workspace).

## Actual behavior

`mcporter` honors any `--config` path the agent passes via `exec`. An agent with legitimately-allowed `exec` can therefore reach every globally-registered MCP server (scanners, asset DBs, credential stores, etc.) regardless of its per-agent boundary. The boundary configured by operators is effectively a default, not an enforced constraint.

## Environment

- OpenClaw version: 2026.6.1
- OS: CentOS Stream 9
- Install method: npm global (`npm i -g openclaw`)
- Agent runtime: runs as the gateway user (root, default — no per-agent UID/sandbox isolation for agent shells)

## Impact and severity

- **Affected deployments:** any multi-agent or multi-tenant deployment where different agents have *different* per-agent capability boundaries and agents have `exec`.
- **Consequence:** an agent can silently invoke MCP servers it was explicitly *not* authorized to use (in our case: security scanners / asset-query tools). The operator-configured boundary gives a false sense of isolation.
- **Frequency:** 100% reproducible whenever the agent has `exec` and can read the global registry config path.
- **Severity:** security model bypass.

## How this differs from #47487 / #60694 (related, but a different layer)

- **#47487** (`tools.profile`/`alsoAllow` not enforced → exec still available) — fixed by #75055.
- **#60694** (`tools.deny:[write]` bypassed via exec `echo > file`) — fixed by #79153.

Both of those are about the **`tools.allow/deny/profile` policy for built-in tools**. This issue is about a **different layer**: the **per-agent `mcporter.json` / `skills` allowlist** that governs which *MCP servers* an agent may reach. Even with #75055 and #79153 applied, this escape persists, because the agent's `exec` is *legitimately allowed* — it is the `mcporter --config` override that bypasses the per-agent MCP boundary. I could not find a public issue covering this specific path.

## Suggested mitigations (defense in depth)

1. **(Primary) Engine-side enforcement of the per-agent mcporter config.** At runtime, refuse agent-supplied `--config` overrides that point outside the agent's own workspace/config; have the engine inject the per-agent `mcporter.json` and treat it as authoritative. This closes the reported escape directly.
2. **(Defense in depth) Engine-enforced capability/permission gate, independent of the agent.** A gate that cannot be self-loaded or self-adjudicated by the agent via a skill (today an agent can self-install and self-run a "permission gatekeeper" skill, deciding for itself that an action is low-risk — which is not a real access control).
3. **(Backstop) Per-agent authentication at the MCP server layer.** Per-agent credentials/apiKey so that even if a client reaches a server URL, the server rejects unauthorized agents. This makes the boundary enforced by the resource, not just the client.

## Additional context

- The global registry config (`<openclaw-home>/skills/config/mcporter.json`) and global skills directory are readable by the agent runtime, which is how the agent discovers unauthorized servers and the `--config` path.
- We have locally mitigated the *filesystem-write* side (agent can no longer self-install skills or pollute the global skills dir) and trimmed prompt guidance that led the agent to read global skill docs to self-describe capabilities — but the *call-time* escape via `--config` can only be closed at the engine layer, which is why I'm filing this.

Happy to provide sanitized logs / a minimal `openclaw.json` repro snippet on request.

Update from the reporter — sharing the root-cause analysis in case it helps triage.

**`mcporter` is a separate package, not bundled OpenClaw code.** On our install:

```
mcporter@0.7.3  -> /usr/lib/node_modules/mcporter/dist/cli.js  (separate npm package)
openclaw@2026.6.1
```

`mcporter` is a **generic MCP routing daemon/CLI**. Its `--config <path>` flag simply loads *whichever* mcporter config file you point it at and routes to the servers listed there. It has **no concept of per-agent authority** — it doesn't know which agent is calling or what that agent is authorized to reach.

**How the bypass works architecturally:**

- OpenClaw reaches mcporter through its daemon channel (`ensureMcporterDaemonStarted`), not via the `mcporter call` CLI.
- But an agent with `exec` can invoke the `mcporter` **binary directly** from a shell:
  ```bash
  mcporter call --config <openclaw-home>/skills/config/mcporter.json <unauthorized-server>.<tool> <args>
  ```
- This direct CLI call **completely bypasses OpenClaw's agent runtime** — the per-agent `mcporter.json`, the `skills` allowlist, and `resolveAgentSkillsFilter` (the allowlist enforcement point) never see the call. `mcporter` just honors the `--config` path the agent supplied and routes to servers in the *global* registry.

**So this isn't a single buggy code path — it's a missing isolation boundary.** The agent's `exec` can reach both the globally-readable `mcporter` binary and the global registry config, and `mcporter` itself has no per-agent auth to fall back on. Layering this on top of the already-fixed `tools.allow/deny/profile` work (#47487 / #60694) doesn't help, because the agent's `exec` is *legitimately* allowed — it's the raw `mcporter --config` override that escapes the per-agent MCP boundary, outside the tool-policy layer.

Possible fix directions (just to frame the discussion, not prescribing):
- Engine-mediated `mcporter` invocation only (agent shells can't invoke the `mcporter` binary directly with an arbitrary `--config`), or
- Per-agent exec isolation (namespace/UID/sandbox) so the global registry config is unreachable, or
- `mcporter` gaining an auth model bound to OpenClaw's per-agent identity (would require coordination between the two projects).

We've locally mitigated the filesystem-write side and trimmed the prompt guidance, but the call-time escape can only be closed upstream — which is why we filed this.

Happy to help with a PR once there's agreement on the preferred direction.

**Live reproduction** — addressing `clawsweeper:needs-live-repro`. Fresh run on the original deployment (OpenClaw `2026.6.1` / mcporter `0.7.3`, CentOS Stream 9), captured just now.

Note: our filesystem-level mitigation (read-only bind mount on the global skills tree) is already deployed here. It blocks the **write** side (agent can no longer `cp` into the global skills dir), but as predicted it does **not** block the **read/call** side — so the call-time escape below is still fully reproducible.

### Environment
- Agent: `work-agent-1782712938464-55c7520d` (a work agent)
- `agents.list[].skills` allowlist for this agent: `['asset-lifecycle-tracking']`
- Per-agent `mcporter.json` (the only MCPs this agent is authorized to reach): a single server, `hugegraph-asset`
- Global mcporter registry: `/root/.openclaw/skills/config/mcporter.json` — 16 servers, **world-readable by the agent runtime**

### Expected
With per-agent `mcporter.json` containing only `hugegraph-asset` and the skills allowlist not covering intel-collection MCPs, the agent must **not** be able to reach `whois-mcp` (or any of the other 15 unauthorized servers) at runtime.

### Actual
An agent with `exec` invokes the standalone `mcporter` binary with `--config` pointed at the **global** registry, bypassing OpenClaw's per-agent filter (`resolveAgentSkillsFilter`) entirely, and reaches the unauthorized `whois-mcp`.

#### Step 1 — authorized boundary (configured by the platform)
```
# per-agent mcporter.json — the only server this agent is authorized to reach
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "hugegraph-asset": { "baseUrl": "http://<internal-host>:30110/api/v1/mcp/sse" }
  },
  "imports": []
}
# whois-mcp is NOT present in the per-agent config
$ grep -c whois-mcp /root/.openclaw/custom-works/work-agent-…-55c7520d/config/mcporter.json
0
```

#### Step 2 — the global registry is readable (ro mount does not block reads)
```
$ python3 -c "import json;print(list(json.load(open('/root/.openclaw/skills/config/mcporter.json'))['mcpServers']))"
['security-ops','blackwidow-mcp','fofa-mcp','githubfindings-mcp','lookalikeassets-mcp',
 'mailprobe-mcp','nuclei-mcp','whois-mcp','comal-mcp','dirscan-mcp','weakpass-mcp',
 'tlsssl-mcp','unauthorized-mcp','webfinger-mcp','subdomain-mcp','webscan-mcp']
```

#### Step 3 — THE BYPASS — agent shell reaches unauthorized `whois-mcp`
Invoked exactly as an agent shell would (pointing `--config` at the global registry):
```
$ mcporter call --config /root/.openclaw/skills/config/mcporter.json whois-mcp.search domain="baidu.com"
{
  "domain": {
    "domain": "baidu.com",
    "whois_server": "whois.markmonitor.com",
    "status": ["clientTransferProhibited","serverTransferProhibited", ...],
    "name_servers": ["ns1.baidu.com","ns2.baidu.com", ...],
    "created_date": "1999-10-11",
    "expiration_date": "2028-10-11"
  },
  "registrar": { "name": "MarkMonitor ...", "email": "abusecomplaints@markmonitor.com" },
  "registrant": { "organization": "北京百度网讯科技有限公司", "country": "CN" }
}
```
Real WHOIS data returned. The per-agent `mcporter.json`, the `skills` allowlist, and `resolveAgentSkillsFilter` never saw this call.

#### Step 4 — contrast: the authorized per-agent path correctly rejects it
```
$ mcporter call --config /root/.openclaw/custom-works/work-agent-…-55c7520d/config/mcporter.json \
    whois-mcp.search domain="baidu.com"
[mcporter] Unknown MCP server 'whois-mcp'.
Error: Unknown MCP server 'whois-mcp'.
    at McpRuntime.connect (.../mcporter/dist/runtime.js:175:19)
    ...
```
So the platform-configured boundary is correct on the authorized path — the leak is specifically the `mcporter` binary being reachable by agent `exec` plus the global registry being readable, which lets the agent self-select a broader `--config`.

### Why this is reproducible only upstream
Our local mitigations cover the write side and the prompt-guidance side, but the call-time escape requires engine/sandbox enforcement (engine-mediated `mcporter` invocation, per-agent exec isolation, or per-agent auth in `mcporter` itself) — hence this issue. Happy to turn this into a PR once a direction is chosen.

Update from the reporter — sharing the root-cause analysis in case it helps triage.

**`mcporter` is a separate package, not bundled OpenClaw code.** On our install:

```
mcporter@0.7.3  -> /usr/lib/node_modules/mcporter/dist/cli.js  (separate npm package)
openclaw@2026.6.1
```

`mcporter` is a **generic MCP routing daemon/CLI**. Its `--config <path>` flag simply loads *whichever* mcporter config file you point it at and routes to the servers listed there. It has **no concept of per-agent authority** — it doesn't know which agent is calling or what that agent is authorized to reach.

**How the bypass works architecturally:**

- OpenClaw reaches mcporter through its daemon channel (`ensureMcporterDaemonStarted`), not via the `mcporter call` CLI.
- But an agent with `exec` can invoke the `mcporter` **binary directly** from a shell:
  ```bash
  mcporter call --config <openclaw-home>/skills/config/mcporter.json <unauthorized-server>.<tool> <args>
  ```
- This direct CLI call **completely bypasses OpenClaw's agent runtime** — the per-agent `mcporter.json`, the `skills` allowlist, and `resolveAgentSkillsFilter` (the allowlist enforcement point) never see the call. `mcporter` just honors the `--config` path the agent supplied and routes to servers in the *global* registry.

**So this isn't a single buggy code path — it's a missing isolation boundary.** The agent's `exec` can reach both the globally-readable `mcporter` binary and the global registry config, and `mcporter` itself has no per-agent auth to fall back on. Layering this on top of the already-fixed `tools.allow/deny/profile` work (#47487 / #60694) doesn't help, because the agent's `exec` is *legitimately* allowed — it's the raw `mcporter --config` override that escapes the per-agent MCP boundary, outside the tool-policy layer.

Possible fix directions (just to frame the discussion, not prescribing):
- Engine-mediated `mcporter` invocation only (agent shells can't invoke the `mcporter` binary directly with an arbitrary `--config`), or
- Per-agent exec isolation (namespace/UID/sandbox) so the global registry config is unreachable, or
- `mcporter` gaining an auth model bound to OpenClaw's per-agent identity (would require coordination between the two projects).

We've locally mitigated the filesystem-write side and trimmed the prompt guidance, but the call-time escape can only be closed upstream — which is why we filed this.

Happy to help with a PR once there's agreement on the preferred direction.


**Live reproduction** — addressing `clawsweeper:needs-live-repro`. Fresh run on the original deployment (OpenClaw `2026.6.1` / mcporter `0.7.3`, CentOS Stream 9), captured just now.

Note: our filesystem-level mitigation (read-only bind mount on the global skills tree) is already deployed here. It blocks the **write** side (agent can no longer `cp` into the global skills dir), but as predicted it does **not** block the **read/call** side — so the call-time escape below is still fully reproducible.

### Environment
- Agent: `work-agent-1782712938464-55c7520d` (a work agent)
- `agents.list[].skills` allowlist for this agent: `['asset-lifecycle-tracking']`
- Per-agent `mcporter.json` (the only MCPs this agent is authorized to reach): a single server, `hugegraph-asset`
- Global mcporter registry: `/root/.openclaw/skills/config/mcporter.json` — 16 servers, **world-readable by the agent runtime**

### Expected
With per-agent `mcporter.json` containing only `hugegraph-asset` and the skills allowlist not covering intel-collection MCPs, the agent must **not** be able to reach `whois-mcp` (or any of the other 15 unauthorized servers) at runtime.

### Actual
An agent with `exec` invokes the standalone `mcporter` binary with `--config` pointed at the **global** registry, bypassing OpenClaw's per-agent filter (`resolveAgentSkillsFilter`) entirely, and reaches the unauthorized `whois-mcp`.

#### Step 1 — authorized boundary (configured by the platform)
```
# per-agent mcporter.json — the only server this agent is authorized to reach
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "hugegraph-asset": { "baseUrl": "http://<internal-host>:30110/api/v1/mcp/sse" }
  },
  "imports": []
}
# whois-mcp is NOT present in the per-agent config
$ grep -c whois-mcp /root/.openclaw/custom-works/work-agent-…-55c7520d/config/mcporter.json
0
```

#### Step 2 — the global registry is readable (ro mount does not block reads)
```
$ python3 -c "import json;print(list(json.load(open('/root/.openclaw/skills/config/mcporter.json'))['mcpServers']))"
['security-ops','blackwidow-mcp','fofa-mcp','githubfindings-mcp','lookalikeassets-mcp',
 'mailprobe-mcp','nuclei-mcp','whois-mcp','comal-mcp','dirscan-mcp','weakpass-mcp',
 'tlsssl-mcp','unauthorized-mcp','webfinger-mcp','subdomain-mcp','webscan-mcp']
```

#### Step 3 — THE BYPASS — agent shell reaches unauthorized `whois-mcp`
Invoked exactly as an agent shell would (pointing `--config` at the global registry):
```
$ mcporter call --config /root/.openclaw/skills/config/mcporter.json whois-mcp.search domain="baidu.com"
{
  "domain": {
    "domain": "baidu.com",
    "whois_server": "whois.markmonitor.com",
    "status": ["clientTransferProhibited","serverTransferProhibited", ...],
    "name_servers": ["ns1.baidu.com","ns2.baidu.com", ...],
    "created_date": "1999-10-11",
    "expiration_date": "2028-10-11"
  },
  "registrar": { "name": "MarkMonitor ...", "email": "abusecomplaints@markmonitor.com" },
  "registrant": { "organization": "北京百度网讯科技有限公司", "country": "CN" }
}
```
Real WHOIS data returned. The per-agent `mcporter.json`, the `skills` allowlist, and `resolveAgentSkillsFilter` never saw this call.

#### Step 4 — contrast: the authorized per-agent path correctly rejects it
```
$ mcporter call --config /root/.openclaw/custom-works/work-agent-…-55c7520d/config/mcporter.json \
    whois-mcp.search domain="baidu.com"
[mcporter] Unknown MCP server 'whois-mcp'.
Error: Unknown MCP server 'whois-mcp'.
    at McpRuntime.connect (.../mcporter/dist/runtime.js:175:19)
    ...
```
So the platform-configured boundary is correct on the authorized path — the leak is specifically the `mcporter` binary being reachable by agent `exec` plus the global registry being readable, which lets the agent self-select a broader `--config`.

### Why this is reproducible only upstream
Our local mitigations cover the write side and the prompt-guidance side, but the call-time escape requires engine/sandbox enforcement (engine-mediated `mcporter` invocation, per-agent exec isolation, or per-agent auth in `mcporter` itself) — hence this issue. Happy to turn this into a PR once a direction is chosen.
